# Overview



Welcome to **ssl-lab** — a research lab for self-supervised learning (SSL). This page is your starting map: what the repository is for, the ideas at its center, how the code is organized, and where to go next. Everything here is written for a first-time visitor; deeper pages in the catalog expand each section.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L8), [mkdocs.yml](mkdocs.yml#L1-L8)

## The Mission: Generative Data You Can Trust

ssl-lab develops methods for **generating biological data that can be trusted like measured data**. Generative models already produce convincing images and video; the goal here is the same capability for experiments. The flagship target is **single-cell perturbation data**: given a population of cells and a genetic perturbation — possibly a combination nobody has ever run in the lab — the model generates the perturbed population, including which genes move, by how much, and how much the response varies from cell to cell.

Crucially, "reliable" is **measured, not assumed**. Generated data are scored on the direction and size of predicted effects and on whether generated populations are calibrated — always against strong references such as a from-scratch model of the same task and a training-free baseline.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L7-L15)

## The Method Line: JEPA at the Center

The core learner is **JEPA** (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture). Instead of reconstructing raw pixels or tokens, JEPA predicts the *embeddings* of masked regions from their context. In this codebase the JEPA module assembles three parts: a **student encoder** that sees only context tokens, an **EMA teacher** (an exponential-moving-average copy of the encoder) that encodes the full input and supplies targets, and a small **predictor** that learns to fill in the hidden positions. The training loss is prediction loss plus an anti-collapse regularizer (**VICReg** or **SIGReg**), and the module also exposes a pooled latent `z` — an unmasked, image-level representation that every downstream piece (decoders, priors, probes) consumes.

Sources: [src/ssllab/jepa/model.py](src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L1-L14), [src/ssllab/jepa/model.py](src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L30-L62)

## Two Research Directions

JEPA is a *representation learner* by default. ssl-lab pushes it past that in two complementary ways:

| Direction | Idea | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Generative JEPA** — make the representation *sampleable* | Add a prior over the latent and a decoder back to data space. The conditional flow prior `v(z, t, c)` with classifier-free guidance is implemented and method-de-risked; the unconditional slice runs end to end. | Method built + de-risked; applications in progress |
| **2. Action operators** — make prediction *active* | Promote JEPA's fixed, blind "predict region *q*" query into a **learned operator the model chooses** — *sensing* (where to look) and *perturbing* (what an action does) — so the system can form and test hypotheses. | Tutorial corpus written; theory still developing |

The two directions are beginning to **converge**: the condition a generative model needs can itself be produced by an action operator. Flagship applications for Direction 1 include the single-cell perturbation study and digital phenotyping (e.g., diabetes monitoring as a generative personal world model).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L36-L61), [docs/index.md](docs/index.md#L9-L24)

## Architecture at a Glance

The repository follows a strict layering discipline. Reusable primitives live in `src/ssllab`; each research direction is a subpackage; application logic lives only in thin `examples/` driver scripts; and cloud infrastructure is deliberately quarantined in a top-level `ops/` package that the SSL library never imports.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph DATA["data/ — datasets & adapters"]
        RAW["MNIST proxy · Perturb-seq · PTB-XL ECG"]
    end
    subgraph SSL["src/ssllab — the SSL library"]
        JEPA["jepa/ — masking, EMA target,<br/>assembled module + objectives/ loss"]
        GEN["generative/ — flow prior, conditional flow,<br/>count decoder, CVAE, operator algebra"]
        AOP["action_operator/ — context-conditioned<br/>latent operators (generator bases, exp/M)"]
        EVAL["eval/ — probes, effect size, calibration,<br/>paired bootstrap, collapse diagnostics"]
    end
    subgraph EX["examples/ — thin study drivers"]
        STUDIES["jepa_basics · generative_jepa ·<br/>perturbation_response · ecg_rhythm"]
    end
    subgraph INFRA["ops/ — remote GPU (decoupled)"]
        SKY["SkyPilot + RunPod"]
    end
    RAW --> JEPA
    JEPA -- "frozen latent z" --> GEN
    JEPA -- "frozen latent z" --> AOP
    STUDIES --> SSL
    SSL --> EVAL
    SKY -.->|"provisions compute only"| STUDIES
```

> [!TIP]
> The **frozen-encoder discipline** is the thread that ties the whole library together: the JEPA encoder is trained once, then everything generative (decoder, flow prior, count decoder) learns on top of its frozen latent `z`. This is why `src/ssllab/jepa/model.py` explicitly documents the pooled `embed` as "used downstream by the decoder, the flow prior, and the linear probe."

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L119), [src/ssllab/jepa/model.py](src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L12-L13), [ops/README.md](ops/README.md#L1-L10)

## Repository Layout

The project uses a **use-case-driven R&D convention**: intuition in `notebooks/`, reusable primitives in `src/`, thin driver scripts in `examples/`, and infrastructure at the root.

```
ssl-lab/
├── src/ssllab/            # the library (installed as `ssllab`)
│   ├── data/              # modality-agnostic adapters → token tensors
│   ├── models/            # TinyViT backbone, encoder/predictor/decoder
│   ├── jepa/              # masking, EMA target, the assembled JEPA module
│   ├── objectives/        # prediction loss + VICReg collapse regularizer
│   ├── generative/        # flow prior, count decoder, CVAE, operator algebra
│   ├── action_operator/   # latent operators: generator bases, exp(M)
│   ├── eval/              # probes, effect size, calibration, paired bootstrap
│   └── anatomy/           # shape traces for the architecture viewer
├── examples/              # one folder per applied study, numbered scripts
├── notebooks/             # intuition-first walk-throughs
├── ops/                   # SkyPilot + RunPod remote training (decoupled)
├── docs/                  # the tutorial corpus (rendered via mkdocs.yml)
├── data/                  # small local datasets
└── tests/                 # pytest suite (tests/ + ops/tests)
```

The package is lightweight by design: core dependencies are just `torch`, `torchvision`, `numpy`, `scipy`, `scikit-learn`, and `matplotlib`. Heavy extras (single-cell tooling, SkyPilot) are optional and installed only when a specific study needs them.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L119), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L6-L30)

## The Two Applied Studies

Two end-to-end studies have run so far, and each follows the lab's methodology: **pre-registered, arms compared within one study, uncertainty reported alongside every number**. Together they answer a narrower question — what JEPA pretraining buys over training the same architecture from scratch.

| | **Perturbation Response** (flagship) | **ECG Rhythm** |
|---|---|---|
| Dataset | Norman 2019 Perturb-seq (single-cell) | PTB-XL, 21,799 twelve-lead ECGs |
| Task | Generate the perturbed cell population for 20 held-out two-gene combinations never measured | Rhythm classification at nested label budgets |
| Pipeline | Cell JEPA pretraining → count decoder → conditional flow / action operator → effect-size eval | Span-masked pretraining → scratch / fine-tune / probe arms → paired patient-cluster bootstrap |
| Key finding | Generative stack graded on effect size and calibration against from-scratch and additive references | With labels for 5% of training patients, pretraining adds **+0.078 macro AUROC** — the advantage fades as labels grow |

The shared lesson: **pretraining pays off when labels are scarce**. Generated samples from the MNIST vertical slice and the ECG label-efficiency curve show the method in action:

![Generated MNIST samples from the generative JEPA slice](https://github.com/pleiadian53/ssl-lab/blob/main/examples/generative_jepa/results/figures/jepa_mnist_samples.png?raw=true)

![ECG label-efficiency: pretraining vs scratch](https://github.com/pleiadian53/ssl-lab/blob/main/examples/ecg_rhythm/results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/figures/label_efficiency.png?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L63-L70)

## Getting Running: Setup and the Vertical Slice

Installation is a standard conda workflow: create the environment from `environment.yml`, activate it, and `pip install -e .`. The fastest way to feel the whole system is the **vertical slice** — five numbered scripts that walk from representation learning to generation:

1. `01_train_jepa_mnist.py` — learn the representation (prints collapse diagnostics each epoch)
2. `02_linear_probe.py` — confirm the frozen latent is semantically useful
3. `03_train_decoder.py` — learn to decode the frozen latent back to pixels
4. `04_train_flow_prior.py` — learn a sampleable prior over the frozen latent
5. `05_sample_and_decode.py` — sample `z ~ prior`, decode → `samples.png`

All artifacts are organized per experiment under `output/<experiment>/` (`checkpoints/`, `samples/`, `reports/`, `logs/`), and every script shares an `--experiment` name so parallel runs stay side by side.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L121-L160)

## Remote GPU Ops (Optional Infrastructure)

Models too large for a laptop train on remote GPU pods. The infrastructure lives in the top-level `ops/` package: **SkyPilot orchestrates, RunPod is the provider**, and provider switching is a config value rather than hard-coded code. The workflow is a straight line — *compute check → provision pod → run job(s) → fetch results* — with dry-runs by default for safety. Architecturally, `ops` is **deliberately decoupled**: nothing in it imports JEPA, and `ssllab` never imports `ops`; it is used from the repo root without being installed.

> [!TIP]
> You can spot this decoupling in `pyproject.toml`: the pytest config adds `pythonpath = ["."]` and lists `ops/tests` alongside `tests`, so the root-level `ops` package works without installation — a clean library/infrastructure split you'll rarely see done this explicitly.

Sources: [ops/README.md](ops/README.md#L1-L25), [ops/README.md](ops/README.md#L27-L49), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L20-L39)

# Quick Start



This page takes you from a fresh clone of **ssl-lab** to your first trained model and your first *generated* samples — five commands, one CPU, no labels required for pretraining. By the end you will have (1) a self-supervised **JEPA encoder** trained on MNIST patches, (2) proof that its frozen latent is semantically useful via a **linear probe**, and (3) a grid of **newly generated digits** produced by a flow-matching prior feeding a latent decoder. Everything below runs comfortably on CPU: the environment is explicitly tuned so that CPU is the local default for development and small proof-of-concept runs, with GPUs reserved for larger training.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L121-L127), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L7-L8)

**Prerequisite reading:** if you have not yet read [Overview](1-overview), skim it first — it explains *why* this lab exists (trustworthy generative models for biological data) and what JEPA is. This page answers only *how to run it*.

## Prerequisites and Environment Setup

Install the pinned conda environment, then install the `ssllab` package in editable mode. All quick-start scripts insert `src/` into `sys.path` themselves, but `pip install -e .` also wires the package (and the test suite) up properly.

```bash
mamba env create -f environment.yml    # or: conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate ssllab
pip install -e .
```

| Requirement | Version / Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Python | ≥3.10, <3.13 | enforced by both `environment.yml` and `pyproject.toml` |
| PyTorch | ≥2.1 | CPU build is sufficient for this page |
| torchvision | ≥0.16 | MNIST data loading |
| numpy / scipy / scikit-learn / matplotlib | latest | probes, metrics, plotting |
| Hardware | CPU default | GPU (CUDA/MPS) only needed for larger runs |

There are also **optional extras** you do *not* need today, listed so you recognize them later: `dev` (pytest), `perturb` (heavy single-cell processing: anndata, scanpy, pertpy), `ops` (PyYAML for remote compute checks), and `remote` (SkyPilot itself for launching GPU pods). None of them are imported by the quick-start path.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L121-L127), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L9-L20), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L10-L30)

## Sanity-Check the Installation

Before training anything, run the smoke tests. They execute in seconds on CPU and assert that the pieces **wire together correctly** — tensor shapes round-trip through the patchifier, the JEPA loss is finite and produces gradients, the EMA teacher actually updates, the flow model trains and samples, and the decoder outputs the right image shape. As the module docstring states, they check plumbing, *not* learning quality.

```bash
pytest -q
```

The test config is pre-wired in `pyproject.toml`: it points at both `tests/` and `ops/tests/` and adds the repo root to `pythonpath` so the top-level `ops` package resolves without installation.

Sources: [test_smoke.py](tests/test_smoke.py#L1-L4), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L32-L38)

## Repository Map for This Tour

You will touch exactly three areas of the repository: the reusable library in `src/ssllab/` (imported by the scripts, never edited by you), the numbered driver scripts in `examples/` (the commands you run), and `notebooks/` (optional intuition-building). The project follows a deliberate convention: **reusable primitives in `src/`, thin driver scripts in `examples/`, intuition in `notebooks/`**.

```
ssl-lab/
├── src/ssllab/          # library: models/, jepa/, generative/, eval/, data/, utils/
├── examples/
│   ├── jepa_basics/     # 01 train JEPA · 02 linear probe        ← steps 1–2 here
│   └── generative_jepa/ # 03 decoder · 04 flow prior · 05 sample ← steps 3–5 here
├── notebooks/jepa_basics/01_jepa_intuition.ipynb                 ← optional detour
├── tests/               # pytest -q smoke suite
└── output/jepa_mnist/   # created by your runs (checkpoints/, samples/, reports/, logs/)
```

The full annotated layout — including the perturbation-response and ECG pipelines you will meet later — is documented in the project README and unpacked page by page in [Repository Layout and Conventions](3-repository-layout-and-conventions).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L119)

## The Path You Will Walk: Five Commands, One Story

The vertical slice tells a single story in five numbered milestones. **Step 1 learns a representation** (predicting masked-patch *embeddings* from context — no labels). **Step 2 verifies it** with a frozen-encoder linear probe. **Step 3 learns to map the frozen latent back to pixels.** **Step 4 learns a sampleable probability distribution over the latent.** **Step 5 draws new latents from that distribution and decodes them into images.** Each script consumes the previous script's checkpoint automatically, because they all read from the same experiment directory.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["① 01_train_jepa_mnist.py<br/>--epochs 5"] -->|"checkpoints/encoder.pt"| B["② 02_linear_probe.py"]
    A -->|"encoder (frozen)"| C["③ 03_train_decoder.py<br/>--epochs 5"]
    A -->|"extracted latents"| D["④ 04_train_flow_prior.py<br/>--epochs 20"]
    C -->|"checkpoints/decoder.pt"| E["⑤ 05_sample_and_decode.py"]
    D -->|"checkpoints/prior.pt"| E
    E --> OUT(["output/jepa_mnist/<br/>samples/samples.png"])
```

Read the diagram left to right: the encoder checkpoint produced in step ① is the *only* upstream dependency of steps ②–④, and steps ③+④ both feed step ⑤. Nothing needs a GPU, nothing needs manual file copying — artifacts flow through the `output/<experiment>/` convention.

| # | Command | Milestone | Produces |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `python examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py --epochs 5` | Learn the representation | `checkpoints/encoder.pt`, `reports/jepa_train.json` |
| 2 | `python examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py` | Verify the frozen latent is useful | `reports/probe.json` |
| 3 | `python examples/generative_jepa/03_train_decoder.py --epochs 5` | Decode latent → pixels | `checkpoints/decoder.pt`, `samples/recon.png` |
| 4 | `python examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py --epochs 20` | Sampleable prior over the latent | `checkpoints/prior.pt` |
| 5 | `python examples/generative_jepa/05_sample_and_decode.py` | Generate | `samples/samples.png` |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L129-L146), [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L9-L18), [03_train_decoder.py](examples/generative_jepa/03_train_decoder.py#L14-L17)

## How the Pieces Fit Together

One concept before the walkthrough: a **latent** (or embedding) is a vector — here 128-dimensional — that summarizes an input. JEPA trains by predicting the embeddings of *masked* patches from the *context* patches, never touching raw pixels. That latent then becomes the hub of everything downstream: the probe reads it, the decoder maps it back to pixels, and the flow prior learns its distribution so new latents can be sampled.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    IMG(["MNIST image"]) --> ENC["JEPA encoder f<br/>trained in ①, frozen afterward"]
    ENC --> Z(["latent z · 128-d"])
    Z --> PROBE["② logistic probe<br/>digit accuracy · chance = 10%"]
    Z --> DEC["③ decoder g: z → pixels"]
    Z --> PRIOR["④ flow prior v(z_t, t)"]
    NZ(["noise ε ~ N(0, I)"]) --> PRIOR
    PRIOR -->|"integrate ODE"| Z2(["new latent z*"])
    Z2 --> DEC
    DEC --> GEN(["⑤ generated digits → samples.png"])
```

Note the single arrow *into* the frozen encoder and four arrows *out of* the latent `z`: the encoder is trained exactly once (step ①), and every later stage treats it as read-only. This two-stage design — representation first, generative machinery second — is the lab's core method line, scaled up to biological data in later pages.

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L1-L7), [04_train_flow_prior.py](examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py#L1-L6), [05_sample_and_decode.py](examples/generative_jepa/05_sample_and_decode.py#L1-L5)

## Step 1 — Train the JEPA Encoder (No Labels)

```bash
python examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py --epochs 5
```

The script patchifies MNIST images into token tensors, trains the encoder to predict **target-patch embeddings** from **context-patch embeddings** with an EMA target encoder supplying targets, and prints **collapse diagnostics every epoch**: loss, `eff_rank` (effective rank of the latent), and `feat_std` (feature standard deviation). It then saves the encoder (config + weights) and a JSON report. For a ~minute-scale smoke run, use the documented quick-smoke variant: `--epochs 1 --limit 2000`.

What a healthy run logs, epoch after epoch:

| Signal | Healthy signature | Failure signature |
|---|---|---|
| `feat_std` | ~0.70–0.77 in the reference run, stable trend | drifting toward 0 → **complete collapse** (all inputs map to one point) |
| `eff_rank` | rising over training; reference run climbed 74 → ~104 of 128 dims | stuck near 1 → **dimensional collapse** (variance crammed into a few axes) |

These two metrics exist precisely because JEPA has a trivial cheat available: collapse the latent space and the loss goes to zero while nothing is learned. The full math and interpretation are in `examples/jepa_basics/docs/representation-diagnostics.md`; the anti-collapse mechanisms themselves (VICReg, EMA) are covered in [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg).

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L1-L19), [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L45-L60), [representation-diagnostics.md](examples/jepa_basics/docs/representation-diagnostics.md#L14-L31), [representation-diagnostics.md](examples/jepa_basics/docs/representation-diagnostics.md#L49-L55)

## Step 2 — Probe the Frozen Representation

```bash
python examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py
```

The script loads the encoder from the experiment's checkpoints, **freezes it**, pools latents for 10,000 train / 5,000 test images (the defaults), and fits a logistic-regression probe on top. Since MNIST has ten digit classes, **chance accuracy is 10%** — the log line prints both train and test accuracy against that floor. In the project's reference run the probe reached 98% train / 95.3% test: structure learned with zero labels. The result is written to `reports/probe.json`. This probe is your first taste of the lab's evaluation philosophy — always score against a floor (chance) and a reference — which scales up in [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics).

Sources: [02_linear_probe.py](examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py#L1-L12), [02_linear_probe.py](examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py#L36-L47), [representation-diagnostics.md](examples/jepa_basics/docs/representation-diagnostics.md#L92-L100)

## Steps 3–5 — Turn the Encoder into a Generator

Three short scripts complete the loop. **Step 3** trains a decoder `g: z → image` with a Bernoulli reconstruction loss while the encoder stays frozen, and saves a before/after grid (`recon.png`: originals on top, reconstructions below). **Step 4** extracts the training set's latents once, standardizes them, and fits a rectified-flow velocity field `v(z_t, t)` so that integrating an ODE from Gaussian noise lands on the data-latent distribution. **Step 5** draws `z ~ prior` by Euler-integrating that ODE (default 100 steps), undoes the standardization, decodes, and writes `samples.png` — a grid of 64 digits by default (`--n 64 --steps 100` to vary).

> [!TIP]
> **Blurry or soft reconstructions in step 3 are expected, not a bug.** JEPA latents are *not trained to be decodable* — the encoder never saw a reconstruction loss — so its latents carry semantic but not pixel-exact information, and reconstructions come out averaged. This is the instructive property that motivates the lab's later co-adaptation research (see [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder)).

Sources: [03_train_decoder.py](examples/generative_jepa/03_train_decoder.py#L1-L18), [04_train_flow_prior.py](examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py#L1-L16), [05_sample_and_decode.py](examples/generative_jepa/05_sample_and_decode.py#L1-L15)

## The Control Panel: Key CLI Options

Every script exposes the same shape of interface; these are the flags a beginner actually needs. All scripts share `--experiment` (default `jepa_mnist`) and `--device auto` (picks CUDA/MPS/CPU), and all training scripts default to seed 42 for reproducibility.

| Flag | Script(s) | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--epochs` | 01, 03, 04 | 5 / 5 / 20 | training duration; README's recommended quick-start values are in the table above |
| `--limit` | 01, 03, 04 | none | cap training examples/latents for smoke runs (e.g. `--epochs 1 --limit 2000`) |
| `--reg-coef` | 01 | 0.0 | VICReg collapse-regularizer weight; 0 disables; usage shows `0.04` |
| `--experiment` | all | `jepa_mnist` | output namespace `output/<name>/`; a new name isolates a new run |
| `--data-dir` | 01–04 | `data` | where MNIST is downloaded/looked up |
| `--n`, `--steps` | 05 | 64 / 100 | number of generated digits; ODE integration steps |
| `--encoder` / `--prior` / `--decoder` | 02–05 | auto | override a checkpoint path instead of using the experiment's |

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L45-L61), [03_train_decoder.py](examples/generative_jepa/03_train_decoder.py#L45-L57), [04_train_flow_prior.py](examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py#L43-L56), [05_sample_and_decode.py](examples/generative_jepa/05_sample_and_decode.py#L40-L48)

## Where Your Results Live

All artifacts land under one self-explanatory hierarchy keyed by the experiment name — never a flat `output/` dir. The layout is created idempotently by a small helper every script calls.

```
output/jepa_mnist/
  checkpoints/   encoder.pt  decoder.pt  prior.pt      # model weights
  samples/       samples.png  recon.png                # image grids
  reports/       jepa_train.json  probe.json           # metrics as JSON
  logs/          train.log
```

> [!TIP]
> **The `--experiment` name is the coupling mechanism of the whole pipeline.** It is deliberately a stable name, not a timestamp, so script 03 finds the encoder script 01 wrote — pass a *new* name to run a variant side-by-side without clobbering anything. On a GPU pod the identical tree is written on the network volume and rsynced back, so the structure you learn here transfers unchanged.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L148-L160), [experiment.py](src/ssllab/experiment.py#L1-L16)

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `eff_rank` ≈ 1 or `feat_std` → 0 during step 1 | representation collapse | rerun with `--reg-coef 0.04` (the documented usage example) |
| probe accuracy near 10% (chance) in step 2 | encoder checkpoint missing or from a failed run | confirm step 1 completed for the same `--experiment`; or pass `--encoder` explicitly |
| decoder reconstructions very soft in step 3 | expected behavior, not an error | see the tip above; sample quality is judged in step 5 and by dedicated metrics |
| "CUDA not available" warnings | no GPU locally | harmless: `--device auto` falls back to CPU, the supported local default for this scale |
| MNIST download fails | restricted network | pre-download to `--data-dir` (default `data`) and rerun |
| steps 3–5 can't find files | scripts 01–04 ran under a different `--experiment` | keep one experiment name across the chain, or pass explicit `--encoder/--decoder/--prior` paths |

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L10-L13), [03_train_decoder.py](examples/generative_jepa/03_train_decoder.py#L4-L7), [02_linear_probe.py](examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py#L38-L43), [environment.yml](environment.yml#L7-L8)

## Optional Detour: Build Intuition in a Notebook

If you would rather *see* the machinery than run it, open `notebooks/jepa_basics/01_jepa_intuition.ipynb`. It is an explicit companion to the training script and visualizes the four ideas this page exercised: **masking** (context vs. target patches), **prediction in latent space** (never pixels, targets from an EMA teacher), **collapse** (watching effective rank / feature std), and **sampling** (prior + decoder turning the representation learner into a generator). Run scripts for training, notebook for pictures.

Sources: [01_jepa_intuition.ipynb](notebooks/jepa_basics/01_jepa_intuition.ipynb#L7-L20)

## Where to Go Next

You have completed the minimal loop: *represent → verify → generate*. The catalog picks up exactly where each of the five scripts left off.

- **Immediately next:** [Repository Layout and Conventions](3-repository-layout-and-conventions) — the `src/` vs `examples/` vs `notebooks/` convention you just experienced, formalized.
- **To understand what you trained:** [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals), then [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span) and [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg) — the `eff_rank`/`feat_std` story from step 1, explained mechanically.
- **To understand what you sampled:** [Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior) — the `v(z_t, t)` velocity field behind step 4.
- **To harden your evaluation habits:** [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics) — the probe from step 2 in its full form.
- **When your model outgrows your laptop:** [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-runpod) — the same five commands, provisioned onto a GPU pod.
- **For the full curated reading order across all tutorial series:** [Tutorial Corpus and Reading Paths](25-tutorial-corpus-and-reading-paths).

Full math rendering of every deep-dive page is available at the documentation site: <https://pleiadian53.github.io/ssl-lab/>.


# Repository Layout and Conventions



This page is the map you reach for before writing any code in `ssl-lab`. It explains *where things live* — the library, the study scripts, the data, the remote-training infrastructure, the tests, and the tutorial corpus — and *why they are arranged that way*. Every convention here exists to answer one beginner question reliably: "I want to do X, so which folder do I touch?" If you have just arrived from [Quick Start](2-quick-start), this page turns the commands you ran there into a mental model of the whole repository.

## The One Rule That Explains the Layout

The repository follows a **use-case-driven R&D convention**, stated in a single line of its README: *reusable primitives live in `src/`, thin driver scripts live in `examples/`, and intuition lives in `notebooks/`*. Everything else follows from this split. The library (`src/ssllab/`) contains no experiment-specific logic; the example folders contain almost no reusable logic — they wire library pieces together into runnable studies; the single notebook exists to build intuition rather than produce results.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph lib["src/ssllab/ — the library (reusable primitives)"]
        direction LR
        ADAPT["data/<br/>modality adapters"]
        JEPA["jepa/<br/>masking · EMA · module"]
        MODELS["models/<br/>TinyViT · heads"]
        GEN["generative/<br/>flow · decoders · CVAE"]
        EVALM["eval/<br/>probes · metrics · bootstrap"]
    end
    subgraph drivers["examples/ — thin numbered study drivers"]
        JB["jepa_basics/"]
        GJ["generative_jepa/"]
        PR["perturbation_response/"]
        EC["ecg_rhythm/"]
    end
    subgraph support["supporting trees"]
        OPS["ops/ — remote GPU infra"]
        DATAIN["data/ — local inputs"]
        TESTS["tests/ + ops/tests/"]
        DOCS["docs/ — tutorial corpus"]
    end
    drivers -- "import" --> lib
    drivers -. "read at runtime" .-> DATAIN
    OPS -. "drives the same scripts remotely" .-> drivers
    TESTS -. "verify" .-> lib
```

Note the dashed line in the diagram: `ops/` drives the example scripts but the library never imports it. That one-way arrow is a deliberate architectural decision covered in its own section below.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L119)

## The Library: `src/ssllab/`

The package is installed with `pip install -e .` and imported as `ssllab`. Its subpackages are organized by *concern*, not by experiment — `jepa/` knows nothing about ECGs or gene counts, and the data adapters know nothing about training loops. The README's layout block documents each folder in one line.

| Subpackage | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `data/` | Modality adapters (MNIST image proxy, single-cell Perturb-seq, PTB-XL ECG) that turn raw data into modality-agnostic token tensors |
| `models/` | The TinyViT backbone, JEPA encoder/predictor, latent decoder |
| `jepa/` | Block masking, the EMA target encoder, and the assembled JEPA module |
| `objectives/` | The prediction loss plus the VICReg collapse regularizer |
| `generative/` | Flow prior (unconditional + conditional with classifier-free guidance), NB/ZINB count decoder, condition encoder, CVAE baseline, perturbation action operator and its algebra |
| `action_operator/` | Context-conditioned latent operators — generator bases, `exp(M)` |
| `eval/` | Collapse diagnostics, linear probe, effect size, calibration, interaction scores, joint paired bootstrap |
| `anatomy/` | Step-by-step shape traces of every component, for the architecture viewer |
| `utils/` | Seeding and device selection |

Two conventions make the library pleasant to use as a beginner. First, the **public API is deliberately lean**: the package's `__init__.py` exports only the essentials (`JEPA`, `JEPAConfig`, `build_jepa`, `set_seed`, `get_device`) and tells you to "reach into submodules for the rest," so the top-level import surface stays small while everything remains accessible. Second, all data adapters converge on a **universal token-tensor shape**, so the same `build_jepa(...)` call works whether the tokens came from MNIST patches or from cells — this is the contract explored in [Modality-Agnostic Data Adapters](23-modality-agnostic-data-adapters).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L91-L105), [\_\_init\_\_.py](src/ssllab/__init__.py#L1-L24)

## The Drivers: `examples/`

Each subfolder of `examples/` is one *study* — a numbered pipeline of scripts that builds on the previous script's artifacts. The four studies progress in difficulty: `jepa_basics/` (train JEPA, probe it), `generative_jepa/` (decoder, flow prior, sampling — the image-proxy slice), `perturbation_response/` (the flagship single-cell pipeline), and `ecg_rhythm/` (the PTB-XL classification study). There is also `ops/` here, holding the thin drivers for the remote-training infrastructure.

### The numbered-script convention

Scripts are named `<number>_<verb_phrase>.py` — `00_process_norman.py`, `01_pretrain_stage_a.py`, `05_sample_perturbed.py` — and the perturbation study's README states the rule plainly: numbers reflect *the order scripts were written, not the order anyone runs them*. The five study READMEs and their `docs/` subfolders explain the actual run order. One deliberate quirk teaches you a second convention: there is no `07` in the perturbation study, and the gap is *kept* so that existing references to script numbers never break. Numbers are identifiers, not just ordering.

> [!TIP]
> Never renumber an existing script when adding a pipeline step — append a new number (or a letter suffix like `00b_data_card.py`) instead. Older READMEs, results ledgers, and pod wrappers reference scripts by their number.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L106-L119), [examples/perturbation_response/README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L68-L82)

### The script anatomy

Every driver script follows the same three-part shape, visible in any file you open. First, a **docstring contract**: it states the milestone in plain words, then a `Usage` block with example commands, then an `Output` block naming exactly which files the script writes. Second, a **path bootstrap**: a three-line `sys.path` insertion that points Python at `src/`, so the script runs from the repo root without any installation step. Third, a **shared argparse interface**: flags like `--epochs`, `--device`, `--seed` appear everywhere, and — most importantly — every script that participates in a pipeline accepts the same `--experiment` and `--output-root` flags.

Sources: [01\_train\_jepa\_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L1-L19), [01\_train\_jepa\_mnist.py](examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L21-L60)

### Five kinds of workflow

The largest study sorts its scripts into five named kinds, and this taxonomy generalizes across the repository. It is the fastest way to answer "what does this script do?" when you encounter an unfamiliar number.

| Kind | What it does | Typical location | Cost profile |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Build** | Trains something; produces an artifact later steps depend on | Numbered low (`00`–`17`) | GPU pod, except data processing |
| **Score** | Grades a trained model on the standing benchmark | Mid-range numbers | CPU, minutes |
| **Diagnose** | Answers a question about where the loss lives; trains nothing | Numbered like data (`00a`, `02`, `11`, `14`) | CPU, minutes |
| **Decide** | Runs a pre-registered statistical verdict on a family of comparisons | One script per round (`20`–`27`) | Seconds |
| **Vary** | `run_*_pod.sh` shell wrappers that retrain one stage at a time on the pod | Top level of the study folder | GPU pod |

The shell wrappers follow their own naming rule — `run_<what>_pod.sh` — and open with a *preflight* that checks staged inputs and stops within seconds, naming whatever is missing, before spending any GPU time. The "decide" scripts carry a further convention worth knowing early: from round 7b onward there is exactly one scoring script per pre-registered round, and the script's docstring *is* that round's protocol, frozen before the run.

Sources: [examples/perturbation_response/README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L84-L128)

## Artifacts: the `output/<experiment>/` Contract

The repository never writes results to a flat pile. A shared helper in the library — `ssllab.experiment.experiment()` — gives every script the same four-subdirectory hierarchy, and its docstring explains the motivation: flat `output/` or `runs/` directories "turn unwieldy fast once you have multiple models, runs, and artifact types." The layout is:

```
output/<experiment>/
  checkpoints/   model weights (encoder.pt, decoder.pt, prior.pt, ...)
  samples/       generated images (samples.png, recon.png, ...)
  reports/       metrics + metadata as JSON
  logs/          run logs
```

Because the experiment name is passed to every script in a pipeline, artifacts *compose*: the probe script finds the encoder the trainer wrote, simply because both were run with `--experiment demo`. The flow below shows the contract in action for the two `jepa_basics` scripts.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T1["01_train_jepa_mnist.py<br/>--experiment demo"] -- "writes" --> CKPT["output/demo/checkpoints/<br/>encoder.pt"]
    T1 -- "writes" --> REP1["output/demo/reports/<br/>jepa_train.json"]
    T2["02_linear_probe.py<br/>--experiment demo"] -- "reads" --> CKPT
    T2 -- "writes" --> REP2["output/demo/reports/<br/>probe.json"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The `--experiment` name is stable on purpose — not a timestamp. Pass a new name to run a fresh experiment side by side with an old one; keep the same name to let pipeline steps hand artifacts to each other. On a remote pod the same tree lands on the network volume and is rsynced back, with only the path prefix changing.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L148-L160), [experiment.py](src/ssllab/experiment.py#L1-L64)

## Data: `data/` and the Data Lake

The `data/` directory holds *local input datasets*, and its first convention is a negative one: **the datasets themselves are not tracked in git** — only the documentation and the folder structure are, because real datasets are too large or sensitive. Small, SSL-specific data lives here as real files; MNIST needs no manual step at all, since torchvision auto-downloads it on first run through the library's data loader.

Large datasets shared across projects follow a different convention: **storage deduplication via symlinks**. Instead of copying a multi-gigabyte dataset into every repository, you keep one physical copy in a project-neutral "data lake" and link only what you use:

```bash
export DATA_LAKE_ROOT=/path/to/shared/data-lake
python -c "from ops.datasets import link_dataset; link_dataset('scrna/perturb_seq/norman2019')"
# -> data/norman2019 -> $DATA_LAKE_ROOT/scrna/perturb_seq/norman2019
```

Note the naming discipline inside that command: the lake is organized as `<modality>/<sub-topic>/<dataset>`, while the link creates a flat alias like `data/norman2019`, which is the path the loaders actually read. The environment variable is deliberately called `DATA_LAKE_ROOT` — the "shared lake" semantics — so no project ever hard-codes another project's name.

Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L25), [ops/README.md](ops/README.md#L51-L67)

## Infrastructure: the `ops/` Decoupling Rule

`ops/` is the remote-training infrastructure (SkyPilot orchestration, RunPod as provider), and it lives at the repository root as a top-level package *next to* `src/` — not inside it. The reason is stated as a strict rule in its README: **nothing in `ops/` imports JEPA, and `ssllab` never imports `ops/`**. Cloud provisioning is scaffolding for practical training, not part of self-supervised learning, so the boundary keeps the science importable on a laptop with no cloud tooling installed.

This decoupling produces three concrete conventions. First, `ops/` is *not installed* — Python finds it because you run commands from the repository root, and the pytest configuration adds the repo root to `pythonpath` for the same reason. Second, its dependencies arrive only through optional extras: `pip install -e '.[ops]'` for dry runs, `.[remote]` to actually launch pods. Third, the tooling defaults to safety: `ops_run_pipeline.py` is a **dry-run until you pass `--execute`**, and it keeps the pod alive afterwards for reuse. The workflow is a fixed four-step chain — compute check → provision pod → run job(s) → fetch results — detailed in [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-runpod). Portability is part of the design too: moving `ops/` into another project means editing exactly two config lines (`project` and `job_prefix`), because nothing else in the package names a project.

Sources: [ops/README.md](ops/README.md#L1-L19), [ops/README.md](ops/README.md#L83-L90), [README.md](README.md#L162-L164), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L19-L37)

## Configuration, Dependencies, and Tests

Packaging is deliberately minimal. The library targets Python `>=3.10,<3.13` and depends on a short core list — torch, torchvision, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, matplotlib. Anything heavy is an *optional extra*, imported lazily by the one script that needs it rather than by the library or the tests' light path. The extras and the test configuration are worth memorizing as a table:

| Extra | Adds | Who needs it |
|---|---|---|
| `dev` | pytest | running the test suite |
| `perturb` | anndata, scanpy, pertpy, scikit-misc | only `00_process_norman.py`; loaders and tests never import it |
| `ops` | pyyaml | compute checks and SkyPilot dry runs |
| `remote` | skypilot\[runpod] | actually launching GPU pods |

Tests live in two places that mirror the two importable packages: `tests/` for the `ssllab` library — with filenames that map one-to-one onto modules (`test_perturbseq.py`, `test_ptbxl.py`, `test_span_masks.py`, `test_smoke.py`, and so on) — and `ops/tests/` for the infrastructure. The pytest configuration declares both: `testpaths = ["tests", "ops/tests"]`. Getting started is three commands from the README: create the conda/mamba environment from `environment.yml`, activate it, then `pip install -e .` so the editable install picks up your changes as you edit `src/`.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L37), [README.md](README.md#L121-L127)

## Documentation Conventions

The `docs/` tree serves two audiences at once. It is the *source* for the published MkDocs Material site — `mkdocs.yml` sets `docs_dir: docs` and notes that a private `dev/` folder is intentionally excluded from the nav — and it is the *tutorial corpus* you browse in the repository. The tutorial series follow a consistent internal pattern you can rely on when reading: each series has an `index.md` overview, numbered chapters (`00-…`, `01-…`, with letter suffixes like `06a-` for digressions), and a `notation.md` reference at the end. The `examples/` studies carry their own documentation in `docs/` subfolders — runbooks, workflow maps, and the results ledger.

Rendering conventions matter if you plan to contribute: mathematics is written in LaTeX and rendered by MathJax via the `arithmatex` extension in generic mode, and ` ```mermaid ` fenced blocks are rendered as diagrams by Material's superfences config. The published nav in `mkdocs.yml` groups the corpus into the series you saw in the README — Generative JEPA, Time-Series JEPA, Action Operators, Operator World Models — each mapped chapter-by-chapter.

Sources: [mkdocs.yml](mkdocs.yml#L17-L18), [mkdocs.yml](mkdocs.yml#L47-L119)

## Conventions at a Glance

| Convention | Rule | Where you'll hit it |
|---|---|---|
| Three-way split | primitives in `src/`, thin drivers in `examples/`, intuition in `notebooks/` | everywhere |
| Script naming | `NN_verb_phrase.py`; numbers are written-order identifiers, never renumbered | any pipeline step |
| Script anatomy | docstring with Usage/Output, `sys.path` bootstrap, shared CLI flags | opening any driver |
| Artifact layout | `output/<experiment>/{checkpoints,samples,reports,logs}` via `ssllab.experiment` | every run |
| Pipeline linking | same `--experiment` name hands artifacts between steps | multi-step studies |
| Data privacy | `data/` contents are git-ignored; only structure is shared | cloning the repo |
| Storage dedup | `DATA_LAKE_ROOT` + `ops.datasets.link_dataset` symlinks | large datasets |
| Infra decoupling | `ssllab` never imports `ops`; extras `[ops]`/`[remote]`; dry-run by default | remote training |
| Pre-registration | one scoring script per round; docstring is the frozen protocol | perturbation study rounds |
| Pod wrappers | `run_<what>_pod.sh` with input preflight | GPU studies |

## Where to Go Next

With the layout in hand, the natural next step is [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview), which opens up the `jepa/` and `generative/` modules this page only listed. If you prefer to see the conventions in motion first, walk the vertical slice again with the map above beside you, then continue into [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals). For the flagship study that exercises every convention at once — numbered scripts, pre-registered scoring, pod wrappers, and the results ledger — read [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline); for the second applied study, [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study). When you outgrow your laptop, [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-RunPod) picks up exactly where the `ops/` section here stops, and [Tutorial Corpus and Reading Paths](25-tutorial-corpus-and-reading-paths) helps you navigate the `docs/` tree as a reader rather than a contributor.

# Architecture Overview



This page maps the architecture of `ssl-lab` as a system: how the repository is organized into tiers, what contract glues the layers together, and how a training study actually flows through the stack. The focus is structural — what each module owns, where the seams are, and which invariants keep the design coherent. For a guided tour of the directory tree itself, see [Repository Layout and Conventions](3-repository-layout-and-conventions); this page goes one level deeper, into module responsibilities and data flow.

## Design Philosophy: A Three-Tier R&D Layout

The repository follows a use-case-driven R&D convention: **reusable primitives in `src/`, thin driver scripts in `examples/`, intuition in `notebooks/`**. Everything that encodes a reusable idea — the JEPA module, the flow prior, evaluation probes — lives in the installable `ssllab` package; everything that encodes a *study* — a pre-registered pipeline with one scoring script per round — lives in `examples/`, importing primitives but owning no reusable logic itself. Documentation corpus and notebooks complete the outer tiers.

```
ssl-lab/
├── src/ssllab/          # the library: primitives only, no study logic
│   ├── data/            # modality adapters -> token tensors (the central contract)
│   ├── models/          # TinyViT backbone, encoder, predictor, latent decoder
│   ├── jepa/            # masking, EMA target, JEPA module assembly
│   ├── objectives/      # prediction loss + VICReg / SIGReg regularizers
│   ├── generative/      # flow prior, count decoders, CVAE, operator algebra
│   ├── action_operator/ # context-conditioned latent operators
│   ├── eval/            # probes, collapse diagnostics, generative metrics
│   ├── coadapt.py       # joint encoder+decoder training modes
│   └── anatomy/         # step-by-step shape traces for the architecture viewer
├── examples/            # one folder per study; numbered thin drivers
├── ops/                 # remote-GPU infrastructure, deliberately decoupled
├── notebooks/           # intuition-first walkthroughs
├── docs/                # the mkdocs tutorial corpus
└── tests/               # pytest suite over both src/ssllab and ops
```

The dependency graph is deliberately shallow: `examples/` depends on `ssllab`, `ssllab` depends on nothing in-repo, and `ops/` depends on neither. Study scripts stay thin — the ECG study, for instance, is a chain of numbered scripts from processing to paired-bootstrap results, each importing library functions rather than re-implementing them.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L86-L119), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L32-L40)

## The Central Contract: Modality-Agnostic Tokens

The single most important seam in the codebase is the data-adapter contract. **Every adapter emits token tensors of shape `(B, n_tokens, token_dim)`**, and every model downstream consumes exactly that shape — nothing below the adapter layer ever knows whether a token came from an image patch, a gene group, or an ECG window.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph adapters["Data adapters — ssllab/data"]
        MNIST["mnist.py<br/>image proxy"]
        PS["perturbseq.py<br/>Perturb-seq counts"]
        PTB["ptbxl.py · signal.py<br/>12-lead ECG"]
    end
    TOK["token tensors (B, n_tokens, token_dim)"]
    subgraph core["JEPA core — modality-blind"]
        MODELS["models/<br/>TinyViT · JEPAEncoder · JEPAPredictor · LatentDecoder"]
        JEPA["jepa/<br/>masking · EMA · module assembly"]
        OBJ["objectives/<br/>prediction loss + VICReg / SIGReg"]
    end
    MNIST --> TOK
    PS --> TOK
    PTB --> TOK
    TOK --> MODELS
    MODELS --> JEPA
    JEPA --> OBJ
```

| Adapter | Modality | Key surface | Design notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mnist.py` | image proxy (MNIST patches) | `patchify` / `unpatchify`, `get_mnist_dataloaders` | defines the reference `(n_tokens, token_dim)` grid |
| `perturbseq.py` | single-cell Perturb-seq counts | `tokenize_cells`, `make_gene_partition`, `ControlSampler` | versioned cache artifacts (`ARTIFACT_VERSION`); gene-group partition defines tokens |
| `ptbxl.py` | 12-lead ECG | `get_ptbxl_dataloaders` | physical-time signal geometry via `signal.py` |
| `signal.py` | generic 1D signals | `patchify_1d`, `SignalGeometry`, `zscore_per_lead` | shared helpers so ECG is one instance of a signal family |

This is why the method line is described as *modality-agnostic*: a new domain drops in as an adapter, and the encoder, objectives, generative heads, and evaluation toolkit all work unchanged.

Sources: [data/\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/ssllab/data/__init__.py#L1-L58)

## The JEPA Core: Student, Predictor, and EMA Teacher

`jepa/model.py` assembles the three components into one `nn.Module`. A single training step runs five moves on a token batch: sample a context/target position split, have the **student encoder** embed the context tokens, have the **predictor** guess embeddings at the target positions, have the **EMA teacher** — a slow-moving average copy of the encoder — encode the *full* token set detached, and score the prediction in latent space. The pooled image-level latent `z` is exposed separately via `embed`, and that frozen latent is what every downstream stage reads.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    TOK["tokens (B, N, D)"] --> MASK["mask sampler<br/>random or span"]
    MASK --> CTX["context idx"] --> STUDENT["student encoder"]
    MASK --> TGT["target idx"] --> PRED["predictor"]
    TOK --> TEACHER["EMA teacher<br/>(no grad, full set)"]
    STUDENT --> PRED
    PRED --> LOSS["prediction loss<br/>+ VICReg / SIGReg"]
    TEACHER --> LOSS
    STUDENT -. "embed(tokens)" .-> Z["pooled latent z"]
```

Masking and anti-collapse are both first-class configuration surfaces, not hard-coded choices. Two masking families exist — scattered random blocks (the MNIST and perturb-seq default) and contiguous spans for ordered 1D sequences — and two regularizer families guard against representation collapse. Because these details each deserve their own treatment, they are covered in [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span) and [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg); the table below just anchors the knobs.

| Config knob | Options | What it controls |
|---|---|---|
| `mask_kind` | `"random"` \| `"span"` | scattered target positions vs. contiguous spans (`span_len × n_spans = n_target` enforced) |
| `reg_kind` | `"vicreg"` \| `"sigreg"` | hinge variance + covariance penalty vs. isotropic-Gaussian Epps–Pulley statistic |
| `reg_target` | `"tokens"` \| `"pooled"` | regularize per-token embeddings or the mean-over-context cell vector |
| `pred_kind` | `"smooth_l1"` \| `"mse"` \| `"cosine"` | latent-space prediction distance |
| `ema_base` / `ema_final` | floats in (0, 1] | teacher momentum schedule |

The loss functions are plain functions returning `(scalar, dict_of_components)` so callers can log every term — a deliberate convention that keeps objectives testable in isolation from the module that calls them.

Sources: [jepa/model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L1-L14), [jepa/model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L30-L74), [jepa/model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L149), [objectives/jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L1-L23), [objectives/jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L31-L41)

## Two Extension Stacks Diverge from the Frozen Latent

Everything downstream of pretraining reads the frozen JEPA latent, and the architecture branches into two complementary directions. **Generative JEPA** makes the representation *sampleable*: a flow-matching prior learns a velocity field over `z` and samples by integrating an ODE from noise to data. **Action operators** make prediction *active*: the latent itself is transformed by a learned, structured operator.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    X["token batch"] --> FENC["frozen JEPA encoder"]
    FENC --> Z["latent z"]
    Z --> FLOW["flow prior<br/>v(z, t) or v(z, t, c)"]
    Z --> ACT["action operator<br/>f(z) = exp(M)·z + b"]
    FLOW --> DEC["decoder z → x<br/>(count-aware / pixel)"]
    ACT --> DZ["counterfactual latents"]
    DEC --> EVALG["generative metrics"]
    DZ --> EVALA["interaction scores"]
```

The generative stack centers on `VelocityMLP`, a velocity field with FiLM-injected time — and optionally a condition vector `c`, FiLM-injected alongside time, turning the marginal `p(z)` into a conditional `p(z | c)`. A learned `null_cond` token with per-sample condition dropping enables **classifier-free guidance** at sampling time. The same module also supports a *data base* source (transporting a control population onto a perturbed one, with independent or `ot_couple` least-action pairing) instead of pure noise. The stack rounds out with NB/ZINB count decoders, a CVAE baseline for reference, and the perturbation operator algebra — the conditional path is what the flagship perturbation study scores.

The action-operator stack implements conditioned latent dynamics `f_θ(c)(z) = exp(M_θ)·z + b_θ` where `M_θ = Σᵢ αᵢ Bᵢ` is a Lie-algebra element built from a **generator basis**. The basis is the main design decision, because it fixes the group the operator can live in:

| Basis | Generator structure | Resulting group |
|---|---|---|
| `FreeBasis` | learnable dense matrices | GL(D): invertible, otherwise free |
| `NamedBasis` | one generator per labeled intervention | GL(D), with interpretable coefficients |
| `SkewBasis` | skew-symmetric generators | SO(D): orthogonal, norm-preserving |
| `SE3Basis` | 3 rotation + 3 translation generators | SE(3): rigid motion |

Invertibility, orthogonality, and rigidity here are *structural* properties — they follow from the basis plus the matrix exponential, never from a training penalty.

> [!TIP]
> The operator's policy head is zero-initialized, so at step zero `α = 0 → M = 0 → A = I`: every action operator literally begins as "do nothing," and training pushes it away from identity only as far as the data demands. If you extend the stack with a new basis, preserve this near-identity property — it is what keeps counterfactual rollouts stable early in training.

Sources: [generative/flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L1-L38), [generative/flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L61-L92), [generative/\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/ssllab/generative/__init__.py#L1-L6), [action_operator/context_operator.py](/src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L1-L39), [action_operator/context_operator.py](/src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L51-L85)

## The Evaluation Toolkit

Evaluation is a first-class architectural layer, not an afterthought: the lab's premise — "reliable is measured, not assumed" — is embodied in `eval/`. The re-exported public surface spans collapse diagnostics, probing, and generative-sample metrics; sibling modules not re-exported (`bootstrap.py`, `calibration.py`, `effect_size.py`, `interaction.py`, `baselines.py`) carry the study-grade statistical machinery, including the joint paired bootstrap with max-t intervals used to compare arms within one study.

| Module | Capabilities |
|---|---|
| `collapse.py` | `effective_rank`, `feature_std`, `collapse_report` |
| `probe.py` | `linear_probe` — the standard readout of representation quality |
| `generative.py` | `fid`, `kid`, `precision_recall`, `density_coverage`, `nn_distance_stats`, `classifier_metrics` |
| `viz.py` | `save_image_grid` |
| `bootstrap.py` | paired-cluster bootstrap, simultaneous max-t inference |
| `effect_size.py` / `interaction.py` | perturbation effect magnitude, epistasis/interaction scores |
| `calibration.py` | whether generated populations match measured variability |

Sources: [eval/\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/ssllab/eval/__init__.py#L1-L28), [README.md](/README.md#L100-L104)

## Study Glue: Co-Adaptation, Latents, and Anatomy

Between the primitives and the study scripts sit a few *glue* modules that encode cross-cutting research decisions. `coadapt.py` trains the cell encoder and count decoder together under three modes that differ only in what may train — `dec` (frozen encoder control), `joint` (both train, encoder at a smaller learning rate), and `joint_anchor` (joint plus the JEPA predictive objective held fixed during reconstruction). `latents.py` provides *row-exact* frozen latents: diagnostics that score an explicit set of cache rows encode exactly those rows, so the cells a metric scores are the cells that were encoded — a subtle but load-bearing reproducibility guarantee. `embeddings/` stores and projects extracted latents, `anatomy/` produces step-by-step shape traces of every component for the architecture viewer, and `checkpoint.py` handles export. These modules exist because two or more numbered study scripts needed the same behavior; the glue layer is the archive of such convergences.

Sources: [coadapt.py](/src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L1-L40), [latents.py](/src/ssllab/latents.py#L1-L8), [README.md](/README.md#L104-L105)

## The Ops Layer: Deliberately Decoupled

Remote training infrastructure lives in a top-level `ops/` package that is **architecturally separated** from the library by an explicit invariant: nothing in `ops/` imports JEPA, and `ssllab` never imports `ops`. Cloud provisioning is treated as scaffolding for practically useful models, not as part of self-supervised learning itself — which is why it is installed through optional extras (`ops` adds PyYAML for compute checks and dry runs; `remote` adds SkyPilot itself) rather than core dependencies. SkyPilot orchestrates while RunPod is merely a config value (`cloud: runpod`), so switching providers is a configuration change, not an API rewrite.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["compute check<br/>ops_compute_check.py"] --> B["dry run<br/>prints SkyPilot YAML + cost"]
    B --> C["launch pod<br/>--execute, kept alive by default"]
    C --> D["run job(s)<br/>re-use pod via --cluster"]
    D --> E["fetch results<br/>rsync to output/"]
    E --> F["teardown<br/>--teardown or sky down"]
```

Notably, the pytest `testpaths` include both `tests/` and `ops/tests/`, so the decoupled package is still verified in one continuous run.

> [!TIP]
> The decoupling invariant ("`ops` never imports `ssllab`, `ssllab` never imports `ops`") is the reason remote training can evolve — provider changes, config schema, dataset staging — without touching a single line of modeling code. When adding features, ask first whether they belong to *learning* or to *scaffolding*; that question is the whole architecture of `ops/`.

Sources: [ops/README.md](/ops/README.md#L1-L11), [ops/README.md](/ops/README.md#L21-L50), [ops/README.md](/ops/README.md#L69-L80), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L20-L30)

## How a Study Flows Through the Stack

To see the layers cooperating end to end, consider the flagship perturbation-response study. Each numbered script is thin; each arrow crosses exactly one architectural seam.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P0["00 process Norman<br/>→ data adapter"] --> P1["01 Stage A<br/>JEPA pretrain"]
    P1 --> P2["02 probe cell encoder<br/>→ eval/"]
    P1 --> P3["03 count decoder<br/>→ generative/"]
    P3 --> P4["04 conditional flow<br/>→ generative/"]
    P4 --> P5["05 sample perturbed<br/>→ sampling"]
    P2 --> P6["06 effect size<br/>→ eval/"]
    P5 --> P6
    P6 --> P7["12 compare arms<br/>paired bootstrap"]
```

Data enters through the Perturb-seq adapter as tokens; Stage A trains the JEPA core; downstream stages read the frozen latent and train generative heads; evaluation scores effect sizes, calibration, and arm differences with paired statistics; and heavy runs are executed remotely through `ops/` with results rsynced back. The ECG study follows the same shape with the span-masking path and scratch-vs-pretrained arms instead. When one script grows reusable logic, it graduates downward into `src/ssllab/` — that migration pressure is the mechanism by which this architecture stays coherent.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L106-L119), [ops/README.md](/ops/README.md#L21-L44)

# Research Directions: Generative and Active JEPA



This page is the pivot of the repository's documentation: it frames the **two research programs** that extend JEPA beyond representation learning — **Generative JEPA** (make the representation *sampleable*) and **Active JEPA via action operators** (make prediction *active*). Here you will learn what each direction adds, how the design space is organized, where each direction lives in `src/ssllab/`, and which catalog pages descend from each. It sits between [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview) and the deep-dive modules ([JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals), [Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior), [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators)).

Sources: [index.md](docs/index.md#L3-L5), [README.md](README.md#L44-L44)

## The Starting Point: JEPA as a Passive Representation Learner

Every direction in this lab begins from the same substrate. **JEPA** (joint-embedding predictive architecture) learns by predicting the *embedding* of a masked region from the embedding of its visible context — never raw pixels, never reconstruction. The reward is a famously good encoder, but only an encoder: it defines no density, has no decoder, and cannot produce new data. It also *watches* rather than *acts* — its predictor's query says only "predict region $q$," a fixed, blind instruction sampled at random. The lab's stated focus is precisely JEPA "and two ways to extend it," and each extension attacks one of those two limitations.

Sources: [index.md](docs/index.md#L3-L3), [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L3-L6), [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L15-L25)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    JEPA["JEPA<br/>passive representation learner<br/>(encoder only, watch-and-predict)"]
    JEPA -->|"Direction 1<br/>add a prior + decoder"| GEN["Generative JEPA<br/>representation becomes SAMPLEABLE"]
    JEPA -->|"Direction 2<br/>make the query a policy-chosen operator"| ACT["Action Operators<br/>prediction becomes ACTIVE"]
    GEN -->|"Route D + action conditions"| WM["World models you can act on<br/>(the convergence point)"]
    ACT -->|"latent operators f_θ(z)"| WM
```

The two extensions are **complementary, not competing**: one gives the learned representation a generative head, the other gives the predictor an actionable structure — and they are documented as beginning to converge (more in [Where the Two Directions Converge](#where-the-two-directions-converge)). The comparison below is the map for the rest of this page.

| | **Direction 1 — Generative JEPA** | **Direction 2 — Action Operators** |
|---|---|---|
| One-line goal | Make the representation *sampleable* | Make prediction *active* |
| What it adds to JEPA | A prior over latents + a decoder back to data space | A learned operator the model *chooses* (sensing + perturbing) |
| Core question | How do I draw new data from this representation? | What does an *action* do to the state? |
| Status | Method built + de-risked; design space mapped; applications WIP | Tutorial corpus written; theory still developing |
| Code seam | `src/ssllab/generative/` | `src/ssllab/action_operator/` |
| Entry tutorial | [Generative JEPA series](docs/generative_jepa/index.md) | [Action Operators](docs/action_operator/00-from-actions-to-operators.md) |

Sources: [index.md](docs/index.md#L7-L24), [README.md](README.md#L44-L52), [README.md](README.md#L97-L100)

## Direction 1 — Generative JEPA: Make the Representation Sampleable

The generative recipe is deliberately the *simplest* thing that closes the loop: **train the encoder once, freeze it, then bolt on two pieces**. JEPA's latent space is a map where meaning is organized; generation needs (a) a way to *pick a point on that map at random* — a prior over latents — and (b) a way to *walk from a latent back to a data point* — a decoder. The v0 route makes three defining choices: train-then-freeze (the encoder never sees the prior or decoder loss), one mean-pooled latent per observation (small, transparent math), and a **rectified-flow** prior (simple regression objective, straight noise-to-data paths).

Sources: [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L8-L13), [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L27-L33)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    X["observation x"] -->|"encoder f_θ (frozen)"| Z["latent z"]
    Z -.->|"train prior on latents"| P["flow-matching prior p(z)"]
    Z -.->|"train decoder on latents"| D["decoder D_ω"]
    P ==>|"sample z* ~ p(z)"| ZS["latent z*"]
    ZS ==>|"decode D_ω(z*)"| XN["generated sample x̃"]
    XN --> EVAL["measure sample quality<br/>without eyeballing"]
```

Read in two passes: **solid arrows** are the forward training path (encode observations into latents); **dashed arrows** are the two heads fitted on frozen latents; **bold arrows** are sampling. Staged as four parts — encoder, latent prior, decoder, sampling-and-evaluation — this is the walking skeleton built on MNIST as a modality-agnostic proof of concept, and it is *verified end to end*: one A40 reference run reports a rich, non-collapsed latent (encoder effective rank 103.7, strong linear-probe accuracy). Each chapter in the series points at the runnable scripts `01`–`06` in `examples/generative_jepa/`.

Sources: [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L15-L26), [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L76-L78), [README.md](README.md#L46-L46)

### The Design Space: Two Gaps, Four Routes

"One realization is not the method." The starter above is a *single point* in a design space the survey chapter maps with a two-question lens. JEPA is not generative for **two independent reasons**, and closing one does nothing for the other:

- **Gap G1 — stochastic prediction.** JEPA's predictor is a deterministic point estimate: one context in, exactly one latent out. Generation needs a *distribution* over outcomes.
- **Gap G2 — no decoder to data space.** JEPA's entire loss lives in latent space; there is no map from a latent back to an actual data point.

A usable generative JEPA must close **both**. The biological example makes the independence concrete: solving only G2 gives one expression profile per drug — a point estimate masquerading as a population, since identical cells respond differently; solving only G1 gives many plausible latents you cannot read or score against a real measurement.

Sources: [05-two-gaps-four-routes.md](docs/generative_jepa/05-two-gaps-four-routes.md#L11-L23), [05-two-gaps-four-routes.md](docs/generative_jepa/05-two-gaps-four-routes.md#L25-L33)

Every route in the survey is a *different pairing of how-it-closes-G1 with how-it-closes-G2*:

| Route | Idea in one line | Closes G1 by… | Closes G2 by… | Landmark |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A: Latent decoder head** | bolt a decoder onto the latent; make the *latent* stochastic | a stochastic predictor or sampled prior | a decoder $D_\omega$ (count-aware for biology) | conditional-VAE / NB-decoder family |
| **B: Variational JEPA** | the predictor emits a *posterior* and *becomes* the conditional prior | learned $q_\phi(z\mid\text{ctx}, c)$ + sampling | a decoder (representation or data space) | **Var-JEPA** |
| **C: Rep-conditioned diffusion** | keep JEPA as encoder; train a *separate* diffusion model on its latent | diffusion noise | the diffusion model decodes to data | **D-JEPA** |
| **D: World-model planning** | freeze encoder, learn an *action-conditioned* predictor, *plan* over actions | not directly | not directly | **V-JEPA 2-AC** |

Two structural facts organize the grid: **Routes A–C produce data; Route D produces decisions** (it searches the space of actions to reach a goal state — which is exactly the bridge to Direction 2), and **the Parts 0–4 starter is a stripped-down hybrid of A and C** (Route C's flow-style machinery used unconditionally, with Route A's plain decoder).

Sources: [05-two-gaps-four-routes.md](docs/generative_jepa/05-two-gaps-four-routes.md#L41-L59)

> [!TIP]
> The route-choice constraint is empirical, not aesthetic: in perturbation biology the benchmark is **effect size** — the correlation between predicted and true differential expression on the genes a drug moved most (the scGen/CPA/scPPDM scoring protocol). Because a stable baseline dominates the latent, a generative head that maps back to *data space* is the mechanism by which effect magnitude is recovered and calibrated — Routes A/B/C, not a pure latent-space model. This is why the flagship application grades on effect size rather than sample realism.

Sources: [05-two-gaps-four-routes.md](docs/generative_jepa/05-two-gaps-four-routes.md#L72-L103)

The survey also plants a through-line to read the deep-dives with: the simplest way to close G1 is a **diagonal Gaussian** head, but that is *unimodal per condition* — one bump of probability where the truth may be genuinely multi-modal. The expressive alternatives (flows, diffusion) buy multi-modality at the cost of closed-form density and cheap sampling; the series treats this as a live trade-off, not a verdict. And the honest open problem, stated plainly: bolt a prior and decoder onto JEPA and you have structurally **rebuilt a VAE or latent-diffusion model with JEPA as encoder pretraining** — the value is that JEPA's encoder is a strong, semantically-organized substrate, not that the surrounding machinery is new.

Sources: [05-two-gaps-four-routes.md](docs/generative_jepa/05-two-gaps-four-routes.md#L104-L137)

### The Implementation Seam: `src/ssllab/generative/`

The generative stack is a small, layered module: the package exports exactly the four primitives of the flow prior — `VelocityMLP`, `linear_interpolant`, `cfm_loss`, `euler_sample` — with the count decoder, CVAE baseline, condition encoder, and the perturbation action operator as siblings in the same package (the latter two belong to the convergence story below).

Sources: [__init__.py](src/ssllab/generative/__init__.py#L1-L6), [README.md](README.md#L97-L99)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph flow.py["flow.py — rectified flow on flat vector latents"]
        V["VelocityMLP<br/>v(z_t, t [, c])<br/>FiLM time + FiLM condition<br/>learned null_cond token"]
        LI["linear_interpolant<br/>z_t = (1−t)z0 + t·z1"]
        OT["ot_couple<br/>minibatch OT pairing"]
        CFM["cfm_loss<br/>‖v − (z1−z0)‖²"]
        ES["euler_sample<br/>integrate ODE t: 0→1"]
    end
    Z["frozen JEPA latents z1"] --> CFM
    LI --> CFM
    OT -.->|"data-base transport"| LI
    V --> CFM
    CFM --> ES
    ES --> SAMPLES["samples (n, dim)"]
```

The module docstring states the conventions compactly: the interpolant $z_t = (1-t)z_0 + t z_1$ with constant target velocity $u_t = z_1 - z_0$; the loss regresses $\|v_\theta(z_t, t\,[,c]) - u_t\|^2$; sampling integrates $dz/dt = v_\theta$ from $t{=}0$ (source) to $t{=}1$ (data). Two design seams are worth knowing before you open the deep dives:

1. **Two choices of source, one loss and sampler.** With `z0=None` the source is Gaussian noise — the standard *noise→data* generative prior. Pass real samples (e.g. control-cell latents) and the same machinery becomes a *distribution-to-distribution transport*, modeling population-level displacement; `ot_couple` optionally re-pairs source and target by minibatch optimal transport for straighter, lower-variance paths. What is identified is the population-level transport, not a per-pair correspondence.

Sources: [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L8-L23), [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L146-L165)

2. **Conditioning and CFG are flags on the same module.** Setting `cond_dim > 0` FiLM-injects a condition vector $c$ alongside time, so the field learns a different flow per condition and samples $p(z \mid c)$ instead of the marginal $p(z)$. A learned `null_cond` token plus per-sample condition dropout (`p_drop`) during training enables classifier-free guidance at sampling time (`guidance` blends conditional and unconditional velocities); with `cond_dim=0` the module is *exactly* the original unconditional field.

Sources: [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L25-L37), [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L61-L126)

> [!TIP]
> `VelocityMLP`'s condition axis is backward-compatible by construction: existing unconditional callers pass no `c`, and the forward pass raises a `ValueError` on any `(c is None)` / `cond_dim` mismatch — so the unconditional prior (tutorial `04`) and the conditional flow (tutorial `07`, the perturbation arm) are the *same class* at different configurations, not two codebases. When you read [Conditional Flow and Classifier-Free Guidance](10-conditional-flow-and-classifier-free-guidance), you are reading one keyword argument's worth of delta.

Sources: [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L29-L38), [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L96-L110)

### Where Direction 1 Lands: The Application Line

The direction's applications are chosen so that "reliable generation" is measurable rather than assumed. The flagship is **single-cell perturbation response**: a staged "cell JEPA" on Norman-2019 Perturb-seq — intra-cell pretraining (Stage A) → variational / conditional-flow perturbation predictor (Stage B) → NB/ZINB count decoder (Stage C) — graded on *effect size* for gene combinations never measured. Second, **digital phenotyping**, where the rollout becomes a *generative personal world model*: a fan of plausible future trajectories under an intervention. Third, **further modalities** drop in as data adapters, because the core is a likelihood-matched conditional generator (the data-modalities primer surveys single-cell counts, EHR codes, and wearable/CGM streams).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L48-L50), [README.md](README.md#L67-L67)

The deep-dive catalog pages for this track are: [Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior), [Conditional Flow and Classifier-Free Guidance](10-conditional-flow-and-classifier-free-guidance), [Latent Transport and Optimal-Transport Coupling](11-latent-transport-and-optimal-transport-coupling), and [Count Decoders and CVAE Baseline](12-count-decoders-and-cvae-baseline), with the applied walk-through in [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline).

Sources: [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L46-L72)

## Direction 2 — Active JEPA: Action Operators

The second direction attacks the *passivity* of prediction. JEPA's predictor takes a context embedding and a **query** $q$ that says only *where* or *when* — which masked region, how far ahead. This leaves two precise blind spots:

| Blind spot | Axis | What the model cannot do | Closure |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1. The query is blind** | *where/when* | Targets are sampled at random; the model cannot choose informative targets — no active perception | **Sensing**: a policy picks *where to look*, rewarded by how much the choice teaches |
| **2. The prediction is unconditioned** | *what acted* | The predictor never sees what intervened between context and target, so it fits the **average** over every unobserved action | **Perturbing**: $\theta$ conditions the prediction on *what acted* |

The gap in one line: *JEPA's query says where and when, never why or under what action* — all causal, exogenous structure (slept-7h, took-meds, gene-KO) is invisible and averaged away.

Sources: [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L43-L59), [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L105-L119)

The fix is to replace the bare query with an **action operator the model configures**: the predictor becomes $f_\theta$, a transformation applied to the latent, with $\theta$ chosen by a policy. Crucially, the operator acts in the **latent**, not on the raw state — the intractable real-world action (a drug on a cell, a week of sleep on a person) stays implicit in the data, while the operator the model builds and applies lives in JEPA's latent space where it can be simple. The perturbing reading gives the action a measurable meaning: $\Delta z = E(\hat O_\theta(x)) - E(x)$, the change the operator induces in the latent, with an energy penalty biasing toward the *smallest* action that produces the effect.

Sources: [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L61-L77), [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L113-L119)

### The Conceptual Move: From Label to Operator

The foundation note makes one shift from which everything follows: an action is **not a label the agent selects** (left / right / jump — a symbol whose meaning hides inside the environment); it is **a function that transforms the state**, $\hat O_\theta : \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{S}$, configured by a parameter $\theta$. Operators buy three properties labels lack: a **description** (so actions become *comparable* — nearby parameters mean nearby transformations), an **energy** (so a model can prefer the smallest sufficient action), and **composition** ($\hat O_2 \circ \hat O_1$ is itself an operator, so a skill is a chain of operators). And the family is *configured, not looked up*: a continuous $\theta$ manufactures $\hat O_\theta$ from scratch, as with $\hat O_\theta(s) = s + \theta$ on the number line or a rotation $R(\omega)s$ in the plane.
