Sources: [00-from-actions-to-operators.md](docs/action_operator/00-from-actions-to-operators.md#L27-L47), [00-from-actions-to-operators.md](docs/action_operator/00-from-actions-to-operators.md#L49-L74), [00-from-actions-to-operators.md](docs/action_operator/00-from-actions-to-operators.md#L83-L115)

The deepest observation connecting this direction to JEPA itself is that the integration is *not* a bolt-on. JEPA's own prediction loss and an **operator equivariance loss** are the same equation under a dictionary:

$$\underbrace{\big\lVert E(\hat O_\theta(s)) - f_\theta(E(s)) \big\rVert^2}_{\text{(A) operator equivariance loss}} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \underbrace{\big\lVert E_{\text{target}}(\text{target}) - \mathrm{Pred}(E(\text{context}), q)\big\rVert^2}_{\text{(B) JEPA prediction loss}}$$

| JEPA (right side) | Operator framework (left side) |
|---|---|
| query / position $q$ | action parameter $\theta$ |
| predictor $\mathrm{Pred}(\cdot, q)$ | latent operator $f_\theta$ |
| "reveal region $q$", a *fixed* rule | action operator $\hat O_\theta$, *configured by a policy* |

**JEPA is the special case where the action is a fixed, passive "look here" that the agent never gets to choose.** Going beyond it means letting a policy configure the operator — which is precisely the two-blind-spot fix. The direction also carries a methodological rule worth internalizing early: a predicted effect is only credible if it agrees with a *genuinely independent* view — an actual measurement, not another predictor reading the same input (that would be distillation, not validation).

Sources: [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L81-L99), [01-jepa-action-operators.md](docs/action_operator/01-jepa-action-operators.md#L121-L131)

### The Implementation Seam: `src/ssllab/action_operator/`

The runnable core is a single module, `context_operator.py`, implementing conditioned latent dynamics

$$f_{\theta(c_t)}(z) = \exp(M_\theta)\,z + b_\theta, \qquad M_\theta = \textstyle\sum_i \alpha_i B_i, \qquad \alpha = \theta \sim \pi_\psi(z, c_t)$$

where $\{B_i\}$ is a **generator basis** and $\alpha$ is emitted by a context policy. The basis is the main design decision: it sets what $\exp(M_\theta)$ is *allowed* to be. Four bases span the expressiveness ↔ structure dial:

| Basis | Generator structure | Resulting operator group | Intended domain |
|---|---|---|---|
| `FreeBasis` | learnable dense matrices | GL(D) — invertible only | phenotyping default; the policy learns dynamics modes end-to-end |
| `NamedBasis` | one learnable matrix per *labeled* intervention; $\alpha$ can *be* $c$ | GL(D) + interpretable | quantified intervention logs; inspect $\mathrm{eig}(B_i)$ |
| `SkewBasis` | skew-symmetric generators ($B^T = -B$) | SO(D) — orthogonal, norm-preserving | cyclic / circadian latent structure; cannot blow up |
| `SE3Basis` | 3 rotation + 3 translation generators, fixed | SE(3) — rigid motion | the protein-frame instance |

Sources: [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L7-L30), [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L51-L60)

> [!TIP]
> Two invariants of this module reward attention before you write any code. First, **near-identity init**: the policy head is zero-initialized, so $\alpha = 0 \Rightarrow M = 0 \Rightarrow \exp(M) = I$ — the operator begins as "do nothing" and training pushes it away from identity only as far as the data demands. Second, **structural constraints, never penalties**: invertibility, orthogonality, and rigidity follow from the basis-plus-$\exp(\cdot)$ construction itself, not from a loss term. Both choices trace directly back to the "energy" and "configure" properties of the foundation note.

Sources: [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L32-L38), [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L61-L96)

The direction's status is honest: *an actively developing theoretical line whose operator formalism is still being worked out, not settled*. Its tutorial corpus is written and ordered — **[Time-Series JEPA](docs/time_series_jepa/index.md)** (the substrate: JEPA on time series, multimodal channels, the blind spot that motivates operators, first runnable as the ECG study), **[Action Operators](docs/action_operator/00-from-actions-to-operators.md)** (the foundation plus a gallery of concrete operators), and **[Operator World Models](docs/operator_world_models/index.md)** (the synthesis). The formalism originates in the sibling **GRL** project, which remains the deep reference for operator families beyond the four bases above (affine, field, potential, kernel).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L52-L61), [00-from-actions-to-operators.md](docs/action_operator/00-from-actions-to-operators.md#L7-L9)

### The World-Model Arc (Direction 2's Destination)

The operator world-model series tells Direction 2's story in three moves: **JEPA watches** (masked-region prediction, passive and label-free) → **JEPA as a world model** (reinterpret "predict the masked region" as "predict the next timestep"; the predictor becomes latent dynamics $z_t \to z_{t+1}$, and prediction error becomes a *surprise* signal) → **JEPA you can act on** (condition the operator on the intervention: $f_{\theta(c_t)}$, unlocking counterfactual rollout and composable interventions). Two anchored domains sit at opposite ends of one dial — **digital phenotyping** (learned `FreeBasis`: you don't know in advance what "a week of more sleep" does to a latent) and **protein ML** (given `SE3Basis`: physics dictates the rigid-motion structure) — and the payoff is that *one piece of operator machinery serves both*.

Sources: [operator_world_models/index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L9-L20), [operator_world_models/index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L22-L43)

The catalog pages for this track are: [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators), [Operator Algebra and Epistasis Tests](14-operator-algebra-and-epistasis-tests), [Operator World Models Series](15-operator-world-models-series), with the accessible on-ramp in [Time-Series JEPA](docs/time_series_jepa/index.md) and the ECG study in [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study).

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L54-L57)

## Where the Two Directions Converge

The README states it directly: the generative slice is one of *two complementary extensions*, and "the two are beginning to **converge**." Three concrete convergence seams are visible in the code and docs:

1. **The condition can be an action.** The generative series treats action-conditioning as the bridge: the conditional flow prior's condition $c$ is modality-agnostic — a class embedding in the MNIST proxy, the perturbation pair $(z_b, z_p)$ in the biology arm — and can equally be an *action operator's* output.

Sources: [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L25-L31), [README.md](README.md#L59-L59)

2. **Route D is the hinge.** World-model planning is the one route that produces *decisions* rather than data, and the survey explicitly names it "the bridge to Operator World Models."

Sources: [05-two-gaps-four-routes.md](docs/generative_jepa/05-two-gaps-four-routes.md#L53-L59), [generative_jepa/index.md](docs/generative_jepa/index.md#L68-L68)

3. **Digital phenotyping is the meeting point.** The diabetes rollout is simultaneously Direction 1's *generative personal world model* and Direction 2's *action-conditioned world model* — one application, both directions.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L49-L49), [operator_world_models/index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L27-L35)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph D1["Direction 1: generative stack"]
        CF["conditional flow prior<br/>v_η(z, t, c)"]
        CD["count decoder / pixel decoder"]
    end
    subgraph D2["Direction 2: active stack"]
        OP["context-conditioned operator<br/>f_θ(c)(z) = exp(M_θ)z + b_θ"]
        WM["action-conditioned world model"]
    end
    C["condition c = (z_b, z_p)<br/>or an action"] --> CF
    OP -.->|"operator output as condition"| C
    CF --> CD
    OP --> WM
    CF --> PHEN["digital phenotyping<br/>fan of futures under intervention"]
    WM --> PHEN
```

A concrete motivating example ties the loop together from the genomics side: given an RNA sequence, *sense* to localize candidate splice sites, then *perturb* (in-silico edits) to learn what they do to splicing — "the kind of active, hypothesis-driven understanding passive prediction alone can't reach."

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L61-L61)

## Status and Evidence So Far

Both directions are grounded in two pre-registered applied studies, each comparing arms within one study and reporting uncertainty alongside every number. Read together they answer a narrower question too: what JEPA pretraining buys over training the same model from scratch — the answer pointing to **label and data efficiency** as the axis that matters.

| Study | Dataset | Question | Headline result |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Single-cell perturbation response](16-perturbation-response-pipeline) | Norman-2019 Perturb-seq, 20 held-out two-gene combinations | Generate the perturbed population for combinations never measured | Generative stack: cell-JEPA encoder + conditional flow or action operator, graded on effect size (flagship, WIP) |
| [ECG rhythm classification](17-ecg-rhythm-study) | PTB-XL, 21,799 twelve-lead ECGs | Does span-masked JEPA pretraining beat training from scratch? | +0.078 macro AUROC with labels for 5% of training patients; advantage fades as labels grow |

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L63-L70)

The repository layout mirrors the two directions under a use-case-driven convention — reusable primitives in `src/`, thin driver scripts in `examples/`, intuition in `notebooks/` — with `generative/` and `action_operator/` as the two research seams and `jepa/`, `objectives/`, `eval/` shared by both.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L86-L105)

## How to Read Onward

This page is the fork in the catalog; the two tracks descend from it as follows. For **Direction 1**, the natural order is the JEPA substrate first — [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals), [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span), [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg) — then the generative stack: [Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior), [Conditional Flow and Classifier-Free Guidance](10-conditional-flow-and-classifier-free-guidance), [Latent Transport and Optimal-Transport Coupling](11-latent-transport-and-optimal-transport-coupling), [Count Decoders and CVAE Baseline](12-count-decoders-and-cvae-baseline). For **Direction 2**, the order is [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators), [Operator Algebra and Epistasis Tests](14-operator-algebra-and-epistasis-tests), [Operator World Models Series](15-operator-world-models-series). Both tracks land in the applied studies — [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline), [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study), [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder) — whose verdicts are adjudicated by [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics) and the methodology series starting at [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series). If you prefer a guided tour across both, [Tutorial Corpus and Reading Paths](25-tutorial-corpus-and-reading-paths) assembles the full reading order.


# JEPA Module Internals



The `ssllab.jepa` package is deliberately small — three files — because the architecture it encodes is a *protocol*, not a pile of layers. The organizing principle is stated right in the module docstring as a five-step contract: sample a (context, target) position split → the student encoder embeds only the context tokens → the predictor predicts embeddings at the target positions → the EMA teacher encodes the *full* token set (no gradients) and the target rows are gathered → `jepa_loss` combines the prediction error with an optional anti-collapse regularizer [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L1-L14).

This page dissects that protocol at the implementation level: the module map, the three network roles, the position-index abstraction that makes it all work, the exact per-step caller contract, the EMA mechanics, the loss assembly, and the backward-compatibility guarantees baked into the configuration. Masking strategy internals deserve their own treatment and are covered in [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span); the mathematical depth of VICReg and SIGReg is deferred to [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg). A higher-level orientation lives in [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview).

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L1-L14)

## Module Map

The package has a clean dependency direction: `jepa/` owns the orchestration and state (config, forward protocol, EMA teacher, mask sampling) and imports *network primitives* from `models/` and the *training signal* from `objectives/`. The package's `__init__.py` exports a narrow, stable surface — `JEPA`, `JEPAConfig`, `build_jepa`, `EMA`, and `sample_block_masks` — so downstream code never needs to reach into internals [__init__.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/__init__.py#L1-L8).

| File | Role | Key exports |
|---|---|---|
| `src/ssllab/jepa/model.py` | Orchestrator: config, five-step forward, factory | `JEPA`, `JEPAConfig`, `build_jepa` |
| `src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py` | Teacher state + cosine momentum schedule | `EMA` |
| `src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py` | Context/target split samplers | `sample_block_masks`, `sample_span_masks`, `batched` |
| `src/ssllab/models/vit.py` | Modality-agnostic transformer primitives | `PatchEmbed`, `TransformerBlock`, `TinyViT` |
| `src/ssllab/models/encoder.py` | Subset-native encoder (student *and* teacher) | `JEPAEncoder` |
| `src/ssllab/models/predictor.py` | Two-stream target-position predictor | `JEPAPredictor` |
| `src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py` | Loss terms and the combinator | `jepa_loss`, `prediction_loss`, `vicreg_reg`, `sigreg`, `epps_pulley` |

The `vit.py` header makes an important scoping claim: everything there operates on token tensors `(B, N, token_dim)` plus integer position indices — there is *nothing image-specific* in the trunk. That is what lets the same primitives serve MNIST patches, ECG time series, and gene-group tokens without modification [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L1-L7).

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/__init__.py#L1-L8), [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L1-L7)

## Three Roles, Three Networks

`JEPA.__init__` wires up exactly three roles. The **student encoder** is a `JEPAEncoder` that will only ever see the context subset during training. The **predictor** is a `JEPAPredictor` — the only component whose job is to close the gap between what the student saw and what it must output. The **EMA teacher** is not a separate class at all: it is an `EMA` object wrapping a frozen deep copy of the *encoder* [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L77-L104).

Two asymmetries are deliberate and structural. First, the teacher tracks the **encoder only** — the predictor has no teacher copy, because the predictor exists precisely to be the imperfect bridge that training sharpens. Second, the capacities differ: defaults give the encoder depth 4 and the predictor depth 2, the standard JEPA design where a shallow predictor prevents the trivial solution of both sides collapsing toward each other [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L31-L40).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    CFG["JEPAConfig<br/>mask_kind / reg_kind / ema schedule"] --> J["JEPA.forward"]
    A["tokens (B, N, token_dim)"] --> J
    J -->|"encoder(tokens, idx=ctx_idx)"| E["student encoder<br/>JEPAEncoder"]
    E -->|"ctx_embed"| P["predictor<br/>JEPAPredictor"]
    J -->|"ctx_idx, tgt_idx"| P
    J -->|"no grad, idx=None"| T["EMA teacher<br/>frozen copy of encoder"]
    P -->|"pred"| L["jepa_loss"]
    T -->|"gathered target rows"| L
    E -->|"z_reg (optional)"| L
    L --> O["(loss, components dict)"]
```

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L77-L104), [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L1-L6), [predictor.py](/src/ssllab/models/predictor.py#L1-L8)

## Position Indices: One Encoder, Many Views

The linchpin abstraction of the whole module is that **positions travel as integer indices, not as tensor slices**. `TinyViT` stores a learned positional table of shape `(1, n_positions, embed_dim)` and exposes `pos_for(idx)`, which gathers rows by index to produce `(B, N, embed_dim)` [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L51-L94). `JEPAEncoder.forward` then does three things: gather the selected tokens via `torch.gather`, add `pos_for(idx)` so every token keeps its *absolute* position regardless of what was dropped, and run the trunk. Pass `idx=None` and the full set is embedded with positions `0..N-1` — identical code path, no special casing [encoder.py](/src/ssllab/models/encoder.py#L41-L76).

> [!TIP]
> This index-gather design is why the same `JEPAEncoder` class serves both the student (context subset via `idx=ctx_idx`) and the teacher (full set via `idx=None`) with zero branching in the training code. It is also why `embed_pooled` — the downstream latent — is literally just `forward(tokens, idx=None).mean(dim=1)` [encoder.py](/src/ssllab/models/encoder.py#L78-L84).

The predictor reuses the same trick in a two-stream construction. The context stream adds position embeddings to embeddings that already carry content; the target stream builds rows from a learned `mask_token` (trunc-normal, std 0.02) plus `pos_for(tgt_idx)` — so the predictor is told *where* to predict by position, not by copying content. Both streams are concatenated, run through the shallow trunk, and the last T slots are read out as the prediction [predictor.py](/src/ssllab/models/predictor.py#L29-L73).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph CS["context stream"]
        CE["ctx_embed (B, C, D)"] --> PA["+ pos_for(ctx_idx)"]
    end
    subgraph TS["target stream"]
        MT["mask_token (1, 1, D)"] --> EX["expand to (B, T, D)"]
        EX --> PB["+ pos_for(tgt_idx)"]
    end
    PA --> CC["concat -> (B, C+T, D)"]
    PB --> CC
    CC --> TR["shallow TinyViT trunk (depth 2)"]
    TR --> RO["read out last T slots -> pred (B, T, D)"]
```

One implementation footnote worth knowing before you touch this code: the read-out slice ends with `.contiguous()` because the non-contiguous view breaks `smooth_l1_loss` on MPS (Apple silicon); on CPU/CUDA it is a no-op [predictor.py](/src/ssllab/models/predictor.py#L70-L73).

Sources: [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L51-L94), [encoder.py](/src/ssllab/models/encoder.py#L41-L84), [predictor.py](/src/ssllab/models/predictor.py#L29-L73)

## Anatomy of One Training Step

`JEPA.forward` executes the five-step protocol in ~40 lines. Mask selection dispatches on `cfg.mask_kind` — `sample_span_masks` for contiguous spans on ordered sequences, `sample_block_masks` for scattered positions otherwise — then the resulting 1-D index vectors are broadcast across the batch with `batched()` [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L116). The student encodes context, the predictor predicts, the teacher encodes the full set under `torch.no_grad()`, and the target rows are gathered out of the full output with `torch.gather` [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L118-L126). Before calling the loss, `forward` selects what the optional regularizer acts on — the `z_reg` tensor — according to `reg_kind` and `reg_target` (covered below) [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L128-L135).

One simplification to internalize early: the (context, target) split is sampled **once per step and shared across the whole batch**, which keeps variable-length subsets rectangular and the code simple — a deliberate POC-level trade-off documented in the masking module itself. Which split to use, and why, is the subject of [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span) [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L10-L15).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Loop as training loop
    participant J as JEPA
    participant E as student encoder
    participant P as predictor
    participant T as EMA teacher
    participant L as jepa_loss
    Loop->>J: forward(tokens)
    J->>J: sample (ctx, tgt) split
    J->>E: encoder(tokens, idx=ctx_idx)
    E-->>J: ctx_embed (B, C, D)
    J->>P: predictor(ctx_embed, ctx_idx, tgt_idx)
    P-->>J: pred (B, T, D)
    J->>T: teacher(tokens, idx=None) under no_grad
    T-->>J: full (B, N, D)
    J->>J: gather rows at tgt_idx
    J->>L: jepa_loss(pred, target, z_reg, ...)
    L-->>Loop: (loss, components)
    Loop->>Loop: zero_grad / backward / step
    Loop->>J: update_target(step, total)
```

The caller contract is strict and visible in the reference training script: per batch, call `jepa(tokens)` for `(loss, comp)`, then `opt.zero_grad()` → `loss.backward()` → `opt.step()` → `jepa.update_target(step, total_steps)` — in that order, every step. The optimizer is constructed over `jepa.parameters()`; as the next section explains, the teacher's weights are deliberately absent from that collection [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L84-L99).

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L154), [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L84-L99), [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L10-L15)

## The EMA Teacher: Frozen State on a Cosine Schedule

`EMA.__init__` builds the teacher as a `copy.deepcopy` of the student encoder, freezes every parameter with `requires_grad_(False)`, and calls `.eval()` — so it contributes no gradients, no dropout, no state-dict entries [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L17-L24). The momentum follows the standard I-JEPA/BYOL cosine ramp: `m = final − (final − base) · (cos(π·frac) + 1) / 2`, moving from `ema_base = 0.996` early in training toward `ema_final = 1.0` at the end — the teacher stabilizes into a slowly-drifting target as the student converges [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L26-L31).

The update itself blends parameters as `pt.mul_(m).add_(ps.detach(), alpha=1−m)` but copies **buffers wholesale** with `copy_` — parameters interpolate, buffers track the student exactly [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L33-L41).

> [!TIP]
> `EMA` is a plain Python object, not an `nn.Module` — so the teacher is invisible to `jepa.parameters()`, `jepa.state_dict()`, and `jepa.to(device)`. This is why every training script contains the explicit line `jepa.ema.to(device)` after moving the model, and why checkpoints save only student-side weights. Forgetting that line silently leaves the teacher on CPU [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L83), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L94).

Sources: [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L17-L41), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L151-L154)

## Loss Assembly: Prediction Term Plus Optional Anti-Collapse

Every loss in `objectives/jepa_loss.py` is a **plain function returning `(scalar, dict_of_components)`** — the house convention that lets every caller log the decomposition of its loss without wrapper machinery. The prediction term supports three kinds against the detached EMA target [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L1-L23):

| `pred_kind` | Form | Character |
|---|---|---|
| `smooth_l1` *(default)* | Huber loss on `(pred, target)` | robust to outliers; the loss the MPS `.contiguous()` note guards |
| `mse` | mean squared error | plain L2 pull |
| `cosine` | `1 − cos(pred, target)` | scale-free; matches direction only [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L31-L41) |

The anti-collapse side offers two regimes with *different combination semantics* — this is the subtlest part of the combinator:

| `reg_kind` | Combination rule | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `vicreg` | `pred + reg_coef · VICReg` | additive; unchanged since before SIGReg existed, so old runs reproduce exactly |
| `sigreg` | `(1 − reg_coef) · pred + reg_coef · SIGReg` | LeJEPA's convex form; paper default `reg_coef = 0.05` [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L167-L170) |

VICReg itself is two terms: a hinge that pushes each embedding dimension's std up to 1, and a penalty on off-diagonal covariance entries (summed over the matrix, divided by `D`), weighted by `var_coef = 1.0` and `cov_coef = 0.04` by default [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L44-L76). SIGReg instead projects embeddings onto 1024 random unit directions — resampled every call — and scores each 1-D projection with the Epps–Pulley statistic comparing the empirical characteristic function to the standard normal's; the internal factor `N` keeps the statistic's scale tied to the group size rather than shrinking with the batch [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L79-L137).

The final piece is *what* the regularizer acts on — the `z_reg` tensor chosen in `JEPA.forward` by a two-axis decision:

| | `reg_target="tokens"` | `reg_target="pooled"` |
|---|---|---|
| `reg_kind="vicreg"` | `(B·C, D)` — all context rows flattened into one pile (the historical behavior) | `(B, D)` — mean over context tokens |
| `reg_kind="sigreg"` | `(C, B, D)` — transposed, so each token position's batch is one "view", averaged | `(B, D)` [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L128-L149) |

The `sigreg` row exists because SIGReg is distribution-shaped rather than moment-shaped: the statistic carries a factor `N`, so testing each token position's `B` rows as one view keeps the token target on the same scale as the pooled target — a scale-matching decision documented directly in the `sigreg` docstring [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L102-L137). With `reg_coef = 0.0` (the config default), both regimes degenerate to the pure prediction loss — the EMA mechanism alone provides the primary defense against collapse, and the regularizer is explicitly positioned as "cheap insurance and an explicit knob" [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L8-L11).

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L1-L23), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L31-L76), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L102-L137), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L140-L194), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L128-L149)

## Configuration Surface and Backward Compatibility

`JEPAConfig` is a single dataclass covering the entire experiment surface, with `__post_init__` validating the enum-like choices and the span-masking arithmetic constraint `n_target == span_len × n_spans` [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L30-L74). The defaults encode the MNIST baseline: 16 tokens of dim 49 (a 4×4 grid of 7×7 patches) predicting 4 targets [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L31-L62). The `build_jepa(**kwargs)` factory accepts any config field as a keyword, mirroring the repo's other builders [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L162-L167).

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `token_dim` / `n_tokens` | 49 / 16 | 7×7 patches on a 4×4 grid (MNIST baseline) |
| `embed_dim` | 128 | shared latent width across encoder, predictor, loss |
| `enc_depth` / `pred_depth` | 4 / 2 | deliberate capacity asymmetry |
| `n_target` | 4 | target positions per step (random masking) |
| `pred_kind` | `smooth_l1` | prediction loss family |
| `ema_base` / `ema_final` | 0.996 / 1.0 | cosine momentum endpoints |
| `mask_kind` | `random` | or `"span"`; validated against `span_len · n_spans` |
| `reg_kind` / `reg_target` | `vicreg` / `tokens` | anti-collapse regime and acting surface |
| `sigreg_slices` / `sigreg_points` / `sigreg_t_max` | 1024 / 17 / 5.0 | projection count, Epps–Pulley knots, integration range |

Backward compatibility is engineered, not hoped for, through three explicit devices. First, the SIGReg random directions come from a **private generator seeded 0**, created lazily on first use, keyed to the embeddings' device, re-created if the device changes, and deliberately excluded from the state dict — so the default VICReg path consumes exactly the same random numbers as it did before SIGReg existed, and old checkpoints load unchanged [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L95-L104). Second, the VICReg combination form is kept additive-and-unmodified precisely so pre-SIGReg runs reproduce bit-for-bit [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L164-L170). Third, new fields carry comments stating which default preserves old checkpoints — the masking defaults are chosen for exactly this reason [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L45-L48).

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L30-L74), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L95-L104), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L164-L170)

## The `embed` Seam: What the Rest of the Repo Reads

Training produces one artifact the rest of the system cares about: `JEPA.embed(tokens)`, the mean-pooled student latent `z` of shape `(B, embed_dim)`, computed over the full token set with no masking. The encoder docstring names its consumers explicitly — the decoder, the flow prior, and the linear probe — making `embed` the single seam between the JEPA core and the generative and evaluation stacks [encoder.py](/src/ssllab/models/encoder.py#L78-L84), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L156-L159).

The reference script also shows the standard health check run against this seam each epoch: pool a held-out batch through `embed` and feed it to `collapse_report`, tracking **effective rank** and **feature std** — effective rank should stay well above 1, the canonical signal that the EMA-plus-regularizer regime is holding back collapse [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L102-L111).

**Where to go next.** Two natural continuations deepen exactly what this page treated at interface level: [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span) explains the split samplers invoked at the top of `forward`, and [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg) develops the mathematics of the `z_reg` regimes tabulated above. To follow `z` downstream into the generative stack, continue to [Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior); to see how `z` is judged, see [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics).


# Masking Strategies: Random and Span



This page explains the masking subsystem of the JEPA core: the two samplers in `src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py`, the `JEPAConfig` seam that chooses between them, and the behavioral contract the test suite pins down. Masking is where the self-supervised prediction task is *defined* — the hidden positions are what the predictor must reconstruct in latent space — so the choice between scattered targets and contiguous spans is a modeling decision, not an implementation detail. It assumes you have already read [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals) for the encoder/predictor/EMA-teacher assembly; the anti-collapse regularizers that ride on the same forward pass are covered in [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg).

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L1-L15)

## Masking Is the Prediction Task

Every JEPA step partitions the `n_tokens` positions of a sample into a **target** subset (what the predictor must predict) and a **context** subset (everything else, what the student encoder sees). The masking module produces this split as two sorted 1-D index tensors, `ctx_idx` and `tgt_idx`, which the forward pass then threads through the three networks. The v0 design used a random target subset of fixed size — enough to drive learning on the 4×4 MNIST grid — and the span sampler was added specifically for ordered 1D token sequences such as ECG windows.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L1-L10), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L126)

The motivation for a second strategy is statistical rather than cosmetic. On a quasi-periodic signal like an ECG, a *randomly scattered* hidden token can be interpolated from its immediate neighbors — a nearly free task that the encoder can solve with local smoothing instead of learning the rhythm's structure. A *contiguous span* covering a whole heartbeat cannot be interpolated away, because the information needed to reconstruct it is not present in adjacent context. The two strategies thus encode different assumptions about redundancy in the token sequence.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L6-L10)

The diagram below places the mask samplers in context: they are the first thing `JEPA.forward` does on every step, and the resulting index tensors flow into the student, the predictor, and the teacher-side gather.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    CFG["JEPAConfig<br/>mask_kind = 'random' or 'span'"]
    FWD["JEPA.forward(tokens)"]
    R["sample_block_masks<br/>n_target scattered positions"]
    S["sample_span_masks<br/>n_spans contiguous spans of span_len"]
    IDX["ctx_idx, tgt_idx<br/>one split per step, shared across the batch"]
    ENC["Student encoder<br/>encodes context tokens only"]
    PRED["Predictor<br/>predicts embeddings at target positions"]
    TCH["EMA teacher<br/>encodes the full token set, no grad"]
    GATH["gather target rows"]
    LOSS["jepa_loss: prediction + regularizer"]

    CFG --> FWD
    FWD -->|"mask_kind == 'random'"| R
    FWD -->|"mask_kind == 'span'"| S
    R --> IDX
    S --> IDX
    IDX --> ENC
    IDX --> PRED
    IDX --> GATH
    ENC --> PRED
    TCH --> GATH
    PRED --> LOSS
    GATH --> LOSS
```

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L149)

## Random Masking: The Scattered Split

`sample_block_masks` implements the random strategy in four lines: draw a `randperm` of all `n_tokens` positions, take the first `n_target` entries as targets and the remainder as context, and sort both halves so the index vectors are monotonically increasing. Sorting matters downstream — the encoder indexes tokens in their natural order, and position-consistent ordering keeps the batch tensors well-formed. The function validates `1 <= n_target < n_tokens` up front, refusing configurations that would predict everything or nothing.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L22-L47)

There is no contiguity structure of any kind here: targets are distinct single positions scattered uniformly at random. That is precisely the right bias for *order-free* token sets — the 4×4 patch grid of an MNIST image and a cell's gene-group tokens have no adjacency semantics worth preserving, so hiding 4 of 16 patches (or 12 gene tokens in the perturb-seq study) gives a rich prediction task without any spatial reasoning. Both of those studies rely on this default; neither passes `mask_kind` at all.

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L74-L82), [01_pretrain_stage_a.py](/examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py#L67)

| Dimension | `sample_block_masks` (random) | `sample_span_masks` (span) |
|---|---|---|
| Target geometry | `n_target` scattered single positions | `n_spans` contiguous runs of `span_len` tokens |
| Sampling algorithm | one `randperm`, split, sort each half | stars-and-bars placement of span starts |
| Overlap guarantee | targets are distinct positions | spans disjoint; may touch, never overlap |
| Target size | exactly `n_target` | exactly `span_len × n_spans` |
| Context size | `n_tokens − n_target` | `n_tokens − span_len·n_spans` |
| Natural home | order-free token grids (MNIST patches, gene groups) | ordered 1D sequences (ECG windows) |
| Reproducibility | optional `torch.Generator` | optional `torch.Generator` |

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L22-L77)

## Span Masking: Contiguous Holes for Ordered Sequences

`sample_span_masks` hides `n_spans` non-overlapping contiguous blocks of `span_len` tokens each. Spans **may touch** — two adjacent spans read as one longer span — but they never overlap, so the target set always has exactly `span_len × n_spans` positions regardless of where the spans land. This fixed size is what lets the model validate the geometry once in `JEPAConfig` and never worry about variable-length targets during training.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L56-L61)

The placement algorithm is a clean stars-and-bars construction. Let `free = n_tokens − span_len·n_spans` be the slack; the sampler chooses `n_spans` distinct values `u_1 < … < u_k` uniformly from `{0, …, free + n_spans − 1}` and shifts each one past the spans before it: `start_i = u_i + i·(span_len − 1)`. Choosing without replacement via `randperm` guarantees distinctness, hence non-overlap; the shift guarantees ordering; and the uniform draw over the shrunken pool makes every valid placement equally likely.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L62-L77)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["free = n_tokens - span_len*n_spans"] --> B["draw n_spans distinct values u<br/>uniformly from 0..free+n_spans-1<br/>(randperm, no replacement)"]
    B --> C["sort u ascending"]
    D["start_i = u_i + i*(span_len-1)<br/>shift each start past previous spans"] --> E["tgt = union of the span blocks<br/>ctx = complement"]
    C --> D
```

A worked example makes the arithmetic concrete. Take `n_tokens=10`, `span_len=3`, `n_spans=2`: the target budget is 6, so `free=4` and `u` is drawn from `{0,…,5}`. Drawing `u=[1,4]` gives `starts=[1, 4+1·2]=[1,6]` — targets `{1,2,3,6,7,8}`, two separated holes. Drawing `u=[2,3]` instead gives `starts=[2,5]` — spans `[2,4]` and `[5,7]`, which *touch* into a single six-token run. Both outcomes satisfy the invariant the tests check: every maximal run of target positions is a multiple of `span_len`. The endpoints are reachable too — the smallest possible start is 0 and the largest is 7 (span `[7,9]`), which is exactly what the coverage test verifies over 2000 draws.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L68-L77), [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L38-L44)

> [!TIP]
> Masking is resampled at *every* optimizer step but held constant *within* a step — so "every sample sees the same context" is a per-step statement, not a per-run one. Over training, each position appears in targets with equal probability; the coverage test verifies this empirically for span mode, including the sequence endpoints.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L12-L14), [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L38-L44)

## One Split Per Step: The Shared-Across-Batch Design

Masks are sampled per step but **shared across the batch**: one context/target split serves every sample in the step. The `batched` helper broadcasts the 1-D index vectors to `(B, len(idx))` so the encoder and predictor can index rectangular tensors. This is a deliberate simplification — per-sample masks would produce jagged subsets and either padding or gather-based bookkeeping, complexity a small-scale JEPA proof-of-concept does not need. The cost is a mild loss of diversity per step, which the per-step resampling amortizes away over training.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L12-L14), [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L80-L83)

Both samplers accept an optional `torch.Generator`, so the split is fully reproducible from a seed. The ECG pretraining script exploits this: its data iteration is driven by an explicitly seeded generator, keeping an entire run replayable. This matters because the masking draw is part of the experiment's noise — the same discipline the methodology pages cover under seeds and reproducibility.

Sources: [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L26-L27), [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L55-L56), [03_pretrain_jepa.py](/examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L101-L102)

## The Configuration Seam: Dispatch and Validation

The strategy is a plain dataclass field on `JEPAConfig`. Three fields parameterize masking: `mask_kind` (the dispatch key, default `"random"`), plus `span_len` and `n_spans` (active only in span mode). `n_target` is shared by both modes — the number of hidden positions the predictor must reconstruct — and in span mode it is not an independent knob but an arithmetic identity with the other two.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L45-L50)

| Field | Default | Role | Constraint |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mask_kind` | `"random"` | sampler dispatch key | must be `"random"` or `"span"` |
| `n_target` | `4` | hidden positions to predict | `1 <= n_target < n_tokens` |
| `span_len` | `0` | tokens per contiguous span (span mode) | `>= 1`; `span_len·n_spans < n_tokens` |
| `n_spans` | `1` | number of spans (span mode) | `>= 1`; `n_target == span_len × n_spans` |

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L45-L50), [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L42-L43), [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L68-L70)

Validation happens at two layers. `JEPAConfig.__post_init__` rejects unknown `mask_kind` values and refuses span configurations where `n_target != span_len × n_spans` — catching the identity violation at construction time, before any GPU work. The sampler layer then re-checks the geometry (`span_len·n_spans` strictly less than `n_tokens`), guarding against programs that call `sample_span_masks` directly and would otherwise leave no context at all; the tests exercise exactly this failure with `sample_span_masks(8, 4, 2)`.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L64-L74), [masking.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/masking.py#L68-L70), [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L47-L57)

At forward time the dispatch is a single branch: `mask_kind == "span"` routes to `sample_span_masks` with `cfg.span_len` and `cfg.n_spans`, everything else (by validation, only `"random"`) routes to `sample_block_masks` with `cfg.n_target`. Both return the same `(ctx_idx, tgt_idx)` shape contract, so everything downstream — the batched broadcast, the context-encoding, the predictor call, the teacher-side `torch.gather` of target rows — is strategy-agnostic. Note also that the pooled `embed` inference path (`encoder.embed_pooled`) is *not* masked; masking exists only inside the training step, and the downstream generative stack consumes the unmasked latent.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L126), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L157-L159)

## Which Strategy Where

The repository's three pretraining consumers map cleanly onto the two strategies, and the mapping follows modality structure rather than preference. Order-free token grids use random masking with the defaults; the one ordered 1D modality — ECG — uses span masking. The ECG study additionally bridges from *physical time* to token counts via `SignalGeometry`, which specifies geometry in Hz and seconds, derives `span_tokens = span_s / patch_s`, and refuses any ratio that is not a whole number or a span that would leave no context — the same "refuse rather than round" discipline the masking validators apply in index space.

Sources: [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L1-L16), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L70-L76)

| Consumer | Tokens represent | Strategy | Mask arguments |
|---|---|---|---|
| `examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py` | 4×4 MNIST patch grid | random (default) | `n_target=4` |
| `examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py` | gene-group tokens per cell | random (default) | `n_target=12` |
| `examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py` | 250 ms ECG patches | span | `span_len=4` (1 s per span at 250 ms patches), `n_spans` from the study config |

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L53), [01_pretrain_stage_a.py](/examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py#L67), [03_pretrain_jepa.py](/examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L87-L92)

The ECG script's `build_jepa` call shows the seam in its applied form: `n_target` is computed as `geom.span_tokens * cfg["n_spans"]`, satisfying the config identity by construction, and `mask_kind`, `span_len`, `n_spans` are passed straight from the study configuration. The docstring states the training semantics this produces: each step hides `n_spans` contiguous spans of `span_s` seconds — 4 tokens of 250 ms each by default — and predicts the EMA teacher's embeddings there, with collapse diagnostics (feature std, effective rank) logged alongside.

Sources: [03_pretrain_jepa.py](/examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L1-L16), [03_pretrain_jepa.py](/examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L87-L92)

## The Test Contract

`tests/test_span_masks.py` pins the subsystem down with property-based checks rather than snapshot values, so the samplers are free to change implementation as long as the contract holds. The suite covers the full lifecycle: sampler properties, config validation, end-to-end training, and storage compatibility.

Sources: [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L1-L74)

| Property | Test | What it pins down |
|---|---|---|
| Exact partition | `test_span_masks_partition_and_contiguity` | target size exactly `span_len·n_spans`; `ctx ∪ tgt` is exactly `{0…n_tokens−1}` |
| Contiguity structure | same test | every maximal run of target positions is a multiple of `span_len` |
| Positional coverage | `test_span_positions_cover_the_whole_sequence` | 2000 draws hit every position, ends included — no dead zones |
| Geometry rejection | `test_span_masks_reject_impossible_geometry` | a span budget consuming all tokens raises `ValueError` |
| Config consistency | `test_config_validates_span_target_count` | `n_target ≠ span_len·n_spans` and unknown `mask_kind` both raise |
| Training + compatibility | `test_span_jepa_trains_and_old_checkpoints_still_load` | span JEPA trains to a finite loss; pre-span checkpoints load unchanged |

Sources: [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L27-L35), [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L38-L57), [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L59-L74)

> [!TIP]
> The compatibility test is the reason `mask_kind` is a defaulted `str` field rather than an enum: a checkpoint saved before the masking fields existed deserializes cleanly and reports `mask_kind == "random"` — so every historical run remains loadable with the exact masking semantics it was trained under, and unknown values still fail fast at `__post_init__` rather than silently training with a garbage strategy.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L45-L48), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L69-L70), [test_span_masks.py](/tests/test_span_masks.py#L59-L74)

## Where to Go Next

The masking seam sits between two other JEPA-core concerns. Upstream, how the encoder and predictor consume `idx` tensors — positional embeddings, pooling, the EMA update schedule — is the subject of [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals). Downstream, the regularizer term that stabilizes training on the *context* embeddings produced under these masks (VICReg on context-token rows, SIGReg per-position or on the pooled vector) is treated in [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg). To see span masking at work end-to-end — study configuration, seeding, collapse diagnostics, and downstream evaluation — follow [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study); the perturb-seq consumer's full pipeline, including the count decoder that reads the pooled latent, is [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline).

# Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg



Every self-supervised objective that predicts embeddings from embeddings has a degenerate solution, and this page documents how ssl-lab fights it. The repository implements three cooperating defenses: a structural one (the EMA teacher), an explicit regularizer with two interchangeable flavors — **VICReg** (second-moment constraints) and **SIGReg** (sketched isotropic-Gaussian testing, from LeJEPA) — and a pair of runtime diagnostics that detect collapse when prevention fails. The core implementation lives in a single module, `src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py`, is wired into the JEPA forward pass in `src/ssllab/jepa/model.py`, and was stress-tested head-to-head in the perturb-seq study's Round 9.

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L1-L23), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L1-L14), [round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md#L1-L5)

## Why Predicting Embeddings Can Collapse

The JEPA objective invites a cheat: if the encoder maps every input to the same embedding vector, the prediction loss reaches its minimum trivially — predicting a constant from a constant needs no understanding. The repository names two flavors of this failure, because the guards attack each with its own term. **Dimensional collapse** means some latent directions shrink to near-constants and stop varying across inputs, carrying no information; in the limit every dimension collapses and all inputs map to one point. **Informational collapse** is subtler: the dimensions vary but are redundant, several encoding the same thing, so the *effective* number of independent directions falls far below the nominal embedding width.

Sources: [03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md#L7-L14), [collapse.py](/src/ssllab/eval/collapse.py#L1-L10)

## Three Layers of Defense

The architecture layers its defenses so that no single mechanism is load-bearing. The first layer is **structural**: the EMA teacher is a frozen, non-trainable copy of the student whose weights track it by exponential moving average, and because targets come from this slowly-moving teacher rather than the student itself, the target manifold drifts slower than the optimizer can collapse it. The second layer is the **explicit regularizer**, off by default (`reg_coef=0`) and enabled as "cheap insurance and an explicit knob." The third layer is **detection**: every training script logs `feature_std` and `effective_rank` on a held-out batch each epoch, so a collapsing run is visible early rather than discovered at evaluation time.

Sources: [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L1-L7), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L8-L11), [03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md#L30-L34), [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L102-L111)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    X["tokens (B, N, token_dim)"] --> S["Student encoder"]
    X --> T["EMA teacher (no grad, cosine momentum 0.996 → 1.0)"]
    S --> C["ctx_embed (B, C, D)"]
    C --> P["Predictor"] --> PL["Prediction loss (invariance)"]
    T --> TG["target embeddings, detached"] --> PL
    C --> SEL{"reg_kind + reg_target"}
    SEL -->|vicreg| V["Variance hinge + covariance penalty"]
    SEL -->|sigreg / tokens| SV["(C, B, D): one view per token position"]
    SEL -->|sigreg / pooled| SP["(B, D): one cell vector per input"]
    V --> J["jepa_loss"]
    SV --> J
    SP --> J
    C --> D["collapse_report: feature_std + effective_rank"]
```

The diagram makes one design decision visible: the prediction loss and the regularizer read the *same* student context embeddings, but the regularizer's reshaping (`SEL` node) depends on which flavor is active — a detail the section on `reg_target` below develops fully.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L107-L149), [ema.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/ema.py#L17-L41)

## VICReg: Second-Moment Insurance

Full VICReg (Bardes, Ponce & LeCun, 2022) has three terms: invariance, variance, and covariance. This codebase does not re-implement all three, and seeing why is the key to reading the code — **the invariance term is already there**: the JEPA prediction loss pulls the student's predictions toward the EMA teacher, which is exactly the term that learns. So `vicreg_reg` adds only the two anti-collapse statistics on a flattened batch of embeddings `(M, D)`:

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L44-L60), [03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md#L26-L34)

```python
# Variance: hinge each dimension's std up to 1.
std = torch.sqrt(z.var(dim=0) + eps)
var_term = F.relu(1.0 - std).mean()

# Covariance: penalize off-diagonal entries of the covariance matrix.
zc = z - z.mean(dim=0, keepdim=True)
cov = (zc.T @ zc) / max(m - 1, 1)
off_diag = cov - torch.diag(torch.diag(cov))
cov_term = off_diag.pow(2).sum() / d
```

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L61-L76)

The variance term is a **one-sided hinge**: each dimension's standard deviation across the batch is pushed up only if it falls below 1, and left alone above it. A dimension drifting toward a constant gets an increasing gradient that inflates its spread again — exactly the counter-force dimensional collapse needs. The covariance term centers the embeddings, forms the $D \times D$ covariance matrix, ignores the diagonal (the variance term's business), and penalizes the sum of squared off-diagonal entries: dimensions that rise and fall together are one dimension wearing two hats, and decorrelation forces each to carry its own slice of information.

Sources: [03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md#L36-L62)

| Term | Statistic | Failure it blocks | Default weight |
|---|---|---|---|
| Variance | `mean(relu(1 − std_dim))` | Dimensional collapse (dead directions) | `var_coef = 1.0` |
| Covariance | `Σ off-diag(cov)² / d` | Informational collapse (redundant directions) | `cov_coef = 0.04` |

The internal split leans hard on variance over covariance: keeping dimensions alive is the first-order defense, decorrelation the finer correction. The defaults `1.0` / `0.04` mirror the original VICReg paper's constants and are never tuned in any run in the repository.

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L44-L49), [03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md#L64-L72)

## SIGReg: Testing for an Isotropic Gaussian

SIGReg (Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization, from LeJEPA — Balestriero and LeCun, 2025, arXiv 2511.08544) takes a different stance: rather than constraining second moments individually, it asks the *whole* embedding distribution to look like an isotropic standard Gaussian. The mechanism is a two-step sketch. First, project the embeddings `z` onto `n_slices` random unit directions (standard Gaussian vectors scaled to unit length, so uniform on the sphere), reducing each projection to a one-dimensional sample. Second, on each 1-D sample, measure how far the empirical characteristic function is from the standard normal's using the **Epps–Pulley statistic**; the loss is the mean over directions.

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L13-L19), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L102-L137)

The statistic itself is worth reading closely, because every constant in the code is a paper value. For a projected sample $x_1, \dots, x_N$, the empirical characteristic function is $\hat\varphi(t) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_j e^{itx_j}$ and the target's is $\varphi(t) = e^{-t^2/2}$. The statistic is $T = N\int|\hat\varphi(t)-\varphi(t)|^2\, w(t)\,dt$ with Gaussian weight $w(t)=e^{-t^2/2}$, integrated by the trapezoid rule on **17 knots over $[-5, 5]$** — the exact values of the LeJEPA code listing. The implementation vectorizes this as means of `cos(tx)` and `sin(tx)` per knot, squares the shortfall against `φ`, and multiplies by `N` so the statistic keeps the scale of a proper test statistic regardless of batch size:

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L79-L99)

```python
t = torch.linspace(-t_max, t_max, n_points, ...)   # 17 knots on [-5, 5]
phi = torch.exp(-0.5 * t * t)                      # target CF, also the weight
xt = x.unsqueeze(-1) * t                           # (..., N, M, n_points)
err = (torch.cos(xt).mean(-3) - phi).square() + torch.sin(xt).mean(-3).square()
return torch.trapezoid(err * phi, t, dim=-1) * n
```

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L95-L99)

Two behavioral properties follow from the math and are pinned by tests. The statistic is near zero for genuinely Gaussian samples (its expected value under the null is ≈ 1.06, and the test asserts shifted or rescaled samples score over 50× higher), and it decomposes exactly over "views": passing `(V, N, D)` averages the statistic computed per view with the *same* directions, never pooling views into one sample — verified to machine precision against per-view evaluation.

Sources: [test_sigreg.py](/tests/test_sigreg.py#L46-L65), [test_sigreg.py](/tests/test_sigreg.py#L103-L109)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Z["z (N, D) or (V, N, D)"] --> DIR["D × 1024 Gaussian vectors → unit length (own RNG, redrawn each step)"]
    DIR --> PJ["project: z @ a → (..., N, S)"]
    PJ --> EP["per slice: empirical CF vs exp(−t²/2) at 17 knots on [−5, 5], trapezoid, × N"]
    EP --> AVG["mean over slices and views"]
```

## Composition: Two Different Algebraic Forms

The two flavors enter the total loss through **structurally different forms**, and `reg_coef` means something different in each. VICReg uses the additive form `pred + reg_coef · VICReg`, so `reg_coef` is a conventional multiplier on top of the prediction loss. SIGReg uses LeJEPA's **convex form** `(1 − reg_coef) · pred + reg_coef · SIGReg`, with the paper's default `reg_coef = 0.05`. The additive form is preserved for VICReg specifically so that every checkpoint saved before SIGReg existed reproduces exactly — the docstring calls this out as "unchanged from before SIGReg existed, so old runs reproduce exactly."

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L154-L194)

> [!TIP]
> The two composition forms are not interchangeable knobs. A VICReg `reg_coef` of 0.04 scales a secondary term on top of an unscaled prediction loss; a SIGReg coefficient of 0.05 *redistributes* the total weight of the prediction loss itself (0.95 × pred). Comparing coefficients across the two flavors without accounting for this is a category error — and it is why Round 9 paired VICReg at 0.04 against SIGReg at 0.05, each "as its source defines it."

| Property | VICReg | SIGReg |
|---|---|---|
| What it constrains | Second moments only: per-dimension spread + pairwise covariances | Full distribution shape: distance to isotropic N(0, 1) via characteristic functions |
| Composition | Additive: `pred + w·reg` | Convex: `(1−w)·pred + w·reg` (LeJEPA) |
| Default weight | `reg_coef = 0.04` (Stage A) | `reg_coef = 0.05` (paper default) |
| Internal constants | `var_coef 1.0`, `cov_coef 0.04` | 1024 slices, 17 knots, `t_max 5`, redrawn per step |
| Centering | Centers internally (mean-subtracts) | Explicitly *not* centered — matching N(0, I) includes mean zero and unit variance |
| Extra state | None | Dedicated `torch.Generator` seeded 0 (not in state dict) |

Sources: [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L44-L76), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L113-L120), [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L51-L62)

## Where the Regularizer Acts: `tokens` vs `pooled`

`reg_target` decides what the regularizer consumes from the student, and the wiring in `JEPA.forward` is flavor-specific. For **VICReg on tokens**, the raw `ctx_embed` of shape `(B, C, D)` is passed straight through — the regularizer flattens it and treats all `B·C` rows as one batch, "as always" in this codebase. For **SIGReg on tokens**, the tensor is transposed to `(C, B, D)`: each token position's `B` rows form one view, tested separately and averaged. The reason is scale: the Epps–Pulley statistic carries a factor `N`, so the group size sets the statistic's scale, and testing one batch per token position keeps the token target on the same scale as the pooled one. For **SIGReg on pooled**, the context tokens are mean-reduced to `(B, D)` — one cell vector per input, "the student's view of the representation downstream stages read."

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L128-L135), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L113-L131)

> [!TIP]
> The pooled target is not just a convenience — it is the regularizer acting on the exact tensor the downstream stack reads: `embed()` pools the same way, and the count decoder, flow prior, and linear probe all consume that `(B, D)` vector. Regularizing tokens shapes the geometry mid-network; regularizing pooled shapes the representation where it is actually sold.

## Reproducibility Engineering

The SIGReg integration is a case study in adding a random component without perturbing existing experiments. SIGReg's random directions are drawn from a **dedicated `torch.Generator`**, created lazily on the embeddings' device, seeded 0, and advanced every step — explicitly so the default VICReg path draws exactly the same random numbers as before SIGReg existed. The generator is deliberately *not* saved in the state dict, so pre-SIGReg checkpoints load unchanged. Three tests pin this contract: the VICReg default path must produce a bit-identical loss and gradient sum to values recorded before SIGReg was added; a pre-SIGReg config dict missing the new fields must load as `vicreg`/`tokens`; and after a SIGReg step, the next draw from the *global* random stream must be identical to a VICReg step's, proving masks and initialization drew exactly as before.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L95-L104), [test_sigreg.py](/tests/test_sigreg.py#L27-L43), [test_sigreg.py](/tests/test_sigreg.py#L88-L100)

## Configuration Reference

All anti-collapse behavior is configured through `JEPAConfig` fields, surfaced as CLI flags in the Stage A trainer. The validation in `__post_init__` rejects unknown `reg_kind`/`reg_target` values at construction time, so a typo fails before any GPU time is spent.

Sources: [model.py](/src/ssllab/jepa/model.py#L30-L74), [01_pretrain_stage_a.py](/examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py#L68-L76)

| Field | CLI flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `reg_coef` | `--reg-coef` | `0.04` (Stage A) / `0.0` (MNIST) | Overall weight; `0` disables. VICReg: `pred + w·reg`. SIGReg: `(1−w)·pred + w·reg` |
| `reg_kind` | `--reg-kind` | `"vicreg"` | `"vicreg"` or `"sigreg"`; default reproduces every earlier run |
| `reg_target` | `--reg-target` | `"tokens"` | `"tokens"` (context-token embeddings) or `"pooled"` (their mean, one vector per input) |
| `var_coef` | — | `1.0` | Weight on the VICReg spread term |
| `cov_coef` | — | `0.04` | Weight on the VICReg decorrelation term |
| `sigreg_slices` | `--sigreg-slices` | `1024` | Random directions per step, redrawn each call |
| `sigreg_points` | — | `17` | Trapezoid knots for Epps–Pulley |
| `sigreg_t_max` | — | `5.0` | Integration half-width, `[-5, 5]` |

The two trainers expose different defaults by design: the MNIST tutorial leaves `reg_coef` at `0.0` — pure JEPA, leaning entirely on the EMA target — while Stage A defaults to `0.04` because a perturb-seq encoder feeds a generative pipeline and the insurance is priced in.

Sources: [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L54), [01_pretrain_stage_a.py](/examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py#L68-L70), [jepa_loss.py](/src/ssllab/objectives/jepa_loss.py#L8-L11)

## Diagnostics: Detecting What the Regularizer Prevents

The loss *prevents* the two failure modes and the diagnostics *detect* whether prevention worked — they line up almost one to one, which is no accident. `feature_std`, the mean per-dimension standard deviation over a batch, is exactly what the variance term defends: a healthy run logs std near or above 1, meaning the floor is holding (or was never needed). `effective_rank`, the entropy-based soft rank `exp(entropy of normalized singular values)` of the centered embedding covariance, is what the covariance term defends: it falls toward 1 as dimensions become redundant and reaches `D` when the representation spans its full width. Every JEPA training script calls `collapse_report` per epoch and logs both numbers, turning collapse from a post-hoc discovery into a visible trajectory.

Sources: [collapse.py](/src/ssllab/eval/collapse.py#L17-L43), [03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/03c-the-vicreg-collapse-guard.md#L74-L81), [01_train_jepa_mnist.py](/examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py#L102-L111)

## Empirical Head-to-Head: the Round 9 Verdict

The repository does not just ship both regularizers — it ran a pre-committed, three-seed head-to-head and wrote down the result. Round 9 of the perturb-seq study trained nine Stage A encoders (three arms × seeds 0–2): VICReg at 0.04 on tokens (the existing recipe), SIGReg at 0.05 on tokens (`sigreg_tok`), and SIGReg at 0.05 on the pooled cell vector (`sigreg_pool`), identical in every other respect. The pre-committed endpoint was the ceiling analysis's linear readout: a closed-form ridge regression from each encoder's cell vector to expression, scored by Δ-correlation on the twenty held-out perturbation pairs' top-20 genes, judged under max-*t* simultaneous 95% intervals from 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples.

Sources: [round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md#L9-L22), [run_sigreg_pod.sh](/examples/perturbation_response/run_sigreg_pod.sh#L8-L10)

**Verdict: neither SIGReg arm passed.**

| Arm | Linear readout Δr | Contrast vs VICReg | Simultaneous 95% interval | Pairs higher than VICReg | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| VICReg (retrained, 3 seeds) | 0.853 | — | — | — | reference |
| SIGReg on tokens | 0.747 | −0.106 | [−0.282, +0.070] | 0/20 | does not pass |
| SIGReg on pooled | 0.756 | −0.097 | [−0.244, +0.050] | 1/20 | does not pass |

The simultaneous intervals include zero, so by the frozen rule neither arm is formally worse — but descriptively they are lower on essentially every pair, both unadjusted intervals lie wholly below zero, and the secondary endpoints agree: size-aware error rose by ~0.25, interaction recovery fell by ~0.21, and effective rank of the cell vectors collapsed from **216–232 of 256** (VICReg) to **16–22** (SIGReg) — above the hard collapse flag of 10, yet a representation putting >99% of its variance in ~20 directions against VICReg's 21%.

Sources: [round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md#L24-L45)

The post-hoc diagnosis is the most instructive part for an advanced reader: SIGReg's cell vectors failed in a way second-moment diagnostics are shaped to catch but a distributional test is not — SIGReg scores a distribution whose variance concentrates in a few directions *provided each 1-D projection still looks Gaussian along its own axis*, and at the paper's default weight in this regime it evidently tolerated exactly the low-rank geometry this pipeline's readout needs. The round's own scope statement is equally honest: this tested SIGReg-in-place-of-VICReg only — not full LeJEPA, which also removes the EMA teacher and the stop-gradient — at no other weight, with the downstream pipeline deliberately not retrained. The swap was set aside, and the standing recipe remains VICReg at 0.04.

Sources: [round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md](/examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-09-sigreg-regularizer.md#L41-L49)

## Running the Swap Yourself

The entire experiment is reproducible through one script with a drift gate: it first re-scores the existing VICReg encoder and stops before spending GPU hours if the harness has drifted (the gate checks the stored md5s of the encoder and the graded gene list). Arm definitions are a three-line `case` statement mapping directly onto the CLI flags above:

```bash
vicreg)      reg=(--reg-kind vicreg --reg-coef 0.04) ;;
sigreg_tok)  reg=(--reg-kind sigreg --reg-target tokens --reg-coef 0.05) ;;
sigreg_pool) reg=(--reg-kind sigreg --reg-target pooled --reg-coef 0.05) ;;
```

Sources: [run_sigreg_pod.sh](/examples/perturbation_response/run_sigreg_pod.sh#L82-L96)

For a cheap local trial without the pod machinery, the Stage A trainer accepts the flags directly, with a CPU smoke profile documented in its usage block:

```bash
# SIGReg in place of VICReg, on the pooled cell vector, at the paper default weight
python examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py --reg-kind sigreg --reg-target pooled --reg-coef 0.05
# local CPU smoke
python examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py --limit 3000 --epochs 3 --embed-dim 128
```

Sources: [01_pretrain_stage_a.py](/examples/perturbation_response/01_pretrain_stage_a.py#L13-L20), [run_sigreg_pod.sh](/examples/perturbation_response/run_sigreg_pod.sh#L23)

## Where to Go Next

The regularizer is one term in a larger objective. To see where the prediction loss and the EMA schedule come from, continue with [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals), and for how the context/target split that determines *which* embeddings get regularized is chosen, see [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span). The frozen head-to-head protocol and its verdict format are part of the broader measurement discipline covered in [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration) and [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics); the ceiling-analysis readout used as Round 9's endpoint is defined in the perturb-seq study itself, [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline). Finally, the Round 9 outcome — that the encoder's representation quality, not the regularizer choice, dominated downstream behavior — motivates the decoder-side follow-up in [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder).

# Flow-Matching Prior



This page documents the **flow-matching prior** — the component that makes a JEPA encoder *sampleable*. JEPA training shapes latents to be predictive but never distributional: after pretraining you own a cloud of vectors $z \in \mathbb{R}^D$, yet no way to draw a new one. The flow-matching prior closes that gap by fitting a learned velocity field over the **frozen** latent space, so that integrating an ODE from Gaussian noise lands on the data-latent distribution. We cover the rectified-flow formulation, the `VelocityMLP` network, the CFM loss, the training and sampling drivers, and the invariants pinned by tests. Conditional fields and classifier-free guidance (Page 10) and optimal-transport coupling (Page 11) are flagged as forward pointers only.

## Why the Prior Exists: Position in the Generative Stack

The generative stack is a three-stage pipeline: an encoder that *embeds*, a prior that *samples*, and a decoder that *renders*. Each stage is trained against a frozen predecessor, which is what makes the prior cheap — it sees precomputed latents, not images. The package's own docstring calls this the "generative head: a sampleable prior over the JEPA latent", and exports exactly four symbols that constitute the public API: `VelocityMLP`, `linear_interpolant`, `cfm_loss`, and `euler_sample`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Training images"] --> B["Frozen JEPA encoder\n(jepa.embed)"]
    B --> C["Latent cloud Z ∈ R^D\n(N, D)"]
    C --> D["Flow-Matching Prior\nVelocityMLP + CFM loss"]
    N["Gaussian noise\nN(0, I)"] --> E["ODE integration\ndz/dt = v(z, t)"]
    E --> D
    D --> F["Sampled latent z*"]
    F --> G["LatentDecoder\nz* → image"]
```

Read the diagram as a left-to-right training order: the encoder is pretrained first (JEPA Module Internals internals), latents are extracted once, then the prior fits the velocity field, and finally the decoder maps samples back to observable space. Because the encoder is frozen during prior training, the latent distribution is a fixed target — no co-adaptation dynamics enter this stage.

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/ssllab/generative/__init__.py#L1-L6), [04_train_flow_prior.py](/examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py#L1-L16), [02-the-latent-prior.md](/docs/generative_jepa/02-the-latent-prior.md#L1-L71)

## The Rectified-Flow Construction

The implementation uses the **linear interpolant** convention of rectified flow. For a source sample $z_0$ and a data latent $z_1$, the path is a straight line in time $t \in [0,1]$ with a velocity that is *constant along the path*:

$$z_t = (1-t)\,z_0 + t\,z_1, \qquad u_t = z_1 - z_0$$

This is implemented literally in `linear_interpolant`, which broadcasts $t$ against the latent dimension and returns the pair $(z_t, u_t)$. The training objective is the **conditional flow-matching (CFM) MSE loss**: sample $t \sim U[0,1]$, draw $z_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ (when no explicit source is passed), and regress the network's predicted velocity against the displacement target:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CFM}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\big\lVert v_\theta(z_t, t) - u_t \big\rVert^2$$

| Mathematical object | Code artifact | Contract |
|---|---|---|
| Path $z_t = (1-t) z_0 + t z_1$ | `linear_interpolant` | returns `(z_t, u_t)` for batched `t` |
| Target velocity $u_t = z_1 - z_0$ | `linear_interpolant` | constant in $t$; shape `(B, D)` |
| Loss $\lVert v_\theta(z_t,t) - u_t \rVert^2$ | `cfm_loss` | draws `z0 = randn_like(z1)` when `z0=None`; `t = rand(B)` |
| ODE $\frac{dz}{dt} = v_\theta(z,t)$ | `euler_sample` | fixed-step Euler, `z ← z + dt·v`, from $t=0$ to $t=1$ |

> [!TIP]
> The per-pair target $u_t$ is almost never the "right" velocity at $z_t$ — yet the regressed field converges to $\mathbb{E}[z_1 - z_0 \mid z_t]$, the *marginal* velocity whose ODE transports the full noise marginal onto the data marginal. This is the quiet miracle of flow matching: regressing conditional velocities yields a globally correct field. The module docstring states this identification explicitly for both noise and data bases.

A useful invariant for reasoning about the sampler: at $t=0$ the interpolant equals $z_0$ exactly and at $t=1$ it equals $z_1$ exactly — so the ODE genuinely starts at the source and ends in the data cloud, which the test suite pins as hard assertions. Because rectified-flow paths are nearly straight, a few dozen Euler steps suffice; the starter default is 50 steps, and the sampling example defaults to 100.

Sources: [flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L1-L24), [flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L121-L128), [flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L148-L175), [test_flow_transport.py](/tests/test_flow_transport.py#L9-L14)

## The Velocity Network: `VelocityMLP`

The field $v_\theta(z, t)$ is a small MLP whose behavior depends on time through a **sinusoidal embedding + FiLM** composition. Time scalars in $[0,1]$ are first mapped to `(B, time_dim)` sinusoidal features by `sinusoidal_time_embedding` (frequencies log-spaced down to $10^{-4}$, sin/cos concatenated, odd dims zero-padded). A two-layer `time_mlp` converts the embedding into per-feature `(scale, shift)` pairs that modulate the projected latent: `h = h * (1 + scale) + shift`. The trunk is a stack of residual blocks — each block is `Linear → SiLU → Linear` added back onto `h` — followed by a linear output projection back to `data_dim`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Z["z_t (B, D)"] --> P["in_proj: Linear(D, hidden)"]
    T["t (B,)"] --> S["sinusoidal_time_embedding → (B, 64)"]
    S --> TM["time_mlp → chunk(2)"]
    TM --> FS["FiLM scale, shift"]
    P --> M["h * (1 + scale) + shift"]
    FS --> M
    M --> B1["Residual block 1\nLinear→SiLU→Linear, + h"]
    B1 --> B2["… n_layers blocks …"]
    B2 --> O["out_proj: Linear(hidden, D)"]
    O --> V["v(z_t, t) (B, D)"]
```

The forward signature `forward(z_t, t, c=None)` carries the module's extensibility seam: the constructor rejects a mismatch between `cond_dim` and whether a condition is supplied, so an unconditional field (`cond_dim=0`) *must* be called with `c=None` and vice versa. The conditional branch (`cond_dim > 0`) adds a second FiLM from a condition vector and a learned `null_cond` token for classifier-free guidance — that machinery is documented in [Conditional Flow and Classifier-Free Guidance](10-conditional-flow-and-classifier-free-guidance); for the unconditional prior discussed here it remains entirely inert.

| Constructor parameter | Default | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `data_dim` | required | latent dimension $D$ (set to `jepa.cfg.embed_dim` in training) |
| `hidden` | `256` | width of trunk and FiLM layers |
| `n_layers` | `4` | number of residual blocks |
| `time_dim` | `64` | sinusoidal time-embedding width |
| `cond_dim` | `0` | `0` = unconditional prior; `> 0` = conditional field (Page 10) |

Sources: [flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L48-L58), [flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L61-L109), [flow.py](/src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L94-L99)

## Training the Prior: `04_train_flow_prior.py`

The training driver is deliberately thin — roughly forty lines of orchestration around the four API functions — because all difficulty was front-loaded into freezing the encoder and extracting latents. The procedure is: load the pretrained encoder from the experiment directory, run `extract_latents` once over the MNIST training loader to obtain the latent matrix `Z (N, D)`, standardize per-dimension, and fit the field with AdamW against `cfm_loss`.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A["load_jepa(encoder.pt)"] --> B["extract_latents(jepa.embed, loader)"]
    B --> C["Z (N, D), encoder never updated"]
    C --> D["Standardize: mean, std per dim\nZn = (Z - mean) / std"]
    D --> E["TensorDataset(Zn) + DataLoader\nshuffle, drop_last"]
    E --> F["per batch: cfm_loss(prior, z1)"]
    F --> G["AdamW step, epochs × batches"]
    G --> H["save prior.pt\n{state, dim, hidden, n_layers, mean, std}"]
```

> [!TIP]
> The standardization statistics are *part of the model contract*, not incidental preprocessing. `prior.pt` serializes `mean` and `std` alongside the weights precisely because sampling must run the ODE in standardized space and invert afterward ($z^* = \sigma \hat z^* + \mu$). If you retrain the prior or swap encoders, the stale stats silently corrupt every sample — always consume stats from the same checkpoint that produced the weights.

Standardization matches the flow target's geometry to the noise source's geometry: the data cloud is centered at the origin with unit per-dimension spread, the same shape as $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$, which is why a plain MLP with no output scaling succeeds at all.

| CLI flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--experiment` | `jepa_mnist` | experiment name; reads `output/<name>/checkpoints/encoder.pt` |
| `--encoder` | `None` | override the encoder checkpoint path |
| `--epochs` | `20` | passes over the latent set |
| `--batch-size` | `256` | latent batch size |
| `--lr` | `1e-3` | AdamW learning rate |
| `--hidden` / `--n-layers` | `256` / `4` | `VelocityMLP` capacity |
| `--limit` | `None` | cap train latents for smoke runs |
| `--seed` | `42` | reproducibility |

Sources: [04_train_flow_prior.py](/examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py#L60-L100), [04_train_flow_prior.py](/examples/generative_jepa/04_train_flow_prior.py#L43-L57), [extract.py](/src/ssllab/extract.py#L13-L40), [02-the-latent-prior.md](/docs/generative_jepa/02-the-latent-prior.md#L55-L71)

## Sampling and Decoding: `05_sample_and_decode.py`

Generation is the reverse composition of training.
