It spans three artifacts that must be read together — the mathematical note `docs/action_operator/03-the-algebra-of-composition.md`, the implementation `src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py` with its property suite `tests/test_operator_algebra.py`, and the epistasis measurement battery in `examples/perturbation_response/` (scripts 15–18 and their comparisons). The prerequisite is [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators); the general, policy-driven context operator from that page remains relevant here only as a contrast case.

The core claim this page documents is a single sentence with a precise formal content: **a pair of interventions is epistatic if and only if their single-intervention generators fail to commute**, and the strength of the interaction is governed by ‖[M_A, M_B]‖. Everything below — the symmetric composition product, the property tests, the empirical-epistasis target, and the correlation endpoint — exists to make that sentence testable rather than rhetorical.

## Why an Algebra Was Needed: The Additive-Composition Failure

The predecessor design (`ssllab.generative.operator_perturb`, round 3 of the perturbation study) applied `exp` exactly once, to a single generator built from an additive gene-set embedding — the same object the NB-VAE baseline consumes. The module docstring is blunt about the consequence: that model "tied the flow" because it composed two genes in the *embedding*, never in the *operator algebra*; the matrix exponential was a reparameterization, not a capability. A model with one shared generator cannot express an order-dependent gap between "A then B" and "B then A," and therefore has no internal quantity that could track interaction even in principle.

Sources: [operator_algebra.py](src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py#L1-L11), [16_train_operator_algebra.py](examples/perturbation_response/16_train_operator_algebra.py#L1-L8)

The algebra variant removes the shared bottleneck. Each single gene `g` owns its own dense generator `M_g` (a `D × D` matrix), and a combination composes **in the group** via the symmetric (Strang) product:

$$A_{A+B} = \exp(M_A/2)\,\exp(M_B)\,\exp(M_A/2)$$

The generators are the *only* parameters — there is no policy network and no basis. A held-out combination composes from single-gene generators the model actually trained, with the interaction supplied by their non-commutativity rather than by a black-box map on an embedding. That is precisely the property that makes combination generalization structural instead of statistical.

Sources: [operator_algebra.py](src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py#L43-L60)

## The Bracket Is the Epistasis: The Formal Core

The theory note builds the claim in four steps, each of which maps onto a test or an eval script. Composition of operators is matrix multiplication (written right-to-left: "A first, then B" is `BA`). The **commutator** `[A, B] = AB − BA` measures the gap between the two orderings, and `[A, B] = 0` exactly when order is irrelevant. The exponential-map theorem then gives the bridge to additivity: when `[A,B] = 0`, the binomial theorem collects `exp(A)exp(B)` into `exp(A+B)`, so composition collapses to generator addition — a no-interaction model. The Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula shows what remains when they do not commute: `log(exp A exp B) = A + B + ½[A,B] + ⋯`, an infinite correction series in which *every* term is a nested commutator, with `½[A,B]` the leading departure from additivity.

Sources: [03-the-algebra-of-composition.md](docs/action_operator/03-the-algebra-of-composition.md#L28-L88), [03-the-algebra-of-composition.md](docs/action_operator/03-the-algebra-of-composition.md#L92-L118)

One structural fact from §5 of the note decides which objects are allowed in this algebra at all: Lie algebras are closed under the bracket but **not** under plain multiplication (the product of two skew-symmetric rotation generators is not skew), so BCH can contain only brackets — and the **anticommutator** `{A,B} = AB + BA`, the swap-even half of the product, never appears in it. The note's comparison table is worth internalizing because the epistasis battery later leans on it: the commutator is swap-odd, vanishes when its arguments commute, and measures *order and direction*; the anticommutator is swap-even, equals `2A²` for a self-pair (so it is zero exactly when nothing interesting is happening), and measures *magnitude and overlap* — an interference term.

Sources: [03-the-algebra-of-composition.md](docs/action_operator/03-the-algebra-of-composition.md#L120-L190)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    MA["M_A — generator of gene A"] -->|exp| AA["A_A = exp(M_A)<br/>single-gene operator"]
    MB["M_B — generator of gene B"] -->|exp| AB["A_B = exp(M_B)"]
    MA -.->|"[M_A, M_B] = M_A M_B − M_B M_A"| BR["Lie bracket"]
    MB -.-> BR
    BR -->|"= 0"| ADD["A_{A+B} = exp(M_A + M_B)<br/>additive — no epistasis"]
    BR -->|"≠ 0"| BCH["BCH correction ½[M_A, M_B] + ⋯<br/>non-additive — epistasis"]
    AA --> SYM["A_{A+B} = exp(M_A/2) exp(M_B) exp(M_A/2)<br/>symmetric product"]
    AB --> SYM
    SYM -->|"commuting limit"| ADD
    SYM -->|"generic case"| BCH
    BCH --> CORR["‖[M_A, M_B]‖ correlates with<br/>measured genetic interaction"]
```

A subtlety that shapes the entire experimental design: the Norman et al. perturbations are delivered with **both guides simultaneously**, so the observable carries no order. The bracket's leading term `½[M_A, M_B]` is swap-odd, hence invisible to a simultaneous experiment as a sign — only its magnitude survives. The symmetric product is chosen deliberately because it cancels the odd first-order term exactly, leaving an even double-commutator contribution whose size scales with ‖[M_A, M_B]‖. Ordered composition — the odd part, path-dependence of a *plan* — becomes observable only in a temporal world model, which is the subject of [Operator World Models Series](15-operator-world-models-series).

Sources: [operator_algebra.py](src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py#L14-L26), [03-the-algebra-of-composition.md](docs/action_operator/03-the-algebra-of-composition.md#L170-L190)

> [!TIP]
> The symmetric Strang split (`exp(M_A/2) exp(M_B) exp(M_A/2)`) is not a numerical-stability trick here — it is a **symmetry-matching device**. Halving the first generator makes the product invariant under `A ↔ B` up to the even double-commutator, so the estimator cannot hallucinate an order-sign from order-free data.

## Implementation Anatomy: `NamedGeneratorOperator`

The module condenses the algebra into one class. `build_pert_gene_matrix` supplies a multi-hot `(n_perts, n_genes)` matrix whose rows mark the genes each perturbation targets; because the gene vocabulary is sorted, ascending column order is the **canonical ordering** the symmetric product reads against — composition is deterministic regardless of how a pair name was written (`"A+B"` vs `"B+A"` yield identical operators). Generators are zero-initialized so every operator starts at the identity: the perturbation begins by doing nothing, and the least-action penalty keeps departures small unless data demand them.

Sources: [operator_algebra.py](src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py#L43-L73)

| Method | Returns | Role in the thesis |
|---|---|---|
| `target_genes(pert_id)` | generator indices, ascending | canonical gene order for deterministic composition |
| `operator(pert_id)` | `A_p`, `(D, D)` | control → `I`; single → `exp(M_g)`; pair → symmetric Strang product; **raises** for >2 genes rather than silently mis-composing |
| `pushforward(z, pert_id)` | `(n, D)` cloud | transports control latents; one operator shared by every cell (intervention-level, not cell-level) |
| `bracket(g_a, g_b)` | `[M_A, M_B]`, `(D, D)` | the Lie bracket itself |
| `bracket_norm(pert_id)` | `‖[M_A, M_B]‖_F` scalar | **model-side quantity** of the round's primary endpoint; 0 for singles/control |
| `action_energy(pert_id)` | scalar | Frobenius penalty summed over the genes a perturbation targets — a pair pays for *both* genes |
| `operator_matrix(pert_id)` | `A_p` under `no_grad` | inspection: eigenvalues, departure from identity |

Sources: [operator_algebra.py](src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py#L75-L131)

Two design contrasts are worth fixing precisely. Against the NB-VAE baseline: it has no generators, hence no bracket, hence *no version of the epistasis claim to make* — it can fit pair interactions only as free parameters on an additive embedding, which is exactly what the held-out split is designed to expose. Against the general `ContextConditionedOperator` of the previous page: that class exposes a `compose` static method whose docstring already warns that `A_second @ A_first` ordering matters ("BCH / [M1, M2]"), but its coefficients are emitted by a policy network per input; here the coefficients *are* the gene multi-hot vector, which is what turns the algebra from a modeling choice into an identification constraint.

Sources: [operator_algebra.py](src/ssllab/generative/operator_algebra.py#L14-L19), [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L313-L317), [condition.py](src/ssllab/generative/condition.py#L1-L1)

## The Executable Thesis: Property Tests as Proof Obligations

`tests/test_operator_algebra.py` is written as a pinned contract — its own docstring says each test exists so "a refactor cannot silently break the thesis." The suite demonstrates the whole argument on synthetic generators: **commuting generators** are constructed as scalar multiples of one matrix (`M_B = 2.3·M_A`, forcing `[M_A, M_B] ≈ 0`), and the test asserts the composed pair operator collapses to `exp(M_A + M_B)`; **generic non-commuting** generators are shown to depart from additivity with bracket norm above threshold. These are not incidental unit tests — they are the theorem §3 of the composition note, instantiated in code.

Sources: [test_operator_algebra.py](tests/test_operator_algebra.py#L1-L13), [test_operator_algebra.py](tests/test_operator_algebra.py#L47-L71)

| Test | Property pinned | Why it is load-bearing |
|---|---|---|
| `test_zero_init_is_identity_everywhere` | every `A_p = I` at init, all seven perturbation names | near-identity prior is structural, not a penalty artifact |
| `test_single_gene_is_matrix_exp` | `A_A = exp(M_A)` exactly | the exponential is the lift from algebra to group |
| `test_commuting_generators_compose_additively` | bracket ≈ 0 ⇒ `A_{A+B} = exp(M_A+M_B)` | commuting ⇒ no epistasis (the ⇐ direction of the theorem) |
| `test_noncommuting_generators_are_not_additive` | bracket > 10⁻³ ⇒ composition departs from additive | non-commutativity *is* the departure from additivity |
| `test_bracket_norm_matches_and_is_antisymmetric` | `[A,B] = −[B,A]`; singles have zero bracket | the bracket's symmetry contract used by the eval scripts |
| `test_heldout_pair_composes_from_trained_singles` | unseen `A+C` equals `exp(M_A/2)exp(M_C)exp(M_A/2)` | **the generalization property**: no combo-specific parameter exists anywhere |
| `test_control_and_action_energy` | control energy 0; a pair pays for both genes | the least-action prior is per-gene, not per-perturbation |

Sources: [test_operator_algebra.py](tests/test_operator_algebra.py#L33-L104)

The held-out test deserves emphasis because it is the architectural heart of the round: setting the two single-gene generators *determines* the held-out combo's operator, since `A_{A+C}` is a fixed algebraic function of `M_A` and `M_C`. There is no mechanism by which the model could have memorized the pair — the parameter count for combinations is literally zero.

Sources: [test_operator_algebra.py](tests/test_operator_algebra.py#L82-L91)

## The Data-Side Target: Empirical Epistasis and Its Two Flavors

A model-side quantity is only meaningful against a data-side quantity that actually **varies**. `15_empirical_epistasis.py` computes the standard model-free definition of genetic interaction entirely from the cached count matrix — no model involved: `Δ(X)` is a perturbation's cell-mean minus the control mean; the additive prediction is `Δ(A) + Δ(B)`; the residual `Δ(A+B) − additive` is the epistasis; `GI = ‖residual‖` on the combo's top-DE genes. The combo's cells come from the held-out split; the two singles come from the training side. The script's stated verdict condition is a viability check performed *before* any model is trained: if `rel_GI` does not span a real range across the twenty held-out pairs, the bracket would have nothing to predict and the round "would be dead before a line of the model is written."

Sources: [15_empirical_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/15_empirical_epistasis.py#L1-L56)

`GI` alone is unsigned — a norm can say the additive model is wrong but never whether the pair did *more* or *less* than the sum of its singles, which is the synergy/buffering distinction a geneticist actually cares about. The script therefore fits a least-squares scale `λ` stretching the additive prediction onto the truth and splits the residual orthogonally: `true = λ·add + perp` with `perp ⊥ add`, giving `GI² = (λ−1)²‖add‖² + ‖perp‖²`. The magnitude term (`λ > 1` super-additive synergy, `λ < 1` sub-additive buffering, with a `--scale-tol` of 0.1) is what a *symmetric, quadratic* object like an anticommutator would predict; the direction term `‖perp‖` is the commutator's natural target. Reporting only `GI` conflates the two flavors the algebra treats differently.

Sources: [15_empirical_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/15_empirical_epistasis.py#L128-L170)

| Metric | Definition | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| `GI` | `‖Δ(A+B) − (Δ(A)+Δ(B))‖` on top-DE genes | absolute (unsigned) epistasis |
| `rel_GI` | `GI / ‖Δ(A+B)‖` | epistasis as a fraction of the effect; the correlation target |
| `scale (λ)` | least-squares fit of `add` onto `true` | >1 synergy, <1 buffering, ≈1 magnitude-ok |
| `GI_mag` | `|λ−1|·‖add‖` | right shape, wrong size — anticommutator-flavored |
| `GI_dir` | `‖perp‖` | genes moved the additive model did not — commutator-flavored |
| `add_r` / `add_cos` | Pearson / cosine of `true` vs `add` | `1.0` = perfectly additive |
| `perp_share` | `GI_dir² / GI²` | how much of the interaction is directional |

Sources: [15_empirical_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/15_empirical_epistasis.py#L56-L100)

## The Epistasis Test Battery: Scripts, Gates, and Endpoints

The round is orchestrated as a four-stage battery plus comparisons, each stage emitting a report into the experiment directory. The dependency structure is strict: stage 15 is a viability precondition, stage 16 produces the only artifact (a checkpoint of generators), stage 17 joins the two sides per pair, and stage 18 supplies the reference a learned score must beat.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Stage A encoder<br/>(frozen, pretrained)"] --> B
    subgraph B["16_train_operator_algebra"]
        B1["precompute + standardize latents"] --> B2["sample perturbation<br/>push control cloud through<br/>composed operator"]
        B2 --> B3["energy distance<br/>+ action energy penalty"]
        B3 --> B4["acceptance gate:<br/>median ‖M_g‖_F ≤ 3.0"]
    end
    B --> C["operator_algebra.pt"]
    D["15_empirical_epistasis<br/>(data-side rel_GI spread)"] -. viability check .-> B
    C --> E["17_eval_bracket_epistasis<br/>Spearman(bracket_norm, rel_GI)<br/>+ permutation p"]
    E --> F["18_eval_additive_baseline<br/>same effect-size metric"]
    E --> G["19_score_interaction<br/>20_compare_composition"]
```

Sources: [16_train_operator_algebra.py](examples/perturbation_response/16_train_operator_algebra.py#L17-L75), [15_empirical_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/15_empirical_epistasis.py#L58-L95)

Training (stage 16) is identical in spirit to round 3 — cells are unpaired, so each step pushes a control cloud through a perturbation's operator and matches the perturbed marginal with an energy distance — but one gradient property is new and decisive: an observed *combination* now flows through the **composed** operator, so its gradient reaches **both** single-gene generators. A single's generator is therefore pinned not only by its own cells but by every combination it participates in, which is how real pair data shapes the bracket. Held-out combinations are never trained; they are composed at eval time.

Sources: [16_train_operator_algebra.py](examples/perturbation_response/16_train_operator_algebra.py#L1-L16), [16_train_operator_algebra.py](examples/perturbation_response/16_train_operator_algebra.py#L128-L130)

The endpoint (stage 17) is a rank correlation with a significance discipline: per pair it reads `bracket = ‖[M_A, M_B]‖_F` off the trained generators and joins it to the model-free `rel_GI` from the cache, reporting **two** Spearman correlations because they answer different questions. In-sample (training combos): did the mechanism engage at all — a null here is fatal, since those combos shaped the generators directly. Out-of-sample (held-out combos): the actual claim, and one that "needs no comparison to the NB-VAE" — a positive, permutation-significant correlation (one-sided, 10,000 resamples via the same permutation machinery family documented in [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference)) is the round's prize.

Sources: [17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py#L1-L33), [17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py#L71-L89)

Stage 18 scores the **additive model** `Δ(A+B) = Δ(A) + Δ(B)` as a *competitor*, not a diagnostic — a deliberate division of labor from stage 15, which builds the same additive prediction only to measure how far each pair departs from it. The additive baseline needs no training, is deterministic (no seeds, combo split only, since that is the only split where the question makes sense: all singles on the training side, twenty held-out combos scored), and is graded through the shared `run_effect_size_eval` seam so its number sits directly beside the flow's and the NB-VAE's in the cross-arm comparison. An exploratory block (single alone; one average effect for every pair; two random singles added) reports, without verdicts, how much of the score depends on knowing the pair at all.

Sources: [18_eval_additive_baseline.py](examples/perturbation_response/18_eval_additive_baseline.py#L1-L31), [18_eval_additive_baseline.py](examples/perturbation_response/18_eval_additive_baseline.py#L66-L95)

| Script | Question answered | Output artifact |
|---|---|---|
| `15_empirical_epistasis.py` | does `rel_GI` vary enough across pairs for the thesis to be testable? | `reports/epistasis.json` |
| `16_train_operator_algebra.py` | can per-gene generators fit unpaired clouds under the least-action prior? | `checkpoints/operator_algebra.pt` |
| `17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py` | does `‖[M_A,M_B]‖` predict measured epistasis, in and out of sample? | `reports/bracket_epistasis.json` |
| `18_eval_additive_baseline.py` | what must a learned score beat? | `reports/effect_size_additive.json` |

Sources: [16_train_operator_algebra.py](examples/perturbation_response/16_train_operator_algebra.py#L53-L75), [17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py#L56-L68)

> [!TIP]
> The training script carries an **acceptance gate** most readers will scroll past: `--max-generator-norm 3.0`. If the median generator norm exceeds it, the near-identity prior has failed — the bracket degenerates into a magnitude proxy and, by the run's own pre-registered standard, the result *cannot test the claim*. This is epistasis testing with the same discipline as the hypothesis ledgers in [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration): the run is disqualified before its numbers can mislead.

## Failure Modes This Design Pre-Commits To

The battery is structured around three specific ways the thesis can die, each detectable at a defined stage rather than after publication. First, **no spread**: if every held-out pair is near-additive, stage 15 reports a tight `rel_GI` cluster and the round stops — a cheap death by design. Second, **prior failure**: if the action penalty cannot hold generators near identity, stage 16's gate fires and the bracket correlation, even if positive, is uninterpretable. Third, **engagement without generalization**: a strong in-sample correlation with a null out-of-sample one means the bracket learned interaction only where it was trained on it — the exact distinction the two-correlation report in stage 17 makes unavoidable. These map directly onto the methodology vocabulary of [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series) and the ceiling analysis of [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics).

Sources: [15_empirical_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/15_empirical_epistasis.py#L44-L56), [16_train_operator_algebra.py](examples/perturbation_response/16_train_operator_algebra.py#L66-L71), [17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py](examples/perturbation_response/17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py#L14-L23)

## Where This Goes Next

Within the catalog, this page sits mid-arc in the Action Operators section. The natural progression: backward to [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators) for the basis/policy machinery this module deliberately strips away; forward to [Operator World Models Series](15-operator-world-models-series), where ordered composition — the swap-odd bracket half that simultaneous perturbation experiments structurally cannot see — becomes observable in temporal rollouts; and sideways to [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline) for the Stage-A/Stage-B context in which this battery runs, and [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder) for what happens when the frozen-encoder assumption behind stage 16 is relaxed.


# Operator World Models Series



This page is the entry point to the repository's capstone tutorial corpus: `docs/operator_world_models/`, a five-part conceptual sequence plus a notation reference and a fully worked example. The series fuses the repo's two foundation threads — the Time-Series JEPA tutorial (a predictor that says *what comes next* in latent space) and the Action Operators foundation (an operator that transforms a latent under a chosen action) — into a single object: **a world model you can act on**. Its runnable counterpart is one module, `src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py`, whose entire forward pass is `f_θ(c_t)(z) = exp(M_θ) z + b_θ`. In the catalog this sits directly after [Operator Algebra and Epistasis Tests](14-operator-algebra-and-epistasis-tests) and before the applied studies.

Sources: [index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L1-L7), [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L1-L33)

## Position in the Corpus

The series assumes two prerequisites and builds a third thing from them. From the Time-Series JEPA series it takes the temporal predictor — encode recent history into a latent `z_t = E_ξ(x_≤t)`, predict the next latent, train against a slow EMA target encoder in latent space. From the Action Operators foundation it takes the operator formalism — an action read as a *function that transforms state*, configured by parameters `θ`. Neither foundation is a world model alone; the series' equation in words is: **world model = Time-Series JEPA's rollout plus the action operator's conditioning**. Within the catalog, the operator foundations are covered by [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators), and the general architecture context by [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview).

Sources: [index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L9-L14), [00-what-is-a-world-model.md](docs/operator_world_models/00-what-is-a-world-model.md#L47-L57)

## The Arc in Three Moves

The series tells one story in three movements, from passive prediction to actionable dynamics. First, **JEPA watches**: hide part of the data, predict its embedding from context — passive, label-free. Second, **JEPA as a world model**: reinterpret "predict the masked region" as "predict the next timestep," so the predictor becomes a dynamics operator on a latent trajectory `z_t → z_{t+1}`, and the prediction-vs-reality gap becomes a **surprise** signal. Third, **JEPA you can act on**: the vanilla temporal query knows only *when* (how far ahead), never *what acted*; conditioning the operator on the intervention `c_t` yields `f_θ(c_t)`, which unlocks counterfactual rollout and composition.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph FOUND["Foundations (prerequisites)"]
        TS["Time-Series JEPA<br/>predictor g_φ(z_t, q) — rollout only"]
        AO["Action Operators<br/>f_θ(z) = exp(M)z + b — conditioning only"]
    end
    subgraph SERIES["Operator World Models series"]
        P0["Part 0 — map vs. world model:<br/>the two defining properties"]
        P1["Part 1 — state vs. latent operator:<br/>the commuting square"]
        P2["Part 2 — predictor = latent operator:<br/>rollout as exp(kM)"]
        P3["Part 3 — the single edit:<br/>f_θ(c_t), counterfactuals, surprise"]
        P4["Part 4 — four generator bases:<br/>one swappable code path"]
        WE["Worked example — diabetes:<br/>every symbol earned"]
    end
    TS --> P0
    AO --> P0
    P0 --> P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> WE
```

Sources: [index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L9-L14), [00-what-is-a-world-model.md](docs/operator_world_models/00-what-is-a-world-model.md#L27-L57)

## Part 0 — What Is a World Model?

Part 0 draws the distinction that does all the work: a representation learner gives you a **map** (where things are in latent space); a world model adds **how the state evolves**. Two properties separate a world model from an ordinary next-step predictor. **Rollout** — apply the one-step map, feed its output back in, iterate; the model imagines trajectories many steps ahead without living through them. **Action-conditioning** — vary the action and get a different trajectory for each, which is what makes "what if I did A?" computable. Part 0 also scopes the term: an action operator on a JEPA latent spans non-temporal arenas too (I-JEPA spatial attention, static in-silico perturbations), but the series builds on the temporal arena because that is where every piece is at its clearest.

| foundation | supplies | missing |
|---|---|---|
| Time-Series JEPA | rollout (the temporal predictor, iterated) | action-conditioning — its query says only *when* |
| Action operator | action-conditioning (trajectories per action) | — (it is the missing property) |

Sources: [00-what-is-a-world-model.md](docs/operator_world_models/00-what-is-a-world-model.md#L11-L57), [00-what-is-a-world-model.md](docs/operator_world_models/00-what-is-a-world-model.md#L59-L94)

## Part 1 — State Operators and Latent Operators

Part 1 is the keystone: one transformation, two spaces. The **state operator** `Ô_θ` acts on the real system state `s` (a person's physiology, a protein's coordinates) — the physically meaningful object, usually inaccessible and nonlinear. The **latent operator** `f_θ` acts on the encoded latent `z = E(s)` — the object you actually compute with. They are tied by the **commuting square**, `E(Ô_θ(s)) = f_θ(E(s))`, which in practice is enforced as the **equivariance loss** `‖E(Ô_θ(s)) − f_θ(E(s))‖²` — exactly the shape of JEPA's own loss, which is why a JEPA encoder can double as the bridge. The Koopman framing legitimizes the parameterization `f_θ(z) = exp(M_θ) z + b_θ`: **the encoder's job is not to compress but to find coordinates in which the physical operator becomes a clean linear latent operator**. JEPA's payoff is that you never instantiate `Ô_θ` and never need a decoder — you predict `f_θ(E(s))` and compare against `E(s')`.

Sources: [01-state-and-latent-operators.md](docs/operator_world_models/01-state-and-latent-operators.md#L14-L70), [01-state-and-latent-operators.md](docs/operator_world_models/01-state-and-latent-operators.md#L82-L112)

### Two Poles of One Dial

The two running application domains are the *same construction* with the expressiveness↔structure dial set to opposite extremes. Digital phenotyping sits at the **learned pole**: no one can write down what "a week of more sleep" does to a behavioral latent, so `M_θ` is free or organized by named interventions, and equivariance is discovered. Protein ML sits at the **given pole**: the relevant transformations are rigid motions, so the SE(3) structure is imposed as a hard symmetry with correctness guaranteed by construction. What differs is only the generator basis that builds `M_θ`.

| | state operator `Ô_θ` | latent operator `f_θ` | equivariance source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Behavioral (phenotyping) | real intervention on true state — inaccessible, nonlinear | `exp(M_θ) z + b_θ`, `M_θ` **learned** | learned from encoded streams |
| Protein (3D) | literal rigid motion `x ↦ Rx + t` — exactly known | SE(3) operator on residue frames | demanded as hard SE(3)-equivariance |
| Image (I-JEPA) | "shift attention to region p" | predictor conditioned on position | learned via the predictor |

Sources: [01-state-and-latent-operators.md](docs/operator_world_models/01-state-and-latent-operators.md#L114-L135), [index.md](docs/operator_world_models/index.md#L16-L40)

## Part 2 — JEPA as a Temporal World Model

Part 2 makes one recognition and exercises one property. The recognition: **the temporal predictor and the latent operator are the same object** — "advance the latent under query q" has exactly the type signature of `f_θ`. Read against the operator formalism, the vanilla predictor is complete in two axes and lacking in two: the map exists but is **unstructured** (no committed algebraic shape), and the query exists but carries **only the time offset** `Δt`, set by a fixed schedule. The property exercised is rollout: iterating the operator composes it, and for the structured operator a k-step rollout collapses to one matrix, `f^k(z) = exp(kM_θ) z` — the series' rhythm example shows a weekly cycle closing exactly because `7 × 51.4° = 360°` in a single matrix multiply.

| action operator | Time-Series JEPA counterpart | status in vanilla model |
|---|---|---|
| latent operator `f_θ` | predictor `g_φ(z_t, ·)` | present, but **unstructured** |
| operator parameter `θ` | query / offset `q_Δt` | present, but carries only *when* |
| policy choosing `θ` | the offset schedule | **fixed, not learned** |
| predicted next state | `ẑ_{t+1}` | present |

Part 2 also states the **anchoring caveat** that shapes everything downstream: during training every prediction is checked against a real EMA-target encoding, but during genuine inference rollout the anchor is gone and small errors compound. The model therefore needs an internal trust signal — the surprise residual — which the vanilla model cannot yet interpret cleanly.

Sources: [02-jepa-as-a-temporal-world-model.md](docs/operator_world_models/02-jepa-as-a-temporal-world-model.md#L27-L70), [02-jepa-as-a-temporal-world-model.md](docs/operator_world_models/02-jepa-as-a-temporal-world-model.md#L74-L98)

## Part 3 — Conditioning JEPA on Actions

Part 3 is the single edit that makes the world model actionable: replace the bare query with an operator configured by the intervention, `g_φ(z_t, q_Δt) → f_θ(c_t)(z_t)`, where `c_t` is the recorded context (hours slept, medication taken; a mutation, a ligand) and a policy `π_ψ` reads state and context to emit `θ`. Everything else about training is unchanged — same EMA target, same latent L2, same stop-gradient. The edit fixes the **averaging defect**: unconditioned, one operator must straddle the good-night and bad-night futures and be wrong on every instance; conditioned, it produces the right answer per case. Three payoffs follow: **counterfactual rollout** (hold today fixed, swap the action, re-roll), **composable interventions** (repeating one intervention scales its generator, `f^7 = exp(7M)`; ordering effects are governed by the commutator `[M₁, M₂]` via Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff), and a **sharpened surprise signal** where the residual measures only what known actions fail to explain.

Sources: [03-conditioning-jepa-on-actions.md](docs/operator_world_models/03-conditioning-jepa-on-actions.md#L14-L58), [03-conditioning-jepa-on-actions.md](docs/operator_world_models/03-conditioning-jepa-on-actions.md#L60-L105)

Part 3 is also careful about its limits on two fronts. It stays **self-supervised**: the policy is trained by the predictive loss with gradients flowing through a reparameterized one-step path — no reward, no critic (the RL attachment is explicitly deferred). And it states the structural risk honestly: if the policy and operator are too expressive, the model can **explain away** a genuine decline as an intervention effect, flattening the very surprise signal you built. The mitigation is structural — keep `Θ` deliberately small and structured, which is why the basis choice in Part 4 is load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

Sources: [03-conditioning-jepa-on-actions.md](docs/operator_world_models/03-conditioning-jepa-on-actions.md#L107-L135)

## Part 4 — Generator Bases and the Operator in Code

Part 4 lands the dial in code. Since `exp(M)` is always invertible, `exp(0) = I` gives a near-identity start, and `M` lives in a flat vector space, the one remaining design decision is *which matrices M is allowed to be* — and that is fixed by choosing a generator basis `{B_i}` with `M_θ = Σ α_i B_i`. The behavioral pole (Free/Named) and the protein pole (SE(3)) are the **same operator class with a different basis argument**.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["context c_t + state z_t"] --> POL["policy π_ψ → α (= θ)"]
    BASIS["generator basis {Bᵢ}<br/>Free · Named · Skew · SE3"] --> GEN["M = Σ αᵢ Bᵢ"]
    POL --> GEN
    GEN --> EXP["A = exp(M)"]
    EXP --> APP["z' = A z + b(c)"]
    APP --> L["L = ‖z' − sg(z_target)‖²"]
    TGT["EMA target E_ξ̄(x_{t+1})"] --> L
```

| basis | `{B_i}` concretely | `exp(Σ αᵢ Bᵢ)` guarantees | where it fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Free / GL(D)** | learnable dense matrices, no constraint | invertible only | phenotyping default; model discovers its own modes |
| **Named** | one learnable matrix per labeled intervention | invertible, **interpretable**; `α` can *be* `c` | quantified intervention logs |
| **Skew / SO(D)** | skew-symmetric (`Bᵀ = −B`) | **orthogonal** — norm-preserving rotation | circadian / cyclic dynamics, cannot blow up |
| **SE(3)** | 6 fixed generators: 3 rotation + 3 translation | **rigid motion** (4×4 homogeneous) | protein residue frames |

Sources: [04-generator-bases-and-the-operator-in-code.md](docs/operator_world_models/04-generator-bases-and-the-operator-in-code.md#L12-L52), [04-generator-bases-and-the-operator-in-code.md](docs/operator_world_models/04-generator-bases-and-the-operator-in-code.md#L54-L72)

### The Runnable Module: `context_operator.py`

The module maps the formalism one-to-one. `GeneratorBasis` has the four subclasses above, each returning `{B_i}` as an `(m, D, D)` tensor — `SkewBasis` returns `R − Rᵀ` (always skew), `SE3Basis` returns the six fixed generators as a buffer. Policies split two ways: `MLPPolicy` emits `α` from `(z, c)` with a zero-initialized head, and `DirectInterventionPolicy` passes `α = c` through an optional learnable gain, so the quantified intervention log *is* the coefficient vector. `ContextConditionedOperator` ties basis and policy together and exposes the inspection surface the series' claims rest on.

| component | role | key lines |
|---|---|---|
| `FreeBasis` / `NamedBasis` / `SkewBasis` / `SE3Basis` | the `(m, D, D)` basis `{B_i}` — the dial | [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L50-L165) |
| `MLPPolicy` | `π_ψ(z, c) → α`; deterministic (Dirac) or diagonal-Gaussian, reparameterized | [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L170-L211) |
| `DirectInterventionPolicy` | `α = c · gain`, requires `c_dim == num_generators` | [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L212-L227) |
| `ContextConditionedOperator` | forward `z' = exp(M)z + b(c)`; `eigenvalues()`, `energy()`, `compose()` | [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L231-L315) |
| `conditioned_jepa_loss` / `ema_update` | Part 3's loss verbatim (`z_target.detach()` = stop-grad); EMA target update | [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L313-L327) |
| `_smoke()` | numerical verification of every structural guarantee | [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L330-L426) |

> [!TIP]
> The structural guarantees are **architectural, not penalized**: invertibility, orthogonality, and rigidity follow from the basis choice plus the matrix exponential, never from a loss term — and the zero-initialized policy head means `α = 0 → M = 0 → A = I`, so every operator starts as "do nothing" and departs from identity only as far as the data demands.

> [!TIP]
> `eigenvalues(z, c)` returns eigenvalues of the *generator* `M`, not of `A` — this is deliberate: a positive real part in any mode of `M` flags locally growing dynamics, which is exactly the "decompensation" read of Part 3 and the worked example. Likewise, the stop-gradient lives inside `conditioned_jepa_loss` via `z_target.detach()`, keeping anti-collapse out of the operator class.

The guarantees are verified, not asserted: the module's smoke test checks skew-basis orthogonality (`AᵀA = I` to ~1e-7), the flow property (`exp(7M) = (exp M)^7` to ~1e-6 — "a week really is one clean matrix"), SE(3) rigidity (`RᵀR = I`, `det R = 1`, bottom row `[0,0,0,1]`), near-identity init, and that the conditioned loss backpropagates into both policy and basis. Two pieces are deliberately left open: the encoders `E_ξ / E_ξ̄` (research artifact vs. on-device product push them in different directions) and the actor–critic attachment (the stochastic policy exposes `log_prob`/`entropy`, but only the predictive one-step path is wired).

Sources: [04-generator-bases-and-the-operator-in-code.md](docs/operator_world_models/04-generator-bases-and-the-operator-in-code.md#L74-L130), [context_operator.py](src/ssllab/action_operator/context_operator.py#L330-L426)

## The Worked Example: A Personal World Model for Diabetes

The closing chapter threads every symbol through one person — Maya, type 2 diabetes, instrumented with CGM, insulin, carbs, exercise, sleep, weight, and an EHR stream of timestamped medical codes (SNOMED diagnoses, RXNORM prescriptions, LOINC labs — the modality most people would not think to feed a glucose model; all data illustrative and synthetic, with the PH caveat stated up front). Diabetes sits at the **learned pole**, so the **named-intervention basis** makes the formalism operational: one learned generator per logged intervention, and the coefficients read straight off the daily log, `α = c_t`:

`M_θ(c_t) = n_insulin·B_insulin + n_carbs·B_carbs + n_exercise·B_exercise + n_metformin·B_metformin`

| generator | learned eigenvalues (illustrative) | what it does to the latent |
|---|---|---|
| `B_metformin` | −0.12, −0.20 | both axes decay toward target — mean-reverting drug |
| `B_exercise` | −0.15, −0.10 | inward pull, strongest on elevation |
| `B_insulin` | −0.30, −0.05 | sharp downward pull on elevation — fast, but risky |
| `B_carbs` | +0.18, +0.05 | **push outward** — the one destabilizing generator |

The headline result is a three-plan counterfactual: fixing today's latent `(0.85, 0.55)` and rolling two weeks under each regimen yields **status quo → TIR ≈ 58%**, **+ daily 30-min walk → TIR ≈ 71%** (no added hypo risk), **intensify insulin → TIR ≈ 67% with elevated hypoglycemia risk** — numbers no passive dashboard can produce. And the eigenvalue read catches **decompensation**: if the elevation-axis eigenvalue of Maya's effective daily operator drifts from −0.05 to +0.04 with her regimen unchanged, `e^{+0.04} ≈ 1.04 > 1` means a slow runaway the logged interventions do not explain — the sharpened surprise signal doing clinical work.

Sources: [05-worked-example-diabetes.md](docs/operator_world_models/05-worked-example-diabetes.md#L14-L175), [05-worked-example-diabetes.md](docs/operator_world_models/05-worked-example-diabetes.md#L197-L265)

## Notation Reference

`notation.md` is a standalone glossary grouping every symbol by role — representation (`E`, `E_ξ`, `E_ξ̄`, `τ`, `sg`), operators (`Ô_θ` vs `f_θ`, `Θ`), construction (`B_i`, `α`, `M_θ`, `A_θ = exp(M_θ)`, `b_θ`), conditioning (`c_t`, `π_ψ`, `Δ(Θ)`, `g_φ`, `q_Δt`), and energy/spectrum (`E(Ô) = ‖M‖²_F`, `Re(λ_i)`) — each with a "read as" column. It flags the one deliberate overload: `E` does double duty as encoder and energy functional, disambiguated by argument. The general policy `π_ψ(z_t, c_t)` exists even though the log can *be* `α`, because real interventions interact with state — 30 g of carbs does something different at `(0.85, 0.55)` than at baseline.

Sources: [notation.md](docs/operator_world_models/notation.md#L1-L62), [05-worked-example-diabetes.md](docs/operator_world_models/05-worked-example-diabetes.md#L267-L290)

The series is conceptual; the applied counterpart lives downstream. [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline) shows the operator machinery doing real experimental work (cell-state encoders, conditional flow, effect-size evaluation), and [Operator Algebra and Epistasis Tests](14-operator-algebra-and-epistasis-tests) develops the non-commuting composition this series' commutator discussion points to — with the load-bearing properties pinned in `tests/test_operator_algebra.py` (zero-init is identity, commuting generators compose additively, the bracket is what differs). For how to evaluate anything you build on this construction, see [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series) and [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics); for the full corpus map, see [Tutorial Corpus and Reading Paths](25-tutorial-corpus-and-reading-paths).


# Perturbation-Response Pipeline



This page documents the single-cell genetic perturbation study in `examples/perturbation_response/` — the biological application of the ssl-lab generative-JEPA toolkit. The pipeline takes the Norman et al. 2019 Perturb-seq dataset, learns a cell representation with an unlabeled JEPA encoder, transports latents from control cells to perturbed populations with a conditional generative model, reads latents back out as gene counts, and grades every arm on a single pre-committed benchmark: effect-size correlation on held-out two-gene perturbations. It is also the repository's worked example for its experimental methodology — the study's negative results are documented as carefully as its wins.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L1-L13), [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L7-L13)

## The Problem Shape: Predicting a Response, Not a State

A genetic perturbation switches a gene on or off inside a cell, and the cell's gene-expression profile shifts in response. The shift is not the same in every cell — genetically identical cells respond differently — so the modeling target is a *distribution* of outcomes, not a point estimate. The benchmark is the scGen/CPA/GEARS lineage test set: K562 cells under CRISPR activation, with both single-gene and two-gene perturbations. Models train on single-gene perturbations and some pairs, then must predict twenty held-out two-gene combinations they have never seen. The combinatorial split is the headline test, because it asks whether a model has learned something about how perturbations compose.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L3-L13)

## The Three-Stage Architecture

The method has three stages, each trained separately so that its contribution can be measured on its own:

1. **Stage A — the encoder.** A JEPA encoder is pretrained on cells with no labels at all: it masks some gene groups in a cell and learns to predict their embeddings from the rest. After pretraining it is frozen and maps every cell to a latent vector.
2. **Stage B — the transition.** A conditional generative model in that latent space turns a perturbation into a cloud of outcome latents. The main version is a conditional flow that transports control-cell latents toward the perturbed population; variants replace the flow with a learned linear operator or a per-gene operator algebra.
3. **Stage C — the readout.** A negative-binomial count decoder turns each latent back into gene counts, because effect size is measured on genes, not on latents.

Before reading the diagram: the arrows into Stage B carry two distinct objects — a *source* latent (either noise or a real control cell) and a *perturbation embedding* `e(p)`. The "cloud" on the output side is the population, which is what the distributional metrics grade; a summary statistic of it feeds the effect-size metric.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph SA["Stage A · Encoder"]
        C["data cache<br/>50 gene-group tokens / cell"] --> E["JEPA cell encoder<br/>z ∈ R^dim · frozen"]
    end
    subgraph SB["Stage B · Transition (latent space)"]
        T{variant} --> F["conditional flow<br/>transport z_b → z_out"]
        T --> O["action operator<br/>A_p = exp(M(e(p)))"]
        T --> OA["operator algebra<br/>per-gene generators"]
    end
    subgraph SC["Stage C · Readout"]
        D["NB count decoder<br/>mu = libsize · softmax(z)"]
    end
    E -->|"control latents"| SB
    P["perturbation embedding e(p)<br/>table or gene-compositional"] --> SB
    SB --> Z["outcome latent cloud"] --> D
    D --> X["sampled counts → log1p-CP10K"]
    X --> H["Δr / e_p harness<br/>one scorer for every arm"]
    G["held-out test cells"] --> H
```

The comparison spine is two references. The first is a from-scratch conditional NB-VAE conditioned on the same perturbation embedding — no JEPA, no flow — which is the strongest learned baseline. The second is a training-free additive reference: the sum of the two single-gene effects, Δ(A) + Δ(B), which requires no model at all and has led on effect size since round 7.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L5-L13)

## The Data Contract: Cells as Token Sequences

The data adapter is the biological sibling of the MNIST adapter, and its job is stated in one line: turn a cell's HVG vector `(n_hvg,)` into gene-group tokens `(n_tokens, token_dim)`, so the *same* `build_jepa(token_dim=..., n_tokens=...)` trains on cells with no architectural change. Where MNIST splits an image into spatial patches, here a cell's 5,000 highly-variable genes are split into a fixed random partition of 50 groups (`DEFAULT_N_HVG = 5000`, `DEFAULT_N_TOKENS = 50`, hence `token_dim = 100`). The partition is deterministic in its seed, so the processing script and every training run agree on which gene sits in which group.

Sources: [perturbseq.py](src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L1-L32), [perturbseq.py](src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L47-L62), [perturbseq.py](src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L72-L99)

The module is deliberately light — torch, numpy, and json only. All heavy single-cell processing (acquiring Norman 2019, QC, HVG selection via scanpy's `seurat_v3` on raw counts, normalization, differential expression) lives in the one-time script `00_process_norman.py`, which imports `anndata`/`scanpy`/`pertpy` lazily inside the functions that need them. The cache it writes is what every later stage consumes:

| Cache file | Role |
|---|---|
| `tokens_meta.npz` | train-time fast path: `hvg_X`, raw `counts`, `libsize`, `pert_id`, `is_control`, `ctrl_group`, split codes, `gene_ids`, `pert_names` |
| `splits.json` | perturbation-level splits — `combo` holds out unseen pairs, `cells` is an in-distribution sanity split |
| `de_genes.json` | top differentially expressed genes per perturbation — the set every metric scores |
| `manifest.json` | provenance and every processing setting, including the token-partition seed |
| `processed.h5ad` | canonical AnnData, for inspection and re-derivation — not read at train time |

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L130-L149), [perturbseq.py](src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L14-L32), [00_process_norman.py](examples/perturbation_response/00_process_norman.py#L98-L108)

The cache lives in the project-neutral data lake, not in the repository: `link_dataset('scrna/perturb_seq/norman2019')` from `ops.datasets` maps the nested lake path to a flat local alias, `data/norman2019`. The batch a loader yields is a dict, not a bare `(x, y)`: perturbation modeling needs the covariates — raw counts for the NB decoder, library size, the perturbation label, and the control grouping for baseline pairing. It also carries a `control_sampler` that draws baseline cells from the matched control pool each step.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L151-L184)

> [!TIP]
> Two panels are lossy by design, and both bind the whole pipeline: the 5,000-gene HVG panel is the model's entire input vocabulary (a perturbation whose response lives outside the panel is invisible downstream), and the fixed gene partition is what makes the encoder's positional table and the `--smoke` end-to-end check mean anything. Change either and every cached artifact must be rebuilt.

## Stage B: One Contract, Three Implementations

The transition is where the pipeline's design space lives, and the code enforces that it stays swappable. Every Stage B checkpoint loads into the same bundle shape and exposes the same operation — produce a cloud of outcome latents for a perturbation — so every downstream evaluator grades all arms through an identical harness. The loader inspects `(flow_base, cond_type)` from the checkpoint and rebuilds the condition module to match: a `control` transport base conditions on the perturbation embedding alone, while a `gaussian` prior fuses the baseline latent and the perturbation.

Sources: [perturb.py](src/ssllab/generative/perturb.py#L1-L52), [perturb.py](src/ssllab/generative/perturb.py#L78-L99)

The conditional flow is a rectified flow over the frozen latents: the interpolant is `z_t = (1-t)·z0 + t·z1`, the target velocity `u_t = z1 − z0`, and training regresses a `VelocityMLP` field onto it by an Euler-integrable ODE. The field is conditioned through FiLM injection alongside a sinusoidal time embedding, with a learned null-condition token enabling classifier-free guidance. The decisive design choice is the source `z0`: a Gaussian noise base generates outcomes from noise, while a `control` base transports a real control-cell latent and therefore models the *displacement* — the effect — directly. A settled ablation: transporting from a real control beats generating from noise (+0.036, significant); optimal-transport coupling of the pairs makes things worse (−0.021, significant) even though it lowers the training loss.

| Stage B variant | Mechanism | Conditioning | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flow, gaussian base | noise → outcome ODE | `cond(z_b, pert_id)` | superseded by control base |
| Flow, control base | transport control latent → outcome | `cond(pert_id)` only | the main method |
| Action operator | `A_p = exp(M(e(p)))`, linear pushforward of control latents | gene-compositional `e(p)` | drop-in, same harness |
| Operator algebra | one generator per gene; pairs compose inside the group | gene vocabulary | refuted for epistasis prediction |
| Conditional NB-VAE | encoder + decoder trained from scratch | perturbation-conditioned | strongest learned baseline |

Sources: [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L1-L38), [flow.py](src/ssllab/generative/flow.py#L61-L109), [04_train_cond_flow.py](examples/perturbation_response/04_train_cond_flow.py#L80-L91), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L47)

The operator variants deserve one paragraph of honesty, because they define what a drop-in replacement means here. `load_operator` and `load_operator_algebra` produce the identical `kind == "operator"` bundle the flow uses: the operator exposes `pushforward(z_ctrl, pert_id)` and reuses the sampling code unchanged. The algebra variant additionally carries a gene vocabulary so the bracket-epistasis eval can compute `‖[M_A, M_B]‖` per pair. The hypothesis — that operator non-commutativity predicts genetic interaction — failed every test it was given, and the refutation is pre-registered in the script's docstring before any run.

Sources: [perturb.py](src/ssllab/generative/perturb.py#L78-L120), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L44), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L112-L113)

## Stage C: Where Effect Size Is Recovered

The count decoder exists because effect size is measured on genes, and single-cell counts are non-negative integers, over-dispersed, and dropout-dominated — a Gaussian/MSE decoder is the wrong measurement model. The decoder instead emits the parameters of a negative-binomial distribution: `rho = softmax(net(z))` is a relative gene-rate profile summing to 1, `mu = library_size · rho` is the NB mean with library size as a given covariate, and `kappa = softplus(per-gene param)` is the dispersion. Training minimizes the NB negative log-likelihood of real counts.

Sources: [count_decoder.py](src/ssllab/generative/count_decoder.py#L1-L29)

The decoder is also where the study's most consequential bug lived. Round 11 of the results ledger found that the NB likelihood was counting each cell's library size over *all* measured genes rather than the 5,000 the decoder models — a factor of about 3.2 mismatch between the likelihood's means and the observed counts, compressing every model's rate profile. The correction is now the default: `LIBRARY_SIZES` offers `all` versus `hvg`, and `DEFAULT_LIBRARY_SIZE = "hvg"`; symmetrically, sampled counts are converted back to log1p-CP10K by dividing each sampled cell by its own total over modeled genes (`DEFAULT_NORMALIZATION = "data"`) rather than by the sampling depth. Fixing one convention lifted *every* model, not just the method — which is exactly why single-sourced scoring code matters.

Sources: [count_decoder.py](src/ssllab/generative/count_decoder.py#L37-L77), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L34)

## The Evaluation Harness: One Scorer for Every Arm

The benchmark function scores the **change** an intervention causes, not the absolute state. For a perturbation, the effect is its differential expression `Δ = mean(perturbed) − mean(control)` in log1p-CP10K; a model is graded on Pearson correlation between its predicted Δ and the true Δ over that perturbation's top-20 differentially expressed genes. The harness is deliberately predictor-agnostic: `run_effect_size_eval` takes a callable `predict_fn(pid, name) → pred_mean`, holds the truth as the mean over the perturbation's test cells, and returns per-perturbation correlations plus a summary. The flow eval (06), the NB-VAE baseline (09), and any future predictor call the same function, so a Δr difference is always an apples-to-apples statement.

Sources: [effect_size.py](src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L1-L44), [effect_size.py](src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L57-L90)

Beyond Δr, the harness family covers the other axes the study committed to: `10_eval_calibration.py` scores the distributional axis (spread correlation, interval coverage, Wasserstein and energy distance), `19_score_interaction.py` scores the *size* of the predicted change — the size-aware error `e_p`, where predicting no change scores 1 — and its departure from additivity. Verdicts on whether any difference is real come from `12_compare_arms.py`, a joint bootstrap with simultaneous intervals over the whole family of comparisons, so contrasts that share arms are resampled jointly rather than independently.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L84-L107)

> [!TIP]
> The scoreboard numbers are re-read, not frozen: every Δr and e_p in the current README is under round 11's corrected likelihood conventions and averaged over three seeds. Older checkpoints reproduce the published numbers only when `library_size=all` and `normalization=depth` are passed explicitly — the defaults are the corrected conventions, not the original ones.

## Script Taxonomy: Build, Score, Diagnose, Decide, Vary

The scripts are numbered `00` to `27` in the order they were written, which is not the order anyone runs them in. The README organizes them by the kind of work they do — a taxonomy worth internalizing before touching the directory:

| Kind | Scripts | Trains? | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Build** an artifact | `00`, `01`, `03`, `04`, `08`, `13`, `16` | yes (only these) | GPU pod, except `00` |
| **Score** on the benchmark | `05`, `06`, `09`, `18`, `10`, `19` | no | CPU, minutes |
| **Diagnose** where loss lives | `00a`, `00b`, `00c`, `02`, `11`, `14`, `15` | no | CPU, minutes |
| **Decide** if a difference is real | `12`, `17`, `20`–`27` | no | CPU, seconds |
| **Vary** one lever at a time | `run_*_pod.sh` wrappers | reuses artifacts | GPU pod |

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L68-L129)

Three of the diagnose scripts changed the direction of the project and are worth reading as instruments rather than utilities. `02_probe_cell_encoder.py` judges the frozen encoder with a linear probe; `11_diagnose_variance.py` attributes predicted spread to the latent distribution versus the decoder; and `14_ceiling_analysis.py` replaces Stage B with an oracle — real held-out cells pushed through encoder and decoder — to establish the best any transition could do with a given representation. That ceiling diagnostic is what proved the transition was never the bottleneck (a perfect-by-construction Stage B reached only 0.679 through the then-current decoder) and located the loss in the readout.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L95-L106), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L42-L43)

## Co-Adaptation and What the Ledger Found

Every round before 12 froze the encoder, which is what made a difference between two arms attributable to the one thing that changed. Co-adaptation relaxes that freeze one stage at a time, and its Phase 1 trainer has three modes sharing one recipe: `dec` re-trains only a fresh decoder (the control), `joint` trains encoder and decoder together on the NB reconstruction loss with a smaller encoder learning rate, and `joint_anchor` adds the JEPA masked-prediction objective with an EMA teacher at a weight fixed by rule — the weight that equalizes the two loss terms at the scale of a *trained* readout, measured before any update. The anchor keeps an objective satisfied during fine-tuning; it does not penalize distance from the original encoder, and how far the representation actually moves is measured separately by CKA.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L1-L56), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L192-L199)

The findings, with Δr meaning effect-size correlation on the twenty held-out combinations and `e_p` the size-aware error:

| Arm | Δr | e_p | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Additive reference, Δ(A)+Δ(B) | **0.961** | **0.289** | training-free; leads since round 7 |
| Conditional NB-VAE, conditioned encoder | 0.939 | 0.455 | strongest learned model |
| Flow on random-start joint encoder+decoder | 0.921 | 0.461 | best full pipeline, round 13 |
| Flow on JEPA encoder fine-tuned with decoder | 0.900 | 0.472 | round 12 |
| NB-VAE, condition-blind encoder | 0.880 | 0.609 | the rounds-1–5 baseline, re-read |
| Action operator on frozen JEPA | 0.848 | 0.579 | round 3, re-read |
| Flow on frozen JEPA | 0.837 | 0.591 | the method as first built |
| Readout ceiling (oracle, diagnostic) | 0.865 / 0.936 / 0.948–0.961 | — | frozen / round-12 / round-13 encoders |

Three findings lead the ledger. Round 11's library-size fix lifted every model by correcting one convention. Round 12's joint training raised the readout ceiling from 0.865 to 0.936 and a retrained flow to 0.900. Round 13 then ran the same joint training from random weights and reached 0.948–0.961 on the ceiling and 0.909–0.921 on the full pipeline — so the JEPA pretraining is *not shown to contribute*, and the honest scoreboard says so. Meanwhile, no learned model has beaten additivity on mean effects, and on the size of the change additivity is far ahead (0.289 versus 1.05 for the conditioned NB-VAE under `e_p`).

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L15-L47)

## Running the Pipeline

The order of operations is strict and follows the dependency graph: cache → encoder → decoder and flow on frozen latents → evaluation; the NB-VAE baseline needs only the cache. A first pass fits entirely in a terminal:

```bash
pip install -e ".[perturb]"
# tiny synthetic smoke run — verifies the whole pipeline, no network, seconds
python examples/perturbation_response/00_process_norman.py --smoke
# real run: pertpy auto-fetch, 5000-gene HVG panel (multi-GB, CPU)
python examples/perturbation_response/00_process_norman.py --source pertpy --n-hvg 5000

export DATA_LAKE_ROOT=~/work/data
python -c "from ops.datasets import link_dataset; link_dataset('scrna/perturb_seq/norman2019')"
```

Training happens on a RunPod GPU pod driven from `examples/ops/`: provision the pod, stage the cache and reused checkpoints to the persistent volume once, launch a `run_*_pod.sh` wrapper, bring outputs back — and evaluate locally, on CPU, where the scoring scripts are fast and cheap by design. Each wrapper reuses every artifact it can and retrains only the stage under test; the decoder and operator wrappers additionally run a preflight that verifies staged inputs and stops within seconds, naming whatever is missing.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L130-L147), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L186-L190), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L113-L115)

## Where This Fits in the Catalog

Every component here has a deeper page: the transition field's mechanics are in [Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior) and [Conditional Flow and Classifier-Free Guidance](10-conditional-flow-and-classifier-free-guidance); the Stage C readout and from-scratch baseline in [Count Decoders and CVAE Baseline](12-count-decoders-and-cvae-baseline); the operator family in [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators) and [Operator Algebra and Epistasis Tests](14-operator-algebra-and-epistasis-tests). The joint-training mechanics cross over into [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder), the probes and ceilings into [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics), the bootstrap verdicts into [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference), and the round-by-round protocol discipline into [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration). For the underlying abstractions, see [Modality-Agnostic Data Adapters](23-modality-agnostic-data-adapters) and [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-runpod).

A recommended reading path through this study: the in-repo data primer (`examples/perturbation_response/docs/reading-perturb-seq/`), then the conditional-flow + JEPA method series up to its results chapter, then the results ledger — and the general methodology it fed, [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series), which is best read as the study's post-mortem turned into a discipline.


# ECG Rhythm Study



This page documents the ECG rhythm study — the first runnable instance of the time-series JEPA line on a real physiological signal. The study asks one controlled question: **does span-masked JEPA pretraining make a fixed encoder more useful for cardiac rhythm classification when only a limited number of labelled patients are available?** Everything here — ten numbered scripts, a frozen protocol, an amendment mechanism, and a results ledger — exists to make that answer trustworthy rather than merely impressive.

## The Question and the Experimental Contract

The comparison is engineered so its answer can be trusted. The same encoder architecture is trained from scratch and from pretraining; labelled patient subsets are identical across methods; test patients stay fixed; and variation across training repeats is reported separately from patient-bootstrap uncertainty. These four decisions form the experimental contract of study v1, and every script in the folder enforces a piece of it.

The substrate is [PTB-XL v1.0.3](https://physionet.org/content/ptb-xl/1.0.3/) (Wagner et al. 2020, *Scientific Data*; PhysioNet, CC BY 4.0): 21,799 ten-second, 12-lead clinical ECGs from 18,869 patients, with a native 500 Hz copy and an official 100 Hz copy. Patient-confined stratified folds ship with the dataset, so patient leakage across splits is prevented by construction rather than by discipline.

Sources: [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L1-L11), [ptbxl.py](src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L28-L30)

## Pipeline at a Glance

The study is organized as a numbered pipeline where each stage consumes the verified artifacts of the previous one. Before reading the diagram: solid boxes are files written to disk, arrows are labelled with the producing script, and the two shared artifacts — the saved subsets and the per-repeat JEPA checkpoints — feed every downstream run.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    RAW["PhysioNet PTB-XL tree<br/>(WFDB records + 2 CSV tables)"] -->|"00_process_ptbxl.py<br/>checksum-verified read"| CACHE["data/ptbxl100/<br/>signals.npy · records.json · manifest.json"]
    CACHE -->|"01_data_card.py"| CARD["reports/data_card.{json,md}"]
    CACHE -->|"01a_plot_records.py"| FIGS["figures/"]
    CACHE -->|"02_make_subsets.py"| SUBS["subsets/subsets.json<br/>nested patient budgets × 5 repeats"]
    CACHE -->|"03_pretrain_jepa.py"| CKPT["checkpoints/jepa_r0..r4.pt<br/>+ reports/pretrain_r*.json"]
    SUBS --> RUNS
    CKPT --> RUNS
    RUNS["04_train_downstream.py<br/>scratch / finetune / probe<br/>60 runs"] --> LRSEL["05_select_lr.py<br/>lr_selection_<tag>.json"]
    LRSEL --> GRID["run_ecg_grid_pod.sh<br/>full grid"]
    GRID --> BOOT["06_compare_arms.py<br/>paired patient-cluster bootstrap"]
    BOOT --> PAGE["07_pilot_report.py + 08_make_results.py<br/>→ results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/"]
```

The status table from the study's README reflects a completed v1: data through comparison are done, with calibration, robustness, external shift, and attribution explicitly deferred to later work.

| Stage | Script | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| Data layer | `00_process_ptbxl.py` | `data/ptbxl100/` cache |
| Data card | `01_data_card.py` | `data_card.{json,md}` |
| Real-record plots | `01a_plot_records.py` | `figures/` |
| Labelled-patient subsets | `02_make_subsets.py` | `subsets/subsets.json` |
| Span-masked JEPA pretraining | `03_pretrain_jepa.py` | `jepa_r{0..4}.pt` |
| Downstream arms | `04_train_downstream.py` | 60 run directories |
| Learning-rate selection | `05_select_lr.py` | `lr_selection_<tag>.json` |
| Paired bootstrap comparison | `06_compare_arms.py` | test-split interval tables |
| Pilot report | `07_pilot_report.py` | runtime and grid estimates |
| Results page | `08_make_results.py` | `results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/` |

Sources: [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L13-L27), [_study.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/_study.py#L1-L5)

## Stage 0 — The Cache: Verification at Ingest

`00_process_ptbxl.py` reads the PhysioNet tree using only the standard library and numpy — WFDB signals are parsed by the small `ssllab.data.wfdb16` reader, which **verifies every record's per-lead checksum** during the build. That choice moves integrity checking to ingest time, so training code never re-pays it.

The cache has three files, and the loader treats them as a unit. `signals.npy` is an `int16` tensor of shape `(21799, 12, 1000)` in microvolts, opened memory-mapped; `records.json` carries per-record identity (`ecg_id`, `patient_id`, `strat_fold`), demographics, quality flags, and parsed `scp_codes`; `manifest.json` records provenance, lead order, sampling rate, the rhythm vocabulary, and the label rules. Two more checks run during the build: every record must have identical geometry and lead order to the first record, and the gains must be exactly 1000/mV with baseline 0 — a record that deviates stops the build instead of silently entering the cache. A `--smoke` mode generates a tiny synthetic PhysioNet-shaped tree and runs it through the identical code path, which is how the pipeline is exercised without a network.

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `signals.npy` | `int16 (21799, 12, 1000)`, microvolts, memory-mapped |
| `records.json` | per record: `ecg_id`, `patient_id`, `strat_fold`, age, sex, quality flags, `scp_codes` |
| `manifest.json` | provenance, leads, sampling rate, rhythm vocabulary, label rules |

Sources: [00_process_ptbxl.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/00_process_ptbxl.py#L1-L20), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L29-L58), [ptbxl.py](src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L238-L291)

## Label Semantics: Present, Unknown, and the Two AF Rules

Label semantics are fixed once, in `ssllab.data.ptbxl`, so that every script agrees. A rhythm statement is **present** when its code appears in a record's `scp_codes`, whatever its stored likelihood — PTB-XL writes likelihood 0 for many rhythm statements, where 0 means "not graded", not "absent". A record with **no rhythm statement at all is unknown** for every rhythm task: it is excluded, never counted as a negative. This is the quiet correctness decision that most naive PTB-XL pipelines get wrong.

The binary AF pilot runs under two rules that trade precision for coverage. Both exclude unknown records and use AFIB as positivity; they differ only on atrial flutter.

| | `af_primary` | `af_sensitivity` |
|---|---|---|
| Unknown-rhythm records | excluded | excluded |
| AFLT records (incl. AFIB+AFLT) | **excluded** | kept |
| Flutter-only records | removed from cohort | counted as **negatives** |
| Rationale | remove ambiguous AF/flutter boundary | keep more patients, accept noisier negatives |

The "non-AF" side is documented as a **clinical population**, not a healthy-control group: it includes other arrhythmias, paced rhythms, and sinus records with diagnoses such as MI or conduction disease.

Sources: [ptbxl.py](src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L7-L37), [ptbxl.py](src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L81-L92), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L76-L85)

## Patient-Level Budgets and Token Geometry

Label budgets simulate scarce annotation, and their unit is the **patient**, not the record. One seeded permutation of *all* training patients is drawn, and a budget of k percent takes the first ⌈k/100 · n⌉ patients of that permutation — which makes budgets **nested**: the 5% patients are part of the 10% set, which is part of the 25% set. Because the permutation ignores the task, the same patients carry labels across tasks and methods for a given seed, so subset noise is *shared* between the arms being compared rather than confounding their difference.

At load time, each record `(C, L)` becomes time-patch tokens `(N, C·P)`: with the study geometry of 250 ms patches over 10 seconds, a batch carries tokens of shape `(B, 40, 300)` — 40 tokens × 12 leads × 25 samples — or `(B, 40, 25)` for single-lead input. The loader refuses a geometry whose sampling rate does not match the cache: a 100 Hz model is never fed 500 Hz input. Each loader attaches a `.meta` dict (geometry, leads, task, label names, budget, record counts), and each batch is a dict with `tokens`, `signal`, `row`, `patient_id` and, unless `task="none"`, `labels`.

| `task` | Cohort | Labels |
|---|---|---|
| `af_primary` / `af_sensitivity` | binary AF pilot under the chosen rule | 1 sigmoid |
| `rhythm` | all rhythm-annotated records | one sigmoid per rhythm statement |
| `none` | every record (pretraining) | none |

Sources: [ptbxl.py](src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L104-L119), [ptbxl.py](src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L421-L479), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L87-L107)

## The Frozen Protocol

Study v1 was written to `configs/study_v1.json` **before any model was evaluated**, and that file stays byte-identical. The core labels (SR, AFIB, STACH, SARRH, SBRAD) were chosen from patient-level class support counted by the data card — and are never revised from model performance. A label with zero positive patients in a given run's subset is masked out of that run's loss and reported as unsupported, rather than silently distorting the macro average.

The protocol's key settings:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Budgets | 5, 10, 25, 100% of all 15,023 training patients |
| Repeats | 5; each redraws subset, downstream seed, and pretraining |
| Per-repeat seeds | `budget_seed = r`, `train_seed = 100 + r`, `pretrain_seed = r` |
| Encoder | embed 128, depth 4, 4 heads |
| Pretraining | 100 epochs, batch 128, lr 5e-4, span masking (2 × 1 s), reg 0.04, train folds only |
| Downstream | mean pool → linear 12 outputs, BCE, AdamW wd 0.05, cosine, 4000 steps, patience 10 evals |
| LR grid (frozen) | `[3e-4, 1e-3]`, selected on validation at repeat 0, budget 10% |
| AF operating point | threshold = highest with validation sensitivity ≥ 0.90, applied unchanged to test |

> [!TIP]
> The three seeds per repeat are deliberately independent dimensions: `budget_seed` redraws *who carries labels*, `train_seed` redraws *stochasticity of downstream training*, and `pretrain_seed` redraws *the pretrained encoder itself*. Because a repeat's checkpoint is reused across that repeat's budgets and by both pretrained arms, the pretraining variance is not hidden inside the downstream runs — it is attributable.

Sources: [study_v1.json](examples/ecg_rhythm/configs/study_v1.json#L7-L62), [study_v1.json](examples/ecg_rhythm/configs/study_v1.json#L63-L74), [_study.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/_study.py#L215-L217)

## Amendments Without Rewriting History

After the pilot, two validation-informed amendments widened the shared learning-rate grid — without touching the frozen base file. The mechanism in `_study.py` is small but strict: an amendment file names its `base` config and the base's hash, which is **verified on load**; it may only change fields listed in `AMENDABLE` (currently only `downstream.lr_grid`); and it may declare an earlier amendment `supersedes`, itself checked by hash. The loaded study dict carries both `_base_sha256` (the frozen protocol) and `_sha256` (base plus amendment).

Every artifact records what it depends on through **relevant hashes**. Three dependency kinds are defined — `subsets`, `pretrain`, and `run` — and each hashes only the protocol sections that matter to it. Crucially, the run hash *excludes* `lr_grid` and `lr_selection`: how a rate was chosen does not change how a run trains once its learning rate is given. `check_compatible` then compares an artifact's recorded hash against the current protocol and **stops the process on any unexplained incompatibility**, printing the exact reason; older artifacts made before relevant hashes existed are accepted only when the amendment provably leaves their relevant settings identical.

| Kind | Hashed sections | Reuse rule |
|---|---|---|
| `subsets` | data, labels, budgets, denominator, repeats | identical relevant hash, or pinned sha256 |
| `pretrain` | data, encoder, pretrain, repeats | plus report shows full epochs, not smoke |
| `run` | all of the above + downstream **minus** `lr_grid`, `lr_selection` | skip only when complete and compatible |

Amendment 2 demonstrates the full machinery: it pins the saved subsets and the repeat-0 pretraining checkpoint by sha256 (byte-identical reuse), declares the 12 amendment-1 runs reusable after per-run compatibility checks, and adds exactly one new rate (`new_rates: [1e-2]`). It also carries a **stop rule**: if any arm selects 1e-2, the edge is reported and the grid is not extended again, and a diverged run is recorded as diverged and never selectable.

> [!TIP]
> The design invariant worth stealing for any experiment codebase: *two protocols with the same relevant hash produce interchangeable artifacts of that kind*. Reuse decisions become hash comparisons instead of human judgment calls, and "why did you reuse this checkpoint?" is answered by a string the artifact itself recorded at creation time.

Sources: [_study.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/_study.py#L13-L15), [_study.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/_study.py#L34-L62), [_study.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/_study.py#L65-L114), [study_v1_amend2.json](examples/ecg_rhythm/configs/study_v1_amend2.json#L1-L42)

## Stage 3 — Pretraining: Span-Masked JEPA on 12-Lead Signals

Pretraining is **inductive**: it sees training-fold recordings only (folds 1–8, all of them, unknown-rhythm records included, labels unused). Validation and test never enter pretraining. One run per repeat, seeded by `pretrain_seed = r`, produces a checkpoint that is reused across that repeat's budgets and by both pretrained arms — so the finetune and probe arms differ only in whether the encoder's weights keep training.

Each step hides `n_spans` (2) contiguous spans of `span_s` (1 second — four 250 ms tokens each) and trains the student to predict the **EMA teacher's** embeddings at those positions, with collapse tracked continuously: every 10 epochs, feature std and effective rank are computed on a fixed sample of 2048 training recordings and logged into the run history.

The run is deliberately **not resumable**: the checkpoint stores the student encoder and predictor only — no EMA teacher, optimiser state, step counter, or RNG state. Instead of half-resumable state, the scripts guarantee something simpler and safer: the checkpoint and report are written atomically at the end via `os.replace`, and the report is the completion marker, written last. An interrupted run leaves no checkpoint that could be mistaken for a finished one, and `pretrain_complete` combines the existence check with compatibility (relevant hash, epoch count, non-smoke flag) before any later script will accept it.

Sources: [03_pretrain_jepa.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L1-L30), [03_pretrain_jepa.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L69-L87), [03_pretrain_jepa.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/03_pretrain_jepa.py#L109-L140), [_study.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/_study.py#L125-L147)

## Stage 4 — Three Arms, One Head

Each downstream run instantiates one arm over the saved subset for its (repeat, budget). All three arms share the encoder architecture, the head (mean pool → linear, 12 outputs), the loss, the optimiser, and the step budget — the *only* intended difference is where the encoder's weights start and whether they move.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph R["repeat r"]
        SUB["saved subset<br/>(budget b, seed r)"] --> A1 & A2 & A3
        CK["jepa_r{r}.pt<br/>(verified compatible)"] --> A2 & A3
        A1["scratch<br/>random init ·<br/>all weights trained"] --> OUT["runs/&lt;tag&gt;/&lt;arm&gt;_b&lt;b&gt;_r&lt;r&gt;_lr&lt;lr&gt;/<br/>report.json + preds.npz"]
        A2["finetune<br/>checkpoint init ·<br/>all weights trained"] --> OUT
        A3["probe<br/>checkpoint frozen ·<br/>head only"] --> OUT
    end
```

| Arm | Encoder init | Weights trained | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `scratch` | random (`train_seed`) | all | **primary baseline** |
