| `finetune` | repeat's JEPA checkpoint | all | **primary comparison** |
| `probe` | repeat's JEPA checkpoint | frozen | secondary readout: representation quality alone |

Model selection is validation-only: every 100 steps the validation core macro AUROC is computed, and the best complete evaluation is kept; test predictions are written only with `--eval-test`, so the pilot never produces them. Two guards round out the script. `--shuffle-labels` permutes whole label vectors across training recordings — prevalence and co-occurrence preserved, signal link broken — as a sanity check that should land near 0.5 AUROC, explicitly documented as *not* a proof that no leakage exists. And a non-finite loss or non-finite validation prediction marks the run **diverged**: it is reported as such and can never be selected by the LR search.

Sources: [04_train_downstream.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/04_train_downstream.py#L1-L44), [04_train_downstream.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/04_train_downstream.py#L100-L135), [04_train_downstream.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/04_train_downstream.py#L137-L200)

## Learning-Rate Selection: Pilot, Amendment 1, Amendment 2

Because scratch must not be under-tuned — the central question is pretraining *versus* scratch — the LR grid was widened twice, and each widening is itself documented. A pilot (repeat 0, validation only, kept untouched as the record) first checked the pipeline and measured runtime. Amendment 1 widened the frozen grid from `{3e-4, 1e-3}` to `{1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3, 3e-3}`; under it, scratch selected 3e-3 — the top edge — with validation core macro AUROC rising monotonically from 0.7603 to 0.7686 across the grid. Amendment 2 added `1e-2` and made the grid final, reusing the twelve amendment-1 runs after per-run compatibility checks so only three new runs were needed.

Selection is deliberately austere: per arm, on validation, at repeat 0 and budget 10% only, then frozen for everything else. That keeps the tuning channel separate from the measurement channel — a pattern the methodology series generalises.

Sources: [study_v1_amend2.json](examples/ecg_rhythm/configs/study_v1_amend2.json#L17-L28), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L109-L113)

## Stage 6 — Comparing Arms Honestly

The headline metric is **core macro AUROC at recording level** on the full eligible rhythm cohort of test fold 10. Differences between arms are quantified with a **paired patient-cluster bootstrap** of 2000 resamples: patients — not recordings — are resampled, and the same patient resample is applied to both arms of a pair, because recordings within a patient are correlated and independent resampling would understate uncertainty. The bootstrap runs per repeat and for the repeat mean, while repeat-to-repeat spread is reported separately rather than being folded into the interval.

The AF operating point gets its own seam. The AFIB output of the main multi-label model is evaluated on the primary AF cohort with a threshold rule fixed in the protocol — the highest threshold achieving validation sensitivity ≥ 0.90 — applied to test unchanged. No calibration is performed in study v1; it is evaluated separately, later.

Sources: [study_v1.json](examples/ecg_rhythm/configs/study_v1.json#L63-L74), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L115-L124)

## The v1 Result

Span-masked JEPA pretraining helps most when labels are scarce. With labels for 5% of training patients, the fine-tuned pretrained encoder beats the same encoder trained from scratch by **+0.078 core macro AUROC**, with a 95% interval over test patients of **+0.064 to +0.091**, and all five repeats agree in direction. The advantage shrinks as the label budget grows toward the full 15,023 training patients — the classic label-efficiency signature, now measured with paired uncertainty rather than asserted from single runs. Full figures, metrics, and narrative live in the generated results page under `results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/`.

Sources: [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L9-L11), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L25-L26)

## Running the Study

The data is open access; the AWS open-data mirror is much faster than the PhysioNet zip, and the downloaded tree is checksum-verified against PhysioNet's `SHA256SUMS.txt`. The smoke path builds a synthetic tree and exercises the identical code path in seconds, no network needed:

```bash
export DATA_LAKE_ROOT=~/work/data
aws s3 sync --no-sign-request s3://physionet-open/ptb-xl/1.0.3/ $DATA_LAKE_ROOT/ecg/ptbxl/raw/1.0.3/
python examples/ecg_rhythm/00_process_ptbxl.py --fs 100 --out-dir $DATA_LAKE_ROOT/ecg/ptbxl/cache100
python -c "from ops.datasets import link_dataset; link_dataset('ecg/ptbxl/cache100', link_name='ptbxl100')"
python examples/ecg_rhythm/00_process_ptbxl.py --smoke   # synthetic tree, same code path
```

The executed study ran on a remote pod, staged once and then driven by the shell entrypoints; comparison and result generation run locally. Note the staging detail: `ops_stage_data.py` names the staged copy after the *symlink target*, so the pod-side `mv cache100 ptbxl100` aligns names before the grid scripts run.

```bash
python examples/ops/ops_stage_data.py data/ptbxl100                                   # once, onto the pod's volume
python examples/ops/ops_run_pipeline.py --execute --cluster <c> -- bash examples/ecg_rhythm/run_ecg_lrsearch_pod.sh
python examples/ops/ops_run_pipeline.py --execute --cluster <c> -- bash examples/ecg_rhythm/run_ecg_grid_pod.sh
python examples/ecg_rhythm/06_compare_arms.py --tag main --split test                 # bootstrap, locally
python examples/ecg_rhythm/08_make_results.py                                         # figures, metrics, results page
```

Sources: [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L29-L48), [README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/README.md#L126-L135)

## Where to Go Next

The ECG study is one application of a shared stack, and each of its seams is documented as a general capability. The masking scheme used here is dissected in [Masking Strategies: Random and Span](7-masking-strategies-random-and-span); the loader pattern follows the conventions of [Modality-Agnostic Data Adapters](23-modality-agnostic-data-adapters); the remote execution layer is covered in [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-rupod-n/a). For the statistics, [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference) formalises the resampling scheme, [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics) covers the probe and AUROC machinery, and the amendment discipline practiced here is the concrete case of [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration). To see the same pipeline applied to single-cell perturbation data, continue to [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline).


# Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder



This page documents the **co-adaptation sub-program**: the experiment in which the perturbation-response stack stops treating the JEPA encoder as a frozen feature extractor and instead lets the encoder and the count decoder shape each other during training. The machinery lives in one library module (`ssllab.coadapt`), one training entry-point script (`co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py`), one diagnostic script (`co-adaptation/01_koopman_linearity_probe.py`), two remote-run pipelines, and a test suite that pins down exactly what each mode trains. The module docstring frames the question precisely: every earlier round trained the negative-binomial decoder on a frozen encoder, and the ceiling analysis showed a linear readout recovers more of the perturbation effect from the same frozen latents than the trained decoder does — so Phase 1 asks whether letting the two networks train together recovers what the decoder loses. Critically, **the transition stage (the conditional flow) is never co-trained**, which is what keeps the result attributable.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L1-L63), [02_coadapt_decoder.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py#L1-L53)

## Why Unfreeze: Two Measurements of the Frozen Encoder

By the end of round 4 the frozen encoder had been measured against two independent requirements, and it split the verdict. It **retained the signal**: a linear ridge readout of the frozen latents scores Δr = 0.852, above the original NB-VAE baseline (0.766) and just below the conditioned NB-VAE (0.858). But it did **not keep the signal in small motions**: fitting the latent response with operator generators demanded norms around 12.4 — a large rotation, not the near-identity motion the operator design assumed. Together with the ceiling's estimate that a large slice of Δr was lost between the linear readout and the trained decoder reading the same latents, this motivated unfreezing: co-training might recover what reconstruction alone loses. One boundary note for interpreting the premise: round 10 later found the headline decoder gap (0.173) only under the convention that reads every predicted change against the *measured* control mean, and Phase 1 was placed on hold pending the corrected-likelihood protocol that round 12 then ran under.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/README.md#L19-L31), [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L1-L63), [26_score_round12.py](examples/perturbation_response/26_score_round12.py#L1-L33)

## The Program in Three Phases

Each phase unfreezes one more stage, so each result stays as attributable as the design allows:

| Script | Phase | Trained jointly with the encoder | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `01_koopman_linearity_probe.py` | Phase 0 — diagnostic | nothing; encoder stays frozen | done (verdict: inconclusive by rule, affine in substance) |
| `02_coadapt_decoder.py` | Phase 1 | the NB count decoder, transition frozen | built; executed as round 12 (and round 13 for the random-init control) |
| `03_coadapt_operator.py` | Phase 2 | the operator, under a Koopman objective | planned, lower priority |

Phase 0 exists to turn the program's central premise into a number before any engineering goes into the delicate Phase 2; its pre-registered decision rule **gates Phase 2 only** — Phase 1 runs regardless because it attacks the largest already-measured loss. The narrative companion lives in the sub-program's `docs/` series, with round-by-round numbers in the results ledger ([Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration)).

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/README.md#L32-L44), [docs/index.md](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/docs/index.md#L1-L17)

## One Trainer, Three Modes

The module's design is deliberately minimal: **one recipe, one optimizer, one training loop**, and the only difference between experimental arms is *what is allowed to train*. This is expressed by a single `mode` string on `CoadaptConfig` and enforced by `prepare_jepa`, which unfreezes exactly the right parameter groups after `load_jepa` returns everything frozen:

| Mode | Encoder | Predictor | Decoder | Learning rates | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dec` | frozen | frozen (unused) | trains | decoder `lr=1e-3` | control: today's decoder recipe, re-seeded under identical optimizer settings |
| `joint` | trains (`encoder_lr=1e-4`) | frozen (unused) | trains | decoder `1e-3`, encoder `1e-4` | does co-training recover the decoder gap? |
| `joint_anchor` | trains (`encoder_lr=1e-4`) | trains (`encoder_lr=1e-4`) | trains | as `joint` | `joint` while maintaining the JEPA predictive objective with a fixed anchor weight |

The shared `CoadaptConfig` defaults are the round-10 recipe: `epochs=30`, `lr=1e-3` (the decoder's Stage C value), `encoder_lr=1e-4` (smaller because the encoder starts pretrained), `clip=5.0` gradient clipping over *all* trainable parameters in every mode, `anchor_batches=20`, and `library_size="hvg"`. The constructor validates the mode against `MODES` and rejects non-positive learning rates or clips, so a misconfigured run fails before consuming compute.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L84-L100), [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L103-L119)

Two checkpoint-handling decisions deserve explicit attention. First, `load_jepa` rebuilds the EMA teacher as an **exact copy of the loaded encoder** — the teacher was never saved in Stage A checkpoints, so under `joint_anchor` the teacher follows the changing student from this new starting point. The module docstring is careful about what this means: the anchor keeps an *objective* satisfied (the masked-prediction loss, with the same EMA mechanics as Stage A); it does **not** penalize distance from the original encoder — that would be a different experiment, and how far the representation actually moves is measured separately (linear CKA against the original encoder). Second, **there is no resume**: saved encoder and decoder are exports, not training checkpoints (no optimizer, teacher, schedule, or RNG state), so an interrupted run restarts from scratch.

> [!TIP]
> The teacher-rebuild subtlety is easy to miss: `load_jepa` constructs `EMA(jepa.encoder, ...)` so the teacher copies the *loaded* weights, and `prepare_jepa` does the same after unfreezing. If you extend the trainer with an objective that reads the teacher (anything that resumes the masked-prediction loss), a stale teacher would silently train the student toward random-init targets.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L1-L63), [checkpoint.py](src/ssllab/checkpoint.py#L19-L41)

## The System at a Glance

The following diagram shows how the pieces interact across a Phase 1 run — from the Stage A checkpoint through the joint training loop to the artifacts downstream scripts consume:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    CKPT["Stage A checkpoint<br/>norman_stage_a/encoder.pt"] --> LOAD["load_jepa<br/>or random_jepa_like"]
    LOAD --> PREP["prepare_jepa(mode)"]
    PREP --> ENC["jepa.encoder<br/>frozen in dec, trainable otherwise"]
    PREP --> PRED["jepa.predictor<br/>trainable only in joint_anchor"]
    PREP --> TCH["EMA teacher<br/>rebuilt as copy of loaded encoder"]
    DECIN["fresh CountDecoder"] --> NB["NB reconstruction loss<br/>on raw counts"]
    ENC -- "z = jepa.embed(tokens)" --> NB
    PRED -- "masked-prediction loss" --> JL["JEPA loss"]
    RULE["anchor_weight_by_rule<br/>w = ref NB loss / JEPA loss<br/>first 20 batches, eval mode"] --> ANCHOR["w times JEPA loss<br/>joint_anchor only"]
    JL --> ANCHOR
    NB --> TOT["total loss<br/>AdamW, clip 5.0"]
    ANCHOR --> TOT
    TOT --> UPD["opt.step + EMA update<br/>joint_anchor only"]
    UPD --> HIST["per-epoch record:<br/>nb_loss, jepa_loss,<br/>grad_nb, grad_anchor,<br/>effective_rank, feature_std"]
    UPD --> EOUT["checkpoints/encoder.pt<br/>save_jepa format"]
    UPD --> DOUT["checkpoints/count_decoder.pt<br/>records latent_source identity"]
    HIST --> REP["reports/coadapt.json"]
    EOUT --> RD["14_ceiling_analysis.py,<br/>02_probe_cell_encoder.py,<br/>04_train_cond_flow.py (flow retrained)"]
```

Everything the trainer emits is in a format downstream scripts already read: the encoder round-trips through `save_jepa`/`load_jepa`, the decoder checkpoint carries `latent_dim`, `n_genes`, the library-size convention, and a `latent_source` identity block (encoder path, md5, width, and the encoder's `space_key`), and `reports/coadapt.json` holds the config, the anchor rule with its measured means, and the per-epoch history.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L149-L238), [02_coadapt_decoder.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py#L100-L204), [checkpoint.py](src/ssllab/checkpoint.py#L13-L21)

## The Anchor Rule: Weighting Two Objectives by Measurement

`joint_anchor` adds the JEPA loss to the NB reconstruction loss with a weight that is **fixed by a rule, not tuned**: `w = mean NB loss of a reference trained decoder / mean JEPA loss`, both measured in eval mode without gradients, before any parameter update, on the first `anchor_batches` (default 20) training batches. The rule's rationale is scale calibration — equal loss values then mean the two terms contribute comparably *at the scale the reconstruction loss will settle at*. A freshly initialized decoder's loss is more than twice a trained one's, so measuring with it would overweight the anchor for most of training; hence `--ref-decoder` must point at an already-trained decoder (round 12 uses `norman_r11_dec_hvg_s0`), and the script refuses to start if the reference was trained with a different `--library-size` convention. A floor guard (`MIN_JEPA_LOSS = 1e-6`) aborts the run if the mean JEPA loss is too small, since the ratio would explode.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L125-L147), [26_score_round12.py](examples/perturbation_response/26_score_round12.py#L24-L33), [02_coadapt_decoder.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py#L100-L204)

Because equal losses do not imply equal *influence* on the encoder, the trainer also instruments the balance directly: on the first batch of each epoch it computes the encoder-gradient norm contributed by each term (`grad_nb`, and `grad_anchor` under the anchor) using `torch.autograd.grad(..., retain_graph=True)` so the measurement never touches `.grad` and the graph survives for the real backward pass. These norms land in the per-epoch history and are read as round-12 secondaries, letting you check whether the nominal weight balance translated into gradient balance.

> [!TIP]
> When reproducing the anchor rule, the measurement must happen with the loaded encoder before the first update and with a decoder trained under the *same* library-size convention — the script enforces both (eval-mode, no-grad measurement; `SystemExit` on a library-size mismatch). The test suite additionally asserts that running the rule changes no parameters, which is the property that makes the pre-registered weight trustworthy.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L149-L238), [test_coadapt.py](tests/test_coadapt.py#L42-L66)

## Training-Loop Instrumentation

Each epoch produces one record with a fixed schema, so arms are comparable without parsing logs:

| Field | Present in | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nb_loss`, `loss` | all modes | mean NB reconstruction loss and mean total loss |
| `jepa_loss` | `joint_anchor` | mean JEPA predictive loss (popped from the record in other modes) |
| `grad_nb`, `grad_anchor` | joint modes | encoder-gradient norm per term, epoch's first batch, before clipping |
| `effective_rank`, `feature_std` | all modes | collapse diagnostics on up to 4,096 cell vectors, detached |

The diagnostics come from `ssllab.eval.collapse`: `feature_std` is the mean per-dimension standard deviation (near zero ⇒ collapse), and `effective_rank` is the entropy of normalized singular values of the centered embedding matrix — a healthy encoder uses many directions, a collapsed one uses ~1. The module docstring is explicit about why these are recorded *during* training while the task-relevant checks run *after*: reconstruction discourages complete information loss, but it does not guarantee the optimizer keeps every useful direction or the perturbation information the benchmark needs — the linear readout and perturbation probe run on the saved encoder via `14_ceiling_analysis.py` and `02_probe_cell_encoder.py`.

Sources: [coadapt.py](src/ssllab/coadapt.py#L149-L238), [collapse.py](src/ssllab/eval/collapse.py#L1-L40)

## Inputs Beyond the Checkpoint: Latents, Library Size, Random Init

The trainer supports two variations that broaden what Phase 1 can compare. Under `--latents <store>` (mode `dec` only), the decoder trains on a precomputed embedding store (`ssllab.embeddings.PrecomputedSource`) instead of the JEPA encoder's vectors: each batch's cell vectors are looked up by cache row, the store's dataset fingerprint is verified against the cache, no encoder is loaded or saved, and the decoder's width becomes the store's dimension. This is how a decoder can be trained on another encoder's embeddings — for example Geneformer's cell embeddings — for a like-for-like stack comparison. Second, `--library-size hvg` (the default since round 11) computes the NB likelihood's total over the modeled genes; `all` reproduces earlier runs.

Sources: [02_coadapt_decoder.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py#L1-L53), [02_coadapt_decoder.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py#L58-L98)

For the attribution question "does JEPA pretraining itself contribute?", `--init random` (mode `joint` only) starts the encoder from freshly initialized weights of the same architecture via `random_jepa_like`, which reads only the checkpoint's config and builds with the same constructor `load_jepa` calls.

> [!TIP]
> The RNG-parity trick in `random_jepa_like` is what makes the control clean: it consumes the global random-number generator exactly as `load_jepa` does before loading weights, so after the same `set_seed` everything drawn afterwards — the decoder's initialization, shuffling — is identical between a pretrained start and a random one. The test suite verifies this draw-for-draw, meaning the *only* difference between `--init pretrained` and `--init random` at a fixed seed is the encoder's starting weights.

Sources: [checkpoint.py](src/ssllab/checkpoint.py#L43-L64), [test_coadapt.py](tests/test_coadapt.py#L126-L146)

## Phase 0: The Premise as a Number

Before reshaping the encoder so perturbations act linearly, Phase 0 checks whether they already do. The Koopman-linearity probe works entirely in latent space — no decoder, no Δr, because the ceiling analysis showed the transition stage has too little headroom for Δr to distinguish a linear latent transition from a nonlinear one. The instrument, per perturbation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph P["per perturbation"]
        CTRL["control cloud"] --> E0["frozen encoder embed"]
        PERT["perturbed cloud"] --> E0
        E0 --> PCA["top-k PCA subspace<br/>standardized per PC by control"]
        PCA --> SP["fit / eval halves<br/>train / val for early stop"]
        SP --> AFF["affine arm<br/>Az + b, Bures-optimal init"]
        SP --> NL["nonlinear arm<br/>z + MLP z, identity init"]
        AFF --> SC["energy distance<br/>on eval halves"]
        NL --> SC
        SC --> GAP["non_koopman_gap =<br/>reduction_nl - reduction_lin"]
    end
    GAP --> CI["bootstrap CI per stratum:<br/>singles, train/val/held-out combos"]
    CI --> GATE["pre-registered rule<br/>gates Phase 2 only"]
```

Three design choices make the verdict honest. **Energy distance, not per-pair error**, because sequencing is destructive — there is no "same cell before and after", so both arms are graded by matching marginals, the project's standing objective. **A PCA subspace (default 20 components)**, because a free 256×256 affine over a few-hundred-cell cloud overfits noise directions; a linear projection preserves the affine-vs-nonlinear question in the directions that carry the response, and the retained variance fraction is reported. **An asymmetric initialization**: the affine arm starts at the closed-form second-moment-optimal (Bures/Gaussian-OT) map with covariance shrinkage so it cannot underfit, while the nonlinear arm is a residual MLP whose final layer is zero-initialized (it starts as the identity), is weight-decayed, and is capacity-swept (hidden widths 8/32/128) so any measured gap must be real structure rather than "the biggest MLP won". An acceptance gate (`--null-tol`, default 0.05) checks that the gap shown on a synthetic exactly-affine cloud is small enough for the artifact subtraction to be trustworthy.

Sources: [01_koopman_linearity_probe.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/01_koopman_linearity_probe.py#L1-L68)

The headline result, run on the frozen `norman_stage_a` encoder (20 principal components, three seeds, acceptance gate passed):

| Stratum | Perturbations | Calibrated nonlinear gap, median | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|
| **single-gene** (primary) | 103 | **0.015** | **[0.003, 0.032]** |
| training combinations | 76 | 0.004 | [−0.002, 0.012] |
| validation combinations | 18 | 0.010 | [−0.003, 0.028] |
| held-out combinations | 15 | 0.010 | [−0.011, 0.023] |

By the pre-registered rule the verdict is **inconclusive**: the singles interval excludes zero, so the advantage is detectable, but the median is far below the 0.10 that would justify Phase 2. In substance, the response is **close to affine** — among the half of singles with the largest responses the median gap is 0.005, and the scattered large values come from perturbations that barely move the cloud. This reconciles round 4: the response is a large *but affine* transformation, so what failed was the near-identity assumption, not linearity. Noted limits: twenty components cover 17% of latent variance, and unpaired data shows distributions rather than individual cells.

Sources: [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/README.md#L46-L73)

## Phase 1 in the Field: The Round-12 Protocol

Round 12 executed Phase 1 under the corrected (round-11) likelihood, with the stakes restated in the pre-registered protocol: the stack's readout ceiling is 0.865 in Δ-correlation, below the conditioned NB-VAE's generative 0.939; the flow transition has about 0.03 of headroom under that ceiling; and about **0.135 is lost by the frozen encoder and the decoder reading real cells** — the quantity co-training attacks. The remote pipeline runs three seeds of `joint` and `joint_anchor`, re-reads round 11's `dec` arm as the control, then gives **every** arm the same readout treatment:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph S1["1. train"]
        T1["norman_r12_joint_s*"]
        T2["norman_r12_joint_anchor_s*"]
        T3["dec arm re-read<br/>norman_r11_dec_hvg_s*"]
    end
    subgraph S2["2. read each arm"]
        C1["14_ceiling_analysis<br/>identity / roundtrip / linear"]
        C2["02_probe_cell_encoder"]
    end
    subgraph S3["3. pipeline per arm"]
        F1["04_train_cond_flow<br/>round-1 recipe on new latents"]
        F2["06_eval_effect_size<br/>19_score_interaction<br/>10_eval_calibration"]
    end
    subgraph S4["4. compare"]
        SC["26_score_round12<br/>max-t contrasts, paired bootstrap"]
    end
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4
```

The **primary endpoint** is the readout-ceiling Δ-correlation (roundtrip) under the measured control, on the 20 held-out pairs, top 20 genes — a single max-t family of two contrasts (`joint − dec`, `joint_anchor − dec`), joint paired bootstrap over pairs (10,000 resamples, seed 0), with a pass rule of estimate ≥ +0.02 and a simultaneous interval wholly above 0. The pipeline script enforces hard **gates before anything is read**: the dec-arm ceiling must reproduce round 11's roundtrip to 1e-4, every identity arm must score 1.000, recomputed Δr must match stored reports to 1e-6, and every joint-arm report must record its mode and corrected library size; plus md5 preflight checks (the `de_genes.json` hash and the Stage A encoder's `38f51067` prefix). Secondaries include the linear readout of each encoder, full-pipeline Δr, transition headroom, population quality and calibration, representation diagnostics (effective rank, feature spread, the perturbation probe, and linear **CKA** against the original encoder to measure how far the representation actually moved), and the training diagnostics above.

Sources: [26_score_round12.py](examples/perturbation_response/26_score_round12.py#L1-L33), [26_score_round12.py](examples/perturbation_response/26_score_round12.py#L35-L49), [26_score_round12.py](examples/perturbation_response/26_score_round12.py#L54-L79), [run_coadapt_pod.sh](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/run_coadapt_pod.sh#L1-L46)

## Round 13: Does Pretraining Contribute?

Round 13 closes the loop opened by `--init random`. Three arms, three seeds each, all `--mode joint` with the corrected likelihood: round 12's pretrained `joint` (re-read, not retrained), `random_lr4` (random init at round 12's encoder learning rate of 1e-4), and `random_lr3` (random init at the decoder's 1e-3). Each random encoder gets its own readout ceiling, perturbation probe, and a transport flow retrained with round 1's recipe, read out through its own decoder; `27_score_round13.py` then compares the arms. The pipeline also demonstrates the project's smoke-first discipline: the entire round is executed at tiny settings (seed 0, one epoch, 2,000 cells) in a separate output directory built from copies of the real inputs, the comparison is run in smoke mode, and **any failure stops the round before full compute is spent**.

Sources: [run_round13_pod.sh](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/run_round13_pod.sh#L1-L31), [02_coadapt_decoder.py](examples/perturbation_response/co-adaptation/02_coadapt_decoder.py#L1-L53)

## What the Tests Pin Down

The test suite is small and fast (tiny synthetic cache, CPU, seconds) but covers the exact properties the experimental claims depend on:

| Test | Property pinned down |
|---|---|
| `test_load_jepa_teacher_is_a_copy_of_the_loaded_encoder` | a loaded JEPA's teacher equals the encoder; every parameter frozen |
| `test_each_mode_trains_what_it_says` (3 modes) | decoder always trains; encoder unchanged iff `dec`; predictor unchanged iff not `joint_anchor`; `grad_nb` recorded iff joint; running the anchor rule changes nothing |
| `test_anchor_mode_requires_a_weight` | `joint_anchor` without a fixed weight raises; invalid modes rejected |
| `test_trained_encoder_round_trips_through_save_and_load` | co-adapted encoder produces identical embeddings after save/load |
| `test_library_size_of…` / `test_depth_normalization…` / `test_hvg_library_size_trains…` | the likelihood's library-size conventions and the published depth-normalization formula |
| `test_cvae_records_library_size_and_normalizations` | checkpoints record the normalization convention; defaults since round 11 |
| `test_random_start_is_fresh_and_draws_like_a_pretrained_load` | `random_jepa_like` uses fresh constructor weights but identical RNG consumption |

The parametrized mode test is the load-bearing one: it converts the module's central contract — "the arms differ only in what trains" — from a docstring claim into an executable assertion, which is precisely what makes the `joint − dec` contrast interpretable.

Sources: [test_coadapt.py](tests/test_coadapt.py#L35-L40), [test_coadapt.py](tests/test_coadapt.py#L42-L66), [test_coadapt.py](tests/test_coadapt.py#L68-L87), [test_coadapt.py](tests/test_coadapt.py#L91-L146)

## Where This Fits and What to Read Next

Two disciplines connect this page to the rest of the catalog. First, **the boundary of attribution**: the conditional flow is never co-trained, so any co-adaptation gain can be credited to the encoder–decoder pair alone; each moved encoder gets its own flow retrained afterward with the unchanged round-1 recipe ([Flow-Matching Prior](9-flow-matching-prior), [Conditional Flow and Classifier-Free Guidance](10-conditional-flow-and-classifier-free-guidance)). Second, **ceiling invalidation**: every co-adapted encoder makes the old ceiling obsolete, because the ceiling is conditional on the frozen encoder — so a new ceiling, oracle, and linear readout are re-measured for each co-adapted encoder ([Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics)).

Suggested reading path: the decoder being co-trained is documented in [Count Decoders and CVAE Baseline](12-count-decoders-and-cvae-baseline); the simultaneous-inference machinery behind the round-12 verdict is [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference); the pre-registration protocol format is [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration); and Phase 2's operator context — the Koopman objective and the near-identity prior that Phase 0's result deprioritized — begins at [Generator Bases and Lie-Group Operators](13-generator-bases-and-lie-group-operators) and continues in [Operator Algebra and Epistasis Tests](14-operator-algebra-and-epistasis-tests). For the encoder-side mechanics the co-trainer relies on (EMA teacher, anti-collapse regularization), see [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals) and [Anti-Collapse: VICReg and SIGReg](8-anti-collapse-vicreg-and-sigreg).


# Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics



Every claim this repository makes about a self-supervised representation — that it is semantically useful, that it has not collapsed, that a generated population matches the real one — passes through one small package: `src/ssllab/eval`. This page documents that toolkit as an integrated system: the instruments, the call contracts that make them reusable across methods, and the conventions that make numbers comparable across experiments. It covers probes, collapse diagnostics, classification metrics, effect-size and calibration harnesses, generative-sample metrics with an independent oracle, and training-free baselines. The statistical machinery for *uncertainty over differences* (paired bootstrap) and the research-methodology essays are deliberately out of scope here — they have dedicated pages downstream in this section.

Sources: [probe.py](/src/ssllab/eval/probe.py#L1-L6), [\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/ssllab/eval/__init__.py#L1-L28)

## The Architecture: One Seam, Many Instruments

The toolkit is organized around a single architectural idea: **separate what produces a prediction from what grades it**. Every harness in `ssllab.eval` accepts a plain callable — a *scoring seam* — so a conditional flow, an NB-VAE baseline, and a hand-written additive reference are all fed through the identical grader and return identical shapes of output. The module inventory below maps each file to the question it answers; note that the harnesses (`effect_size`, `calibration`) never import a model, and the models never import each other.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Supply["Latent supply"]
        JEPA["JepaSource<br/>frozen encoder on demand"]
        PSTORE["PrecomputedSource<br/>embedding-store lookup"]
    end
    JEPA --> EXT["extract_latents<br/>(N, D) frozen features"]
    PSTORE --> EXT
    EXT --> PROBE["probe.linear_probe<br/>train / test accuracy"]
    EXT --> COLL["collapse.collapse_report<br/>feature_std · effective_rank"]

    subgraph Harness["Single-sourced harnesses"]
        EFF["effect_size.run_effect_size_eval<br/>predict_fn(pid, name) → mean profile"]
        CAL["calibration.run_calibration_eval<br/>predict_population_fn(pid, name) → population"]
    end
    ADD["baselines.additive_predictor<br/>(training-free reference)"] --> EFF
    LEARNED["learned predictor<br/>(flow / decoder / CVAE)"] --> EFF
    LEARNEDGEN["learned generator"] --> CAL
    ORACLE["oracle features<br/>(MnistCNN · domain model)"] --> GEN["generative metrics<br/>FID · KID · P/R · D/C · NN · classifier"]
```

| Module | Instrument | Question it answers | Input contract |
|---|---|---|---|
| `probe.py` | `linear_probe` | Is the frozen latent semantically useful? | `(z_train, y_train, z_test, y_test)` |
| `collapse.py` | `collapse_report` | Has the representation collapsed? | embedding batch `(M, D)` |
| `classification.py` | `per_label_metrics`, `macro_auroc`, `operating_point` | Are scores ranked well, and where do we cut? | binary labels `(n, K)`, scores `(n, K)` |
| `effect_size.py` | `run_effect_size_eval` | Does predicted Δ match true Δ? | `predict_fn(pid, name)` + eval split |
| `calibration.py` | `run_calibration_eval` | Does predicted *spread* match true spread? | `predict_population_fn(pid, name)` + eval split |
| `generative.py` | `fid`, `kid`, `precision_recall`, … | Are generated samples a faithful distribution? | feature vectors `(N, D)` or probs `(N, C)` |
| `oracle_mnist.py` | `MnistCNN` | An honest, independent feature space for grading samples | images |
| `baselines.py` | `additive_predictor` | What would a biologist write down with no model? | training cells only |
| `viz.py` | `save_image_grid` | A quick visual artifact of generated samples | image batch in `[0, 1]` |

Sources: [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L52-L111), [calibration.py](/src/ssllab/eval/calibration.py#L72-L140), [generative.py](/src/ssllab/eval/generative.py#L1-L16), [\_\_init\_\_.py](/src/ssllab/eval/__init__.py#L1-L28), [viz.py](/src/ssllab/eval/viz.py#L1-L18)

## Probing Frozen Representations: The Linear Probe

The linear probe is the headline instrument of self-supervised learning: freeze the encoder, fit a logistic regression on its embeddings, and report test accuracy. Well-above-chance accuracy means the encoder learned label-aligned structure without ever seeing a label — `probe.py` states this explicitly in its opening lines. The function is deliberately minimal: scikit-learn `LogisticRegression` with two knobs (`max_iter`, `C`), torch-or-numpy inputs, and a two-number return `{"train_acc", "test_acc"}`. The chance rate is *your* job to compute — 1/10 for MNIST digits, `1 / n_perturbations` for perturbation labels — and both example scripts log it alongside the probe score so the number is never read unanchored.

Sources: [probe.py](/src/ssllab/eval/probe.py#L1-L44), [02\_linear\_probe.py](/examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py#L62-L64), [02\_probe\_cell\_encoder.py](/examples/perturbation_response/02_probe_cell_encoder.py#L89-L98)

The canonical usage flow is three calls in `examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py`: load the frozen encoder from a checkpoint, extract pooled latents for the train/test loaders via `extract_latents`, then hand the four tensors to `linear_probe` and write the result into an experiment report. The same three-step pattern recurs in `examples/perturbation_response/02_probe_cell_encoder.py`, which probes whether cell latents linearly separate perturbation identities — explicitly framed as the *encoder-quality gate* before any generative stage, and as a representation check, not the effect-size benchmark that comes later.

Sources: [02\_linear\_probe.py](/examples/jepa_basics/02_linear_probe.py#L42-L77), [02\_probe\_cell\_encoder.py](/examples/perturbation_response/02_probe_cell_encoder.py#L1-L27)

## Latent Provenance: Sources, Stores, and Space Keys

Probes and generative harnesses both need "the vector of these dataset rows," however it is produced. The `embeddings` package formalizes this as a `LatentSource` interface with `encode(rows) -> (len(rows), dim)` plus an `identity()` dict that scripts embed into their reports — so every number can say which vectors it was computed on. Two implementations exist: `JepaSource` runs the frozen encoder on demand, and `PrecomputedSource` looks rows up in an embedding store written by any encoder.

| Source | `space_key` basis | `encode` behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `JepaSource` | MD5 over the online encoder's `state_dict` (names + tensor bytes), not the checkpoint file | runs `encode_rows` per call |
| `PrecomputedSource` | the store manifest's `space_key`; `open()` also verifies a dataset fingerprint | row lookup; a missing row raises |

> [!TIP]
> The `space_key` hashes *parameters*, not file bytes, so a re-saved checkpoint (as decoder-only co-adaptation runs produce) keeps its key — and because two different encoders can share a width (the project's JEPA and Geneformer V1 are both 256-d), `check_same_space` refuses to pair a flow and decoder trained in different latent spaces. Without that guard the mismatch would run silently and every downstream score would be meaningless.

When a wide embedding must be compared at equal width, `embeddings.project` fits a PCA on **training rows only** and writes the projection as a store of its own, recording the explained-variance share in the manifest — another number worth reporting, since it says how much of the wide embedding's spread survives the projection.

Sources: [source.py](/src/ssllab/embeddings/source.py#L1-L20), [source.py](/src/ssllab/embeddings/source.py#L31-L39), [source.py](/src/ssllab/embeddings/source.py#L121-L137), [project.py](/src/ssllab/embeddings/project.py#L1-L18), [project.py](/src/ssllab/embeddings/project.py#L49-L88)

## Collapse Diagnostics: The Cheap Signals

The failure mode a JEPA must avoid is *collapse* — every input mapping to nearly the same embedding — and `collapse.py` watches for it with two cheap signals computed straight off a batch of embeddings. **Feature std** is the mean per-dimension standard deviation; near zero means collapse. **Effective rank** is more interesting: it exponentiates the entropy of the centered matrix's normalized singular values, giving a soft rank in `[1, D]` — a healthy encoder spreads its energy across many directions and scores well above 1, while a collapsed one uses roughly one. The module notes that `svdvals` runs on CPU even on MPS devices, keeping this a tiny always-on diagnostic rather than a profiling chore.

```python
rep = collapse_report(Ztr)
# {"feature_std": ..., "effective_rank": ..., "embed_dim": ...}
```

In practice the probe and the collapse report are issued together as a single gate: `02_probe_cell_encoder.py` logs probe accuracy *and* effective rank in one line, with the comment that effective rank "must stay well above 1". This pairing matters because the two instruments fail in opposite directions — a probe can look fine on a partially collapsed representation that still preserves the label-relevant axis, while a high effective rank says nothing about semantics.

Sources: [collapse.py](/src/ssllab/eval/collapse.py#L1-L10), [collapse.py](/src/ssllab/eval/collapse.py#L18-L44), [02\_probe\_cell\_encoder.py](/examples/perturbation_response/02_probe_cell_encoder.py#L89-L98)

## Classification Metrics: AUROC, AUPRC, and Operating Points

For multi-label scoring tasks (the ECG rhythm study is the primary consumer), `classification.py` opens with a short conventions block that governs everything downstream: only the *order* of scores matters for AUROC/AUPRC, and an undefined metric is returned as NaN with a `defined=False` flag — **never dropped silently**, so a macro average over a fixed label set can be flagged incomplete. `per_label_metrics` returns AUROC, AUPRC, prevalence, and the positive count per label; `macro_auroc` averages over an explicitly given label index set and returns `(value, complete)`, refusing to shrink the set when one label has no positives or negatives on the evaluation side.

Sources: [classification.py](/src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L1-L12), [classification.py](/src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L27-L50)

> [!TIP]
> When you later bootstrap a *difference* between two methods over these metrics, those NaN conventions become load-bearing: undefined resamples are dropped and counted in `n_valid` rather than quietly zeroed, so an incomplete label set degrades your confidence interval's validity instead of faking a tighter one.

Beyond ranking metrics, the module provides threshold discipline for clinical-style operating points. `threshold_at_sensitivity` finds the *highest* (hence most specific) threshold meeting a sensitivity target, and its docstring carries the rule the whole system follows: **fit on validation, apply unchanged to test**. `operating_point` then converts a threshold into the full confusion picture — TP/FN/FP/TN counts plus sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and F1, each NaN-safe. The paired patient-cluster bootstrap that shares this module — how a difference between methods acquires a confidence interval — is documented separately in [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference).

Sources: [classification.py](/src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L55-L86)

## Effect Size: Grading the Change, Not the State

`effect_size.py` encodes the discipline from the project's design-space essays: score the **change** an intervention causes, not the absolute state. For a perturbation, the effect is its differential expression Δ = mean(perturbed) − mean(control), and a model is graded by Pearson correlation between its predicted Δ and the true Δ restricted to the **top differentially-expressed genes** — the genes the perturbation actually moved. This is the metric scGen / CPA / scPPDM report, so reproducing it makes the project's numbers comparable to published work.

Sources: [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L1-L10), [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L27-L41)

The harness is where the toolkit's architecture pays off. `run_effect_size_eval` takes a `predict_fn(pid, name) -> (G,)` callable plus the evaluation arrays, walks every evaluable perturbation, guards against tiny test sets (`min_test_cells`, default 20), and returns `(per_pert, summary)` with mean/median correlation and a perturbation count. The docstring states the point of the seam directly: it is used by the flow eval, the NB-VAE baseline, *and any future predictor*, so every method is graded identically. An optional `profiles` dict captures each perturbation's predicted mean profile so later metrics (magnitude, interaction) can be computed from exactly the predictions this score used — and the harness also logs best/worst perturbations for quick triage. NaN handling here is explicit rather than silent: `summarize` drops NaN correlations as a documented step.

Sources: [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L43-L62), [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L63-L111)

## Calibration: Grading the Spread, Not Just the Mean

Two models can produce identical mean predictions while disagreeing completely about *how much a perturbed population varies, and which genes vary* — and that is exactly where a full distribution over latents should beat a cruder generator. `calibration.py` is the instrument that decides whether the generative machinery earns its keep once the means tie, and it grades four complementary reads on each perturbation's top-DE genes, comparing a generated population against held-out real cells.

| Metric | What it compares | Healthy reading |
|---|---|---|
| `spread_r` | Pearson between predicted and true per-gene stds | → 1: model knows *which* genes vary |
| `coverage` | fraction of true cells inside the predicted central interval | ≈ nominal `hi − lo` (0.8 default); below = over-confident, above = under-confident |
| `mean_wasserstein` | per-gene 1-Wasserstein, averaged | lower |
| `energy` | multivariate 2-sample energy distance `2·E‖P−Q‖ − E‖P−P'‖ − E‖Q−Q'‖` | lower; 0 iff identical joint distributions |

The first three reads are per-gene marginals; `energy_distance` is the one that sees the *joint* distribution, so it is sensitive to gene-gene correlations and multimodality — structure a rich latent flow can capture but marginals cannot. `run_calibration_eval` mirrors the effect-size harness exactly (same callable seam, same `min_test_cells` guard, same `(per_pert, summary)` return shape) and anchors its summary with `nominal_coverage = hi − lo` so the coverage number is always read against its own target.

Sources: [calibration.py](/src/ssllab/eval/calibration.py#L1-L15), [calibration.py](/src/ssllab/eval/calibration.py#L29-L69), [calibration.py](/src/ssllab/eval/calibration.py#L72-L140)

## Generative Sample Metrics: Feature Space, Not Pixel Space

`generative.py` implements intrinsic sample-evaluation metrics with one hard rule stated in its docstring: every function operates on **feature vectors `(N, D)` or class probabilities `(N, C)` — never on raw images**. The same code therefore evaluates MNIST samples (features from a small CNN oracle) or DNA/protein samples (features from a domain encoder). The metric families:

| Family | Functions | Input | Question answered |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distributional distance | `fid`, `kid` | `(N, D)` features | Do Gaussian moments / polynomial-kernel MMD match? KID is more reliable at small N |
| Fidelity vs diversity | `precision_recall` (Kynkäänniemi 2019), `density_coverage` (Naeem 2020) | `(N, D)` features | Is the generated manifold inside the real one (precision/density), and vice versa (recall/coverage)? |
| Memorization | `nn_distance_stats` | query vs reference features | Tiny NN distances to train ⇒ copied data; compare against a real-test baseline |
| Classifier oracle | `classifier_metrics` | `(N, C)` probs | Confidence, normalized coverage entropy, classes covered — a mode-collapse readout |

Sources: [generative.py](/src/ssllab/eval/generative.py#L1-L16), [generative.py](/src/ssllab/eval/generative.py#L33-L71), [generative.py](/src/ssllab/eval/generative.py#L86-L143), [generative.py](/src/ssllab/eval/generative.py#L148-L172)

The feature space these metrics run in is supplied by an **independent oracle**, and `oracle_mnist.py` explains why independence is non-negotiable: evaluating a generator with its own encoder is circular, because the decoder was trained to satisfy that encoder. `MnistCNN` is a small Conv-Conv-FC classifier exposing two methods — `features()` returning the 128-d penultimate layer, and `proba()` returning class probabilities — and the module states the portability contract for other modalities: swap this oracle for a domain model (the docstring suggests a splice predictor or ESM) exposing the same `features`/`proba` API, while the metrics themselves stay untouched. `train_oracle` / `load_or_train_oracle` handle training-from-scratch and caching so scripts never silently probe with a half-trained grader.

Sources: [oracle_mnist.py](/src/ssllab/eval/oracle_mnist.py#L1-L12), [oracle_mnist.py](/src/ssllab/eval/oracle_mnist.py#L26-L99)

## Training-Free Baselines: The Additive Reference

A learned model's score means little until it sits beside the obvious answer a biologist would write down without any model. For a two-gene combination that answer is the **additive model** of genetic interaction — assume the interventions don't interact, so Δ(A+B) = Δ(A) + Δ(B), with each single-gene Δ estimated from *training-side* cells only, so the predictor never sees a held-out cell. The module notes that published work finds this hard to beat on Norman-style combination benchmarks, which is precisely why it exists as a graded peer rather than a footnote.

Sources: [baselines.py](/src/ssllab/eval/baselines.py#L1-L19)

`additive_predictor` returns a `predict_fn(pid, name)` closure in exactly the seam's shape, so it drops straight into `run_effect_size_eval` alongside the learned models. Because it produces a mean profile rather than a population, it has no calibration score — a documented limitation, not an oversight. One design detail is worth copying in your own baselines: if a gene in a combination has no matching single perturbation or no training cells, the call *raises* rather than dropping the term, because silently scoring a different model than the one you named is the kind of bug that survives for months.

Sources: [baselines.py](/src/ssllab/eval/baselines.py#L30-L71)

## Conventions That Make Scores Comparable

Across every module, the same five conventions recur. They are the reason a number written by `06_eval_samples.py` and a number written by `09_eval_cvae_baseline.py` (or their ECG-side counterparts) can be placed in one table and compared.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q["What are you measuring?"] --> A["Representation quality"]
    Q --> B["Predictive performance"]
    Q --> C["Generative fidelity"]
    A --> A1["linear probe<br/>semantics"]
    A --> A2["collapse report<br/>geometry"]
    B --> B1["AUROC / AUPRC<br/>ranking"]
    B --> B2["operating point<br/>thresholding"]
    C --> C1["Δ-correlation<br/>mean shift"]
    C --> C2["calibration<br/>spread"]
    C --> C3["FID / KID / P&R<br/>distribution"]
```

| Convention | Mechanism | Enforced in |
|---|---|---|
| Undefined ≠ zero | NaN + `defined` / `complete` flags, explicit drop in `summarize` | `classification`, `effect_size` |
| One grader, many models | `predict_fn` / `predict_population_fn` callable seams | `effect_size`, `calibration` |
| Split hygiene | probe on the `cells` split; additive reads `is_train` only; PCA fit on fit rows | `02_probe_cell_encoder`, `baselines`, `embeddings.project` |
| Fit on validation, apply to test | documented threshold contract | `classification.threshold_at_sensitivity` |
| Provenance per number | `identity()` / `space_key` recorded in checkpoints and reports; `check_same_space` | `embeddings.source` |
| Oracle independence | generator never grades with its own encoder | `oracle_mnist` + `generative` |

The split-hygiene row deserves one concrete example: pretraining uses the `combo` split so held-out combinations never leak, while the cell-encoder probe runs on the `cells` split — random per-cell hold-out — because a multiclass probe over perturbation labels is only well-posed when the same perturbation vocabulary appears on both sides. The example script documents this as two independent, intentional choices, not an oversight.

Sources: [02\_probe\_cell\_encoder.py](/examples/perturbation_response/02_probe_cell_encoder.py#L18-L22), [classification.py](/src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L1-L12), [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L43-L50), [baselines.py](/src/ssllab/eval/baselines.py#L8-L18), [source.py](/src/ssllab/embeddings/source.py#L53-L137)

## Where the Toolkit Ends and Inference Begins

The toolkit produces point estimates — one probe accuracy, one mean Δ-correlation, one FID. It deliberately stops before answering the question every verdict eventually faces: *is the difference between two methods real, or noise?* That question is answered downstream by the paired patient-cluster bootstrap and simultaneous-inference machinery, and the broader discipline of turning differences into verdicts is the subject of the methodology series. The applied pages show the toolkit in deployment: the perturbation-response pipeline wires the effect-size and calibration harnesses into its rounds, the ECG study consumes the per-label metrics, and the co-adaptation work exercises the space-key provenance guarantees.

Sources: [classification.py](/src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L88-L167), [effect_size.py](/src/ssllab/eval/effect_size.py#L52-L57)

## Next Steps

Natural reading order from here, following the Evaluation and Methodology section:

1. **[Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference)** — how the metrics above acquire confidence intervals when you compare two methods on the same patients.
2. **[Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series)** — the reasoning behind weak instruments, ceilings, and failure modes the toolkit's design assumes.
3. **[Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration)** — where these numbers get recorded so they can be trusted later.

To see the instruments in a full experimental arc first, read the applied studies: [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline), [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study), and [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder).


# Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference



This page documents the machinery behind every "A beats B" claim in ssl-lab: a **joint paired bootstrap** that resamples the evaluation units once and reuses that resample across an entire family of contrasts, then controls multiplicity with **max-t simultaneous intervals**. It exists as a library (`ssllab.eval.bootstrap`) and a cluster-bootstrap sibling (`ssllab.eval.classification`), consumed by the arm-comparison scripts in both the perturbation-response and ECG pipelines. The design goal is precise: intervals that are valid *simultaneously* over a family of claims, with verdicts permitted only on a pre-committed primary endpoint.

## The Unit of Analysis: Why Pairing Comes First

Every comparison in this repository is anchored to a deliberate choice of statistical unit. In the perturbation-response pipeline, the unit is the **held-out perturbation** — not the cell, not the gene, not the training seed. Each arm produces one number per perturbation (seed-averaged first), yielding a vector of ~20 values per arm; that vector, not a scalar, is the only sample available. A contrast such as `transport - gaussian` is then a **paired difference** computed over the same perturbations for both arms, which cancels per-perturbation difficulty (some perturbations are simply hard for everyone) and isolates the between-arm signal [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L5-L15). The ECG study makes the identical move one level up: the unit is the **patient**, and both arms are scored on the same patient resample with all of each patient's recordings kept together [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L9-L12).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph ARM["Arm A"]
        A1["metric per perturbation 1"]
        A2["metric per perturbation 2"]
        A3["..."]
    end
    subgraph ARMB["Arm B"]
        B1["metric per perturbation 1"]
        B2["metric per perturbation 2"]
        B3["..."]
    end
    A1 -->|"d₁ = A₁ − B₁"| D["paired differences d (n,)"]
    A2 -->|"d₂ = A₂ − B₂"| D
    A3 -->|...| D
    B1 --> A1
    B2 --> A2
    B3 --> A3
    D --> BOOT["joint bootstrap over perturbation indices"]
    BOOT --> CI["family of intervals with one shared resample"]
```

The pairing is what makes the resampling below meaningful: because both arms are evaluated on identical units, one resample of units serves every contrast at once, and the dependence between contrasts is preserved by construction rather than modeled after the fact.

Sources: [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L5-L15), [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L9-L12)

## One Resample for Everything

The contrasts in a typical comparison are **not independent**: `transport - gaussian` and `transport - vae` share an arm, and every contrast is computed on the same perturbation set. Bootstrapping each contrast in a separate call discards this dependence and forces a Bonferroni correction — which assumes independence — to be needlessly conservative [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L10-L15). The library's answer is a single index matrix drawn once and shared by every contrast:

- `resample_indices(n, n_boot, seed)` returns an `(n_boot, n)` integer matrix of bootstrap indices, drawn from one seeded RNG and intended to be passed to *every* contrast and metric in the family [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L26-L28).
- In the CLI consumer, the same discipline appears inline: `idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=(args.n_boot, n))` is computed once before any contrast is evaluated, with the comment "THE joint resample: one set of indices, reused for every contrast and metric" [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L144-L146).

The composition ablation demonstrates the intended library reuse pattern: it imports exactly `maxt_family, percentile_interval, resample_indices` and obtains the same arithmetic as script 12 without duplicating it [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L97-L101). This is the module's stated purpose — the procedure of `12_compare_arms.py` extracted as library functions so other comparisons use identical arithmetic [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L1-L7).

> [!TIP]
> One shared RNG seed (default `seed=0`) makes the entire inference run reproducible: re-running script 12 or 20 with the same inputs regenerates the identical index matrix, so every interval in the family — and the critical value derived from it — is bit-for-bit reproducible.

Sources: [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L10-L15), [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L26-L28), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L97-L101)

## Max-t Simultaneous Intervals: The Arithmetic

For each contrast with paired differences `d` (one value per perturbation), `contrast_stats` computes four quantities [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L31-L43):

1. `obs` — the observed mean difference.
2. `se` — its standard error, `std(d, ddof=1) / √n`.
3. `bmean` — bootstrap means: the differences are indexed by the shared `idx` matrix, giving an `(n_boot, n)` array whose row means are the bootstrap distribution of the contrast.
4. `t` — the **centered studentized statistic** per bootstrap iteration: `(bmean − obs) / bse`, guarded against division by near-zero standard errors (`bse > 1e-12`, else `t = 0`).

The multiplicity control then happens in `maxt_family`. Given a dict mapping contrast names to their per-perturbation differences and the shared index matrix, it stacks the absolute studentized statistics of all contrasts into a `(n_contrasts, n_boot)` matrix and takes, per bootstrap iteration, the **maximum |t| across the whole family**; the critical value `crit` is the `(1 − α)` percentile of that max distribution [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L52-L54). Each contrast then receives two intervals:

| Interval | Formula | Validity | Verdict role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ci_unadjusted` | percentile interval of `bmean` at `α/2`, `1−α/2` | per-contrast only | descriptive |
| `ci_simultaneous` | `obs ± crit · se` | **simultaneously over the family** | the only significance claim |

Because the same resample produced every contrast's studentized distribution, the max over the family captures the joint sampling behavior — contrasts sharing an arm move together in the bootstrap world exactly as they do in the real one. A contrast is called significant only if its simultaneous interval excludes zero [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L178-L192). The script logs the critical value next to the familiar unadjusted benchmark (1.96), making the price of family-wide error control explicit [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L174-L175).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D1["d₁ = transport − gaussian (per perturbation)"] --> CS["contrast_stats<br/>obs, se, bmean, t (studentized, centered)"]
    D2["d₂ = OT − transport"] --> CS
    D3["d₃ = transport − NB-VAE"] --> CS
    CS --> TMAX["T = |t| stacked over family<br/>per-iteration max → crit = 95th percentile of max"]
    TMAX --> SIM["ci_simultaneous = obs ± crit·se<br/>holds at 95% over ALL contrasts"]
    CS -->|"bmean only"| PCT["ci_unadjusted = percentile(bmean)<br/>per-contrast, descriptive"]
    SIM --> V{"interval excludes 0?"}
    V -->|yes| SIG["** significant (family-level claim)"]
    V -->|no| NS["not significant"]
```

Sources: [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L31-L43), [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L46-L62), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L159-L192)

## Primary and Secondary: Where Verdicts Are Allowed

Multiplicity is handled not only statistically but **procedurally**. With several contrasts times several metrics, testing each at α = 0.05 guarantees false positives under the global null, so the protocol splits metrics into two tiers [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L17-L27):

- **Primary** — exactly one metric, pre-committed via `--primary` (default `delta_r`, the effect-size Δ-correlation). Its contrast family receives max-t simultaneous intervals, and the `**` marker on a row is the *only* significance claim the script makes [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L159-L192).
- **Secondary / exploratory** — every other metric (the calibration family: `spread_r`, `coverage`, `wasserstein`, `energy`, with `LOWER_IS_BETTER` flags for direction) is reported with plain percentile CIs and **no verdict**, because a difference discovered on a secondary endpoint after the fact is a hypothesis, not a result — it needs confirmation on fresh held-out data or it does not get claimed [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L64-L65), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L194-L212).

The composition ablation applies the same discipline with a two-contrast primary family (`flow_ds - flow_add`, `vae_ds - vae_add`) and a decision rule expressed directly on the simultaneous interval: DeepSets improves on its additive predecessor if the interval lies wholly below 0, is worse if wholly above 0, otherwise inconclusive [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L112-L117), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L150-L155). It additionally hardens the protocol: the primary verdict stands only if at least 18 of the expected 20 pairs survive missing-value filtering (`MIN_PAIRS = 18`), otherwise the primary is reported as not evaluable [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L170-L179).

Sources: [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L17-L27), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L194-L212), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L150-L155)

## API Reference

The inference toolkit is intentionally small — four library functions plus one cluster-bootstrap workhorse:

| Function | Location | Signature (essentials) | Returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| `resample_indices` | [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L26-L28) | `(n, n_boot=10000, seed=0)` | `(n_boot, n)` shared index matrix |
| `contrast_stats` | [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L31-L43) | `(d: (n,), idx)` | `(obs, se, bmean, t)` tuple |
| `maxt_family` | [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L46-L62) | `(diffs: dict[str, (n,)], idx, alpha=0.05)` | `{"critical_value", "contrasts": {name: {diff, se, ci_unadjusted, ci_simultaneous}}}` |
| `percentile_interval` | [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L65-L70) | `(values: (n,), idx, alpha=0.05)` | `{"mean", "ci"}` on the shared resample |
| `paired_cluster_bootstrap` | [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L117-L161) | `(metric, y, scores_a, scores_b, clusters, n_boot=2000, seed=0, alpha=0.05, repeats=False)` | `BootstrapResult` |
| `macro_auroc_metric` | [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L164-L166) | `(label_idx)` closure | `metric(y_subset, s_subset)` adapter returning NaN if a label is undefined |

`BootstrapResult` carries `estimate` (the metric difference on the original sample), `ci_low`/`ci_high` (percentile interval), `n_boot`, `n_valid` (resamples where the metric was defined for *both* methods), and the raw `samples` array [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L100-L107). The `metric` callable must return a float and may return NaN; undefined resamples are dropped and counted rather than silently averaged [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L136-L137).

Sources: [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L26-L70), [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L100-L161)

## Two Bootstrap Variants: Perturbation-Unit vs Patient-Cluster

The repository runs two sibling implementations of the same philosophy — pair the arms, resample the units once — differing in unit structure and output shape:

| Dimension | Perturbation-unit bootstrap | Patient-cluster bootstrap |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | held-out perturbation (one scalar per arm) | patient (a cluster of recordings) |
| Implementation | `ssllab.eval.bootstrap` (vectorized, all contrasts at once) | `ssllab.eval.classification.paired_cluster_bootstrap` (per-contrast loop) |
| Resample mechanics | index matrix `(n_boot, n)` via `d[idx]` fancy indexing | `_cluster_index` groups recording indices by patient; each iteration resamples whole clusters via `np.concatenate([groups[g] for g in pick])` [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L110-L114), [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L152-L158) |
| Multiplicity | max-t over the contrast family | per-pair percentile intervals (one primary pair family of three) |
| Repeats handling | seeds averaged per unit *before* the bootstrap | two modes: per-repeat bootstraps, and `repeats=True` where the statistic is the mean over repeats scored on the **same** patient resample [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L131-L134) |
| Undefined resamples | studentized t guarded to 0 at near-zero SE | dropped from the percentile computation, counted in `n_valid` |
| Primary consumer | `12_compare_arms.py`, `20_compare_composition.py` | `06_compare_arms.py` |

The cluster variant exists because ECG recordings from the same patient are not independent draws — resampling patients with replacement, keeping all their recordings, is the only resampling that reflects how the test set was sampled [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L9-L12). In `06_compare_arms.py`, each (pair, budget) task produces three layers: per-repeat paired bootstraps (seeded `1000 + r` for reproducibility), a repeat-mean bootstrap where every repeat is scored on the same patient resample (seed 999, `repeats=True`), and — kept deliberately separate — the raw repeat-to-repeat spread of per-repeat differences, which measures training variability without pretending it is test-set uncertainty [06_compare_arms.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/06_compare_arms.py#L57-L72).

> [!TIP]
> The seed conventions (`1000 + r` per repeat, 999 for the repeat mean, 0 for the perturbation bootstrap) are not cosmetic — they let a rerun reproduce any single layer of the comparison independently, which is essential when a 250-line comparison script is debugged one layer at a time.

Sources: [classification.py](src/ssllab/eval/classification.py#L110-L161), [06_compare_arms.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/06_compare_arms.py#L57-L72)

## Pipeline Integration: From Reports to Verdict

The comparison scripts never recompute metrics; they consume the per-perturbation (or per-recording) reports written by earlier pipeline stages and operate purely on aggregation and resampling. This is the module interaction structure:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph PRODUCERS["Scoring stages (per arm, per seed)"]
        E["06_eval_effect_size.py → effect_size.json (per_pert)"]
        C["10_eval_calibration.py → calibration_flow/vae.json (per_pert)"]
    end
    subgraph COMPARE["Comparison stage"]
        LA["load_arm: seed-average per perturbation<br/>keep only perts with all seeds finite"]
        SUP["common support: perts every arm scored<br/>(n &lt; 5 → abort)"]
        IDX["joint resample idx (n_boot, n)"]
        MF["primary: maxt_family → crit + simultaneous CIs"]
        SEC["secondary: percentile CIs only"]
        OUT["JSON summary + logged verdict table"]
    end
    subgraph LIB["ssllab.eval"]
        BS["bootstrap.py (12, 20)"]
        CLS["classification.paired_cluster_bootstrap (06)"]
    end
    E --> LA
    C --> LA
    LA --> SUP --> IDX
    IDX --> MF --> OUT
    IDX --> SEC --> OUT
    BS -.-> MF
    BS -.-> IDX
    CLS -.->|"ECG: patient clusters, repeats"| MF2["per-repeat + repeat-mean intervals"]
```

The aggregation order is strict and documented: load each arm's reports, seed-average per perturbation, keep a perturbation only if *every* requested seed produced a finite value [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L82-L105), intersect across arms and metrics to find the common support [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L130-L142), then resample once and evaluate the primary family and secondaries on that one resample [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L144-L157). The output JSON records everything needed for audit: `n_perturbations`, `n_boot`, `alpha`, the primary metric name, `maxt_critical_value`, the perturbation list, and per-contrast intervals with a `significant_simultaneous` boolean [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L164-L166), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L186-L191).

Sources: [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L82-L105), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L130-L157), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L186-L191)

## What the Intervals Cover — and What They Deliberately Do Not

The module is unusual in how explicitly it states the limits of its own output. Three caveats are stated in both the library docstring and the consumer's final log block, and none are hidden:

- **Test-set uncertainty only.** Seeds are averaged per perturbation *before* the bootstrap, so the intervals describe uncertainty from the finite set of held-out perturbations, not from training randomness. With three seeds, seed variance cannot be estimated well enough to propagate, so the intervals are conditional on the seed-averaged model and understate total uncertainty — "stated, not hidden" [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L29-L32), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L214-L217).
- **Units are not strictly i.i.d.** Perturbations share genes (the ECG analogue: patients share demographics), so the exchangeability assumption the bootstrap relies on is approximate — if anything, this makes the reported CIs too narrow [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L216-L217), [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L17-L18).
- **Minimum sample guards.** Fewer than 5 shared perturbations aborts script 12 outright [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L138-L139); the composition ablation demotes the primary to "not evaluable" below 18 of 20 pairs [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L170-L179).

For the ECG study, the split discipline adds one more boundary: with `--split val` only the machinery is exercised — "numbers on validation are not results" — and the AF operating point is fitted on validation by a pre-declared threshold rule, then applied unchanged to test [06_compare_arms.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/06_compare_arms.py#L15-L19). Together these rules implement a single epistemic stance: an interval is a statement about a specific, finite, named sampling frame, and a verdict is a claim made once, on the primary endpoint, with family-level error control.

Sources: [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L29-L32), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L214-L217), [bootstrap.py](src/ssllab/eval/bootstrap.py#L17-L18), [06_compare_arms.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/06_compare_arms.py#L15-L19)

## Where This Fits in the Evaluation Stack

This page sits between metric computation and experimental protocol. Upstream, the metrics that feed the bootstrap — Δ-correlation on top-DE genes, calibration spreads, macro AUROC — are defined in [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics); the metric that is usually chosen as primary (`delta_r`) is the effect-size correlation documented there. Downstream, the procedural half of this page — pre-committing the primary, treating secondary findings as hypotheses, logging caveats in machine-readable JSON — connects directly to the discipline described in [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series) and to the audit trail maintained per [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration). If you want to see the machinery exercised end-to-end on a real benchmark, the arm-comparison entry points are `12_compare_arms.py` (four model arms, three contrasts), `20_compare_composition.py` (the composition ablation with an evaluable-primary guard), and `06_compare_arms.py` (the ECG study's patient-clustered comparison across finetune / probe / scratch).


# Experimental Methodology Series



This page documents the repository's **Experimental Methodology Series** — an eight-chapter treatise living in `docs/experimental-method/` that teaches how to run experiments you can trust. Its scope is deliberately narrow and deliberately deep: not modeling ideas, but the *scaffolding* around them — how to measure, how to compare, and how to know when a number is telling you something. Every principle is illustrated on one real, mostly losing project (a generative-JEPA system for single-cell perturbation response), because a loss forces the question *is this real, or did I measure it wrong?* — and that project answered "measured it wrong" more than once. This page sits in the **Evaluation and Methodology** cluster, alongside the practical companions [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics) and [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference).

Sources: [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L1-L8)

## The Series Architecture at a Glance

The series is structured as a narrative arc, not a reference manual. Chapters 1–5 build a **trust chain** (measure → locate → denoise → design → verdict), Chapter 6 is a catalogue of the ways the chain breaks, and Chapters 7/7a turn trusted measurement into a *decision instrument* for research direction. The two defining habits of the whole series are stated in its index: **make every stage assert something about its own output before the next stage consumes it**, and **before you improve a component, measure whether it can matter**.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Trust Chain — building a verdict"
        C1["Ch 1<br/>Unit of analysis<br/>per-item vectors"] --> C2["Ch 2<br/>The scoring seam<br/>support selection"]
        C2 --> C3["Ch 3<br/>Seeds & noise<br/>seed vs metric noise"]
        C3 --> C4["Ch 4<br/>Ablations vs controls<br/>one lever per arm"]
        C4 --> C5["Ch 5<br/>Paired bootstrap<br/>max-t simultaneous CI"]
    end
    C5 --> C6["Ch 6<br/>Failure modes<br/>specimen catalogue"]
    C2 -. "self-guarding criterion" .-> C7a
    C5 --> C7["Ch 7<br/>The ceiling<br/>oracle ladder"]
    C7 --> C7a["Ch 7a<br/>Weak instruments<br/>probes & diagnostics"]
    C6 -. "assert-at-stage habit" .-> C1
```

Sources: [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L16-L27), [01-what-are-you-measuring.md](docs/experimental-method/01-what-are-you-measuring.md#L1-L148), [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L1-L12)

| Chapter | File | Core claim | One-line countermeasure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `01-what-are-you-measuring.md` | The *shape* of a metric (unit of analysis) decides whether statistics are possible | Emit per-item vectors; pre-commit one primary endpoint |
| 2 | `02-the-scoring-seam.md` | Support selection code is upstream of every check and can silently define what your benchmark can see | Rank by test statistics; gate the seam with assertions |
| 3 | `03-seeds-and-noise.md` | Seed noise and metric noise are different quantities with different fixes | 3-seed sweep minimum; check the ruler before buying compute |
| 4 | `04-ablations-and-controls.md` | Ablations isolate, controls calibrate — never read one as the other | One lever per arm; design stages for separability |
| 5 | `05-from-difference-to-verdict.md` | A difference is not a verdict; dependent contrasts need joint resampling | Paired bootstrap; max-$t$ simultaneous intervals |
