| 6 | `06-failure-modes.md` | Broken measurements don't announce themselves; broken ideas do | Catalogue of five specimen failures with countermeasures |
| 7 | `07-the-ceiling.md` | Before improving a stage, replace it with an oracle and measure the ceiling | Build a ladder of oracles; commit to decision rules in advance |
| 7a | `07a-probes-and-weak-instruments.md` | The most informative diagnostic is the weakest one that can answer the question | Choose instruments by what they are *structurally unable to fake* |

Sources: [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L16-L27)

## The Worked Example as the Series' Spine

Every chapter is grounded in a single project: making a JEPA representation *generative* for gene perturbation prediction and trying to beat the established conditional generators (the CPA/scPPDM lineage) at their own game. The project structure is a three-stage pipeline — **Stage A** (frozen self-supervised JEPA encoder), **Stage B** (generative model over frozen latents: conditional flow or action operator), **Stage C** (count decoder) — and the test set is twenty held-out two-gene perturbation combinations. The design made the project a superior teaching vehicle: a win hides your methodology because nobody audits a result they like, while this project's central early result turned out to be an artifact of two lines of gene-selection code.

Sources: [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L10-L14), [03-seeds-and-noise.md](docs/experimental-method/03-seeds-and-noise.md#L92-L98)

The full method writeup lives in the example tree at `examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/index.md`, with a running scoreboard in its results ledger; the pipeline itself is documented on [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline). The series and the code are tightly coupled: Chapter 5 names its implementation script explicitly as `12_compare_arms.py`, which loads each arm's per-item reports, seed-averages them, intersects arms onto a common support, and runs the joint bootstrap.

Sources: [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L31-L35), [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L186-L189), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L1-L52)

## Chapters 1–2: What You Measure and Where the Seam Is

**Chapter 1** argues that a metric has a *shape*, not just a value, and that the load-bearing question is **what is one observation?** An aggregate score is a sample of size $n=1$ — unbootstrappable, unrepairable after the fact. The fix is structural: define the metric per item and emit a vector (`{"per_item": scores, "mean": ...}`), so the aggregate becomes a summary of the vector rather than a substitute for it. The worked example's unit is the perturbation (n = 20), never the cell, the gene, or the seed — the classic **pseudoreplication** trap, since the numerous thing (thousands of cells) lives *inside* the exchangeable thing (perturbations). The chapter then demands a **single primary endpoint declared before you look**, with arithmetic as the argument: ~20 available tests at α = 0.05 means you *expect one* false finding under the global null — and it will look exactly like the real ones.

Sources: [01-what-are-you-measuring.md](docs/experimental-method/01-what-are-you-measuring.md#L4-L8), [01-what-are-you-measuring.md](docs/experimental-method/01-what-are-you-measuring.md#L40-L48)

The chapter closes with the project's own cautionary tale: the flow beat the VAE baseline on joint energy distance (3.578 vs 3.962), on the metric its architecture was justified by — announced as a finding, then withdrawn when the bootstrap interval $[-0.960, +0.172]$ crossed zero. Secondary, post-hoc, found on a metric changed mid-project: every rule of the chapter violated at once. Its final habit: **write down, next to your primary metric, the thing it cannot see** — for the effect-size correlation, that is spread, shape, modality, and cross-gene structure, which is precisely why the calibration metrics exist.

Sources: [01-what-are-you-measuring.md](docs/experimental-method/01-what-are-you-measuring.md#L104-L128), [01-what-are-you-measuring.md](docs/experimental-method/01-what-are-you-measuring.md#L131-L148)

**Chapter 2** — flagged by the series as its most important chapter — names the **scoring seam**: the support (subset of items/features) every metric is computed on, chosen by criterion code that nobody audits because it looks like plumbing. Its general law: *a metric computed on the wrong support does not fail loudly; it returns a well-formed, stable, plausible, meaningless number.* The project's seam was a gene list ranked by $\log_2$ fold change, whose pseudocount-guarded ratio explodes exactly on silent genes — selecting, with high reliability, genes detected in **0% of cells**. Consequences cascaded through the entire scoreboard: coverage forced to exactly 1.00 for every model at every seed, per-gene spread correlation driven by floating-point noise, and the effect-size correlation degenerated into a constant (every perturbation's true $\Delta$ reduced to the same fixed vector $-\bar{x}^{\text{ctrl}}_g$), producing the false headline that the elaborate method *tied* its baseline.

Sources: [02-the-scoring-seam.md](docs/experimental-method/02-the-scoring-seam.md#L9-L16), [02-the-scoring-seam.md](docs/experimental-method/02-the-scoring-seam.md#L76-L89)

The fix is stated as a design principle, not a heuristic: **rank by a test statistic, not an effect ratio.** The Wilcoxon rank-sum $z$-statistic is **self-guarding** — built from rank orderings, it is *structurally unreachable* by the two-stray-transcripts pathology, with no pseudocount and no filter to remember. Selection quality transformed (mean expression 0.0006 → 2.40; detection 0% → 83%; significance 0% → 100%) and the arms stopped tying. On top of the ranking sit detection/significance filters and an assertion that refuses to write its cache on an invalid support — guards that almost never fire, which is the point: a guard that never fires is a **tripwire** converting future silent failures into loud ones. The chapter generalizes the seam to other fields (LLM benchmark subsets, RL episode filters, forecasting windowing, IR gold sets) and prescribes the practice: find the line of code that chooses your support, ask what its criterion *maximizes*, inspect the selected items directly, then gate it.

Sources: [02-the-scoring-seam.md](docs/experimental-method/02-the-scoring-seam.md#L120-L146), [02-the-scoring-seam.md](docs/experimental-method/02-the-scoring-seam.md#L160-L195)

> [!TIP]
> The fold-change failure and the fix share one property worth carrying everywhere: the winning criterion has the null hypothesis built into its denominator. When evaluating any selection rule, ask whether its failure mode is *structurally impossible* or merely *usually filtered* — the second kind survives until someone copies the two lines without the filter.

## Chapters 3–4: Noise You Can Measure, Designs You Can Attribute

**Chapter 3** decomposes what a seed actually controls (weight initialization, minibatch order, stochastic regularization, and — the one that bites generative work — sampling at generation time), then introduces the **seed sweep** as the non-optional minimum: three seeds per configuration, recording individual scores because they *are* the noise floor. Its rule: **any claimed improvement smaller than the noise floor is not a claim, it is a coin flip.** But the chapter's central insight inverts the diagnosis: when the scoring seam was fixed, the Gaussian flow's three seeds went from spanning 0.061 to spanning 0.012 — same models, same seeds, only the scoring changed. **Most of what had been attributed to seed noise was measurement noise**, and a better-conditioned metric bought statistical power for free, retroactively, at zero GPU-hours.

Sources: [03-seeds-and-noise.md](docs/experimental-method/03-seeds-and-noise.md#L18-L27), [03-seeds-and-noise.md](docs/experimental-method/03-seeds-and-noise.md#L52-L68)

The chapter is honest about its own hole: the sweep re-seeds Stages B and C but not the frozen Stage A encoder, so reported seed noise excludes encoder-initialization variance; and the from-scratch NB-VAE baseline trains end-to-end, so its seed perturbs everything — which is exactly why the baseline got its own three-seed sweep before its win ($\bar{s} = 0.766$ vs 0.648, a gap ~10× either noise floor) could be declared. The diagnostic question when the noise floor looks bad is not "how many more seeds can I afford?" but **"is this variance coming from the model, or from the ruler?"** — only one of those fixes is expensive.

Sources: [03-seeds-and-noise.md](docs/experimental-method/03-seeds-and-noise.md#L70-L98), [03-seeds-and-noise.md](docs/experimental-method/03-seeds-and-noise.md#L100-L115)

**Chapter 4** draws the series' sharpest conceptual line: **ablations isolate, controls calibrate.** An ablation changes exactly one lever (flow source: Gaussian vs real control latent; minibatch coupling: independent vs OT; decoder flags; operator-vs-flow). The NB-VAE control changes *every* lever simultaneously — different encoder, prior, decoder, all trained end-to-end — so it cannot attribute the 0.118 gap, but it answers a different question: *does all this machinery beat a simple, honest alternative?* Reading the control as an ablation ("the gap is the JEPA encoder's fault") is the specific failure mode the chapter exists to prevent. The project also confesses its own two-lever arm (stochastic coefficients + per-condition residual bundled together), which regressed and produced a coherent mechanism story the experiment **cannot test** — recorded in the ledger as a hypothesis, not a finding.

Sources: [04-ablations-and-controls.md](docs/experimental-method/04-ablations-and-controls.md#L18-L27), [04-ablations-and-controls.md](docs/experimental-method/04-ablations-and-controls.md#L63-L80)

The chapter's structural contribution is why ablations are cheap here: given the frozen latents, **Stage B and Stage C are conditionally independent** — no training signal crosses the boundary — so *an experiment retrains only the stage it changes*. A decoder ablation with four variants reuses cached encoder latents and flow samples; an operator-vs-flow comparison shares a byte-identical evaluation pipeline. The general research argument: separability is not engineering hygiene, it is what makes a monolithic end-to-end system *harder to learn from*, because every question costs a full retrain. The chapter closes with the fair-comparison checklist (same evaluator code, same test split including Stage A's pretraining data, shared seeds, same control reference, and — the most-violated rule — **the baseline gets the same conditioning information**; the VAE was deliberately given the identical compositional gene-set embedding rather than one-hot conditioning it could not generalize with) and the instruction: *build the strongest, fairest baseline you can, and want it to be strong.*

Sources: [04-ablations-and-controls.md](docs/experimental-method/04-ablations-and-controls.md#L82-L121), [04-ablations-and-controls.md](docs/experimental-method/04-ablations-and-controls.md#L123-L174)

## Chapter 5: From a Difference to a Verdict

This chapter specifies the statistical machinery, implemented one-to-one in `12_compare_arms.py`: form per-item differences $d_i = A_i - B_i$, resample item indices with replacement $R = 10{,}000$ times, and read 95% intervals from the replicate distribution. **Pairing is not optional** on a small test set: items differ enormously in intrinsic difficulty, and differencing cancels hardness out of $d_i$, whereas comparing unpaired intervals lets between-item variance swamp a between-arm effect one or two orders of magnitude smaller. Seeds are averaged per perturbation *before* the test — a stated, not hidden, limitation: intervals capture test-set uncertainty, not training randomness, because three draws cannot support a seed-variance estimate worth propagating.

Sources: [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L13-L30), [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L70-L78), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L9-L25)

The multiplicity arithmetic is done explicitly: ~4 contrasts × 5 metrics ≈ 20 tests, so under the global null you *expect one false positive*. Bonferroni is rejected for a structural reason — the contrasts share arms (transport appears in two of them) and share items, so they are positively dependent and Bonferroni's independence assumption over-corrects. The fix is a **joint bootstrap**: resample item indices once per iteration and evaluate every contrast on that same resample, preserving the dependence structure by construction. Max-$t$ **simultaneous intervals** then bootstrap the family-wide studentized maximum $M^{(r)} = \max_c |t_c^{(r)}|$, yielding one critical value ($q \approx 2.95$ vs the unadjusted 1.96) whose intervals hold at 95% *simultaneously* across the family.

Sources: [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L86-L110), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L60-L75)

The verdicts table shows the method earning its keep: transport − Gaussian $+0.036$ $[+0.019, +0.052]$ **significant**; OT − transport $-0.021$ $[-0.039, -0.002]$ **significant** (the clever coupling *hurts*); transport − NB-VAE $-0.118$ $[-0.228, -0.008]$ **significant** (the baseline wins); operator − transport $-0.003$ $[-0.030, +0.024]$ an honest null reported with an informative interval. Secondary endpoints get intervals, **no verdicts** — the rule enforced in code, born from the retracted joint-energy finding of Chapter 1. The chapter also audits itself: the bootstrap assumes i.i.d. items, and the twenty held-out combinations *share genes*, so effective sample size is below twenty and the intervals understate true uncertainty. The moral: **the machinery is not there to help you argue for your findings; it is there to stop you from believing your own favourite result** — it earns its keep on the day it takes something away from you. The deeper implementation walkthrough lives on [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference).

Sources: [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L115-L131), [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L166-L189)

## Chapter 6: A Catalogue of Ways an Experiment Lies

Five specimen failures, all real, none of which crashed anything — every pipeline ran to completion and produced plausible, stable, wrong numbers. They are presented with general form and countermeasure:

| # | Failure | Instance | Countermeasure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Better training loss, worse model | OT coupling: flow-matching loss 1.96 → 1.48, effect score *significantly worse* $[-0.039, -0.002]$; repeated with a dispersion anchor and the stochastic operator — **three times** | Report target metric alongside loss, same table, every arm; treat divergence as a finding |
| 2 | The two-lever arm | Stochastic coefficients + residual displacement bundled; result uninterpretable three ways | One lever per arm, always; a bundle is a demo, label it as one |
| 3 | The silently clobbering fetch | Blanket `rsync` overwrote seven locally-correct reports with stale remote ones | Hash artifacts inside results; fetch selectively; make sync direction explicit |
| 4 | The meaningless silence | Dead-looking log stream over a healthy job; "pod left running" printed on failure | Check the authoritative source (job queue), never the wrapper |
| 5 | Pseudoreplication | Thousands of cells per perturbation tempting an $n$ four orders of magnitude too large | Fix the unit at the top of the analysis script; no code path to any other level |

Sources: [06-failure-modes.md](docs/experimental-method/06-failure-modes.md#L9-L16), [06-failure-modes.md](docs/experimental-method/06-failure-modes.md#L63-L90)

Failure 1 deserves emphasis because it is the signature: the training objective is a **proxy** — differentiable, stable, and correlated with the goal, and each of those properties is why it is not the goal. The sharpest version: *a loss that improves while the target metric does not is not noise — it is information that the gap between your proxy and your goal is real and load-bearing.* The chapter's unifying countermeasure is the series' opening habit: in every case a stage received input it should have rejected and processed it happily, so **make each stage the last place its own bugs can hide** — the feature-selection stage now refuses to write its cache if the selected features are not actually detected in the data. Discovered anywhere downstream, the number is already wearing a suit.

Sources: [06-failure-modes.md](docs/experimental-method/06-failure-modes.md#L17-L35), [06-failure-modes.md](docs/experimental-method/06-failure-modes.md#L108-L124)

## Chapters 7 and 7a: The Ceiling and the Instruments That Find It

Chapter 7 is the constructive turn. Three rounds of transition-model improvement (0.612 → 0.648 → 0.645) never asked the deciding question: **given this encoder and this decoder, what is the best score *any* transition could achieve?** The answer, measured without training anything, was 0.679 — meaning the stage under three months of active development held at most 0.031 of headroom. The method is **oracle substitution**: replace a stage's output with the ground truth it was trying to produce (the skyline twin of a baseline), and build a **ladder**, not a single rung, so the loss decomposes by stage.

Sources: [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L14-L27), [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L40-L52)

The project's four-rung ladder and its loss budget:

| Rung | Score | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| Identity (metric fed the truth itself) | 1.000 | Harness sanity gate — must be perfect |
| Roundtrip (real latents → real decoder) | 0.679 | **The ceiling** for this decoder |
| Latent-mean (real latents, collapsed to mean) | 0.706 | Spread does not help a mean-comparing metric |
| Linear readout (real latents → plain linear map) | 0.852 | The representation, read out linearly |

| Step | From | To | Lost | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Encoder (under a *linear* readout) | 1.000 | 0.852 | 0.148 | what a linear map cannot recover |
| Decoder | 0.852 | 0.679 | 0.173 | ~6× the transition's loss — the real bottleneck |
| Transition | 0.679 | 0.648 | 0.031 | the stage everyone was improving — saturated |

Sources: [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L40-L72)

Three readings changed the project: the transition is **saturated**; the readout is where the score is actually lost; and — the rung nobody was built to find — a *linear* readout of the frozen representation (0.852) sat above the baseline that had been beating the method (0.766), relocating the problem entirely. The chapter's subtleties keep it honest: a ceiling is not a result, it is specific to what you held fixed, it inherits its reference, and every rung is cheap because **it trains nothing** — substitution plus a forward pass. The recipe transfers universally (gold-context for RAG retrievers, hand-written correct plans for agents, privileged state in RL, true future covariates in forecasting).

Sources: [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L62-L96), [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L98-L116)

Companion **7a** reveals that the ceiling's linear arm and the pipeline's long-standing encoder probe (`02_probe_cell_encoder.py`) are the same instrument — the **linear evaluation protocol** from representation learning — wearing two heads: logistic regression asks *which* perturbation (identity), ridge regression asks *what it did* (quantity). Its selection rule unifies the whole series' diagnostic philosophy: **a diagnostic is only informative if it is structurally unable to give you a good answer for the wrong reason**, which is the same property Chapter 2 called *self-guarding* and Chapter 7's oracle embodies (a perfect stage cannot score better than perfect). Hence the corollary: **the most informative instrument is usually the weakest one that can still answer the question** — a linear probe's weakness makes its claim a *lower bound* on accessible signal, and a flexible probe would confound representation quality with probe capacity. The chapter then organizes the full toolbox by question — representation quality (linear/k-NN/nonlinear probes, effective rank via eigenvalue entropy, CKA/RSA), bottleneck location (oracle ladder, ablations), generator health (posterior collapse via per-dimension KL, prior-vs-aggregate-posterior mismatch, reconstruction-generation gap, two-sample energy distance, the total-variance split $\mathrm{Var}[x_g] = \sigma^2_{\text{dec}} + \sigma^2_{\text{bio}}$ computed in `11_diagnose_variance.py`, calibration/coverage), and training sanity (target metric beside the loss, init-time no-op assertions, shuffled-label permutation nulls).

Sources: [07a-probes-and-weak-instruments.md](docs/experimental-method/07a-probes-and-weak-instruments.md#L6-L32), [07a-probes-and-weak-instruments.md](docs/experimental-method/07a-probes-and-weak-instruments.md#L84-L129)

> [!TIP]
> When you adopt the oracle-ladder practice, gate it with the identity rung and pre-commit the decision rule (what counts as "saturated" numerically) *before* reading the ceiling — otherwise the ceiling becomes decoration for the direction you had already chosen, which is exactly the failure Chapter 5 exists to prevent.

## How the Series Maps to Code

The series is not abstract: each chapter's discipline is enforced by a script in the perturbation-response example. The relationship between the methodology and its enforcement points:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph docs["docs/experimental-method"]
        M1["Ch1 unit"] --> M2["Ch2 seam"] --> M3["Ch3 seeds"] --> M4["Ch4 arms"] --> M5["Ch5 verdict"] --> M7["Ch7 ceiling"]
    end
    M2 -. "gates support" .-> S1["effect_size.json<br/>calibration_*.json<br/>per_pert reports"]
    M3 -. "seed-averages" .-> S2["load_arm()<br/>12_compare_arms.py"]
    M4 -. "one lever per arm spec" .-> S2
    M5 -. "joint resample +<br/>max-t intervals" .-> S2
    M7 -. "oracle rungs" .-> S3["14_ceiling_analysis.py"]
    S2 --> L["results ledger<br/>verdicts + hypotheses"]
    S3 --> L
```

Sources: [05-from-difference-to-verdict.md](docs/experimental-method/05-from-difference-to-verdict.md#L186-L189), [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L98-L120), [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L36-L39)

The comparison script's design encodes the chapters directly: `load_arm()` seed-averages per perturbation and counts a perturbation only if *every* requested seed produced it; a `--primary` flag names the one pre-committed metric whose contrasts get max-$t$ intervals; every other metric is reported with a plain CI and no verdict; and arm specs declare `label=experiment_pattern:kind:seeds`, making the one-lever-per-arm contract explicit at the CLI. NaN values are dropped, and secondary metrics carry a `LOWER_IS_BETTER` registry — every rule from Chapters 1, 3, and 5 is visible as a line of code.

Sources: [12_compare_arms.py](examples/perturbation_response/12_compare_arms.py#L56-L120)

The disciplines transfer beyond this example: the ECG study applies the same arm-comparison and seed-sweep structure (see [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study)), the encoder/decoder separation analysis extends Chapter 4's separability argument (see [Co-Adaptation of Encoder and Decoder](18-co-adaptation-of-encoder-and-decoder)), and pre-registration plus verdict recording operationalize Chapters 1 and 5 (see [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration)).

Sources: [03-seeds-and-noise.md](docs/experimental-method/03-seeds-and-noise.md#L100-L115), [04-ablations-and-controls.md](docs/experimental-method/04-ablations-and-controls.md#L123-L140)

## The Two Habits, and Where to Go Next

Everything above compresses into two instincts pointed in opposite directions. **Backward-facing trust**: make every stage assert something about its own output before the next stage consumes it — not because assertions catch bugs, but because the alternative is discovering the bug at the metric, where it is wearing a suit. **Forward-facing direction**: before you improve a component, measure whether it can matter — the oracle ladder costs an afternoon and redirects months. Together they define what the series means by an experiment you can trust: a measurement whose support you have audited, whose noise floor you have measured, whose arms differ by one lever, and whose verdicts were pre-committed to a single primary endpoint.

Sources: [index.md](docs/experimental-method/index.md#L29-L33), [06-failure-modes.md](docs/experimental-method/06-failure-modes.md#L108-L124), [07-the-ceiling.md](docs/experimental-method/07-the-ceiling.md#L98-L112)

For readers continuing through the catalog: the statistical mechanics summarized here are implemented and expanded step-by-step on [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference); the probe family of Chapter 7a connects to [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics); the ledger discipline that stores verdicts and demoted hypotheses is detailed in [Results Ledger and Pre-Registration](22-results-ledger-and-pre-registration); and for placement of this series among the repo's other tutorial threads, see [Tutorial Corpus and Reading Paths](25-tutorial-corpus-and-reading-paths).


# Results Ledger and Pre-Registration



Every experimental result in ssl-lab passes through two artifacts before it is allowed to influence a decision: a **pre-registered protocol** that fixes the question, the endpoint and the decision rule before any number exists, and an **append-only results ledger** that records what was asked, what was found, and what was later superseded. This page documents both mechanisms as they are actually implemented in this repository — the per-round ledger under `examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/`, the per-setting results folder under `examples/ecg_rhythm/results/`, and the comparison scripts whose docstrings *are* the pre-registration. It assumes familiarity with the evaluation endpoints described in [Evaluation Toolkit: Probes and Metrics](19-evaluation-toolkit-probes-and-metrics) and the statistics behind verdicts in [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference); the underlying experimental philosophy is developed separately in [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series).

Sources: [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L1-L31), [results/README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/README.md#L1-L3)

## The Problem the Ledger Solves

The motivating failure is documented, not hypothetical. The `04-decide` workflow records a retraction in this project: a flow "win" on joint energy distance was announced on a single seed, discovered after changing the metric, on a secondary endpoint — and on three seeds the simultaneous interval came out $[-0.960, +0.172]$, crossing zero. Every ingredient of a garden-of-forking-paths false positive was present, and the only structural defense is committing to the endpoint and the decision rule *before* looking. That is why the discipline here is described as "mostly about what you commit to before you look": the ledger then becomes the durable, append-only memory in which every round's pre-committed question and its honest answer are permanently paired.

Sources: [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L1-L3), [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L44-L56)

The ledger is also what makes negative results useful. The perturbation-response study refuted its own headline hypothesis (the operator-algebra bracket), watched its baseline rise twice, and re-read every published number under corrected conventions — and all of that history remains readable in one place rather than being reconstructed from git archaeology. The ledger's own intro states the contract plainly: *"a living, append-only record of every experimental round on this method… so that progress against the baseline can be read in one place."*

Sources: [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L1-L31), [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L58-L63)

## Architecture: How Pre-Registration Flows into the Ledger

The two mechanisms form a pipeline with a deliberate trust boundary between it. Protocols are frozen in version control *before* runs are scored; run outputs stay uncommitted; the only committed numbers are ones that a script can re-derive from the frozen outputs. The diagram below shows how a claim travels from pre-commitment to the permanent record:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph PREREG["Pre-registration layer (committed)"]
        P["Round protocol<br/>frozen in the comparison<br/>script's docstring"]
    end
    subgraph RUNS["Frozen run outputs (not committed)"]
        R["per-run report JSONs<br/>output/experiment/reports/"]
    end
    subgraph SCORE["Scoring and verdict layer"]
        S["score + compare scripts<br/>with reproduction guards"]
        V["verdict JSON<br/>echoing the frozen protocol"]
    end
    subgraph LEDGER["Results ledger (committed)"]
        L["round page:<br/>settings, endpoint, verdict"]
        SB["running scoreboard:<br/>current + published tables"]
    end
    P -->|"locks endpoint,<br/>decision rule, arms"| S
    R --> S
    S --> V
    V --> L
    L --> SB
```

Two properties of this architecture do most of the work. First, the protocol lives in a *script docstring*, so pre-registration inherits version control for free — the commit timestamp is the registration timestamp, and any later edit to the protocol is a visible diff. Second, scoring scripts refuse to produce numbers that cannot be tied to stored reports, which closes the gap between "what was planned" and "what was actually graded."

Sources: [results-ledger.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/conditional-flow-jepa/results-ledger.md#L1-L11), [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L186-L212)

> [!TIP]
> The docstring-as-protocol pattern works because Python docstrings are data: the protocol text travels with the code that implements it, and `git log` on that one file gives you the complete registration history without any external system.

## Inside the Perturbation-Response Ledger

The ledger index at `examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md` is organized as five blocks, each with a distinct job. The round table is the entry point — one row per round, numbered in the order runs happened, with 7b marked as a companion ablation and the re-baseline explicitly noted as "not a round: it tests nothing."

| Component | Location | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| The rounds | table at top of index | question → answer → link, one row per round |
| The standing verdict | narrative section | the two questions the study keeps apart, and each round's contribution to them |
| The two rules | short section | how comparisons are allowed to be made |
| The running scoreboard | two tables | current conventions and published pre-correction numbers |
| Shared settings | bullet list | data, split, endpoints, frozen component md5s, seed policy, statistics, pre-registration, compute |
| Open / retired | closing section | what is still live and which levers are permanently closed |

Sources: [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L1-L31), [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L33-L75)

**The round page is the unit of record.** Each page follows a fixed anatomy, visible in round 1: a one-paragraph *What was tested*, an *Experimental settings* section with an arm table (exact training flags, experiment names like `norman_sweep_control_s{0,1,2}`, grading settings and compute), the *Primary endpoint* with max-$t$ simultaneous intervals over the pre-declared contrast family, *Secondary endpoints* reported as intervals with no verdicts, and a closing *Verdict*. Round 1's page, for instance, declares the three-contrast family up front, reports the critical value (2.95 against the unadjusted 1.96), and concludes "the flow loses to the VAE" — a negative result recorded as carefully as a positive one would be.

Sources: [round-01-head-to-head.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-01-head-to-head.md#L1-L9), [round-01-head-to-head.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-01-head-to-head.md#L11-L33), [round-01-head-to-head.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-01-head-to-head.md#L45-L50)

**The two rules govern every claim in the ledger.** First, *compare within a round*: rounds are not run under identical conditions, so a difference is meaningful only against the other arms of its own round, with two references carried across rounds (the strongest learned baseline and, since round 7, the additive reference). Second, *one primary endpoint per round, everything else exploratory*: significance is claimed on exactly one pre-named metric, and rounds whose questions correlation cannot answer (4, 5, 7b, 8, 9) each named a different primary endpoint on their own page. A difference found on a secondary endpoint after the fact is a hypothesis, not a result.

Sources: [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L108-L124), [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L44-L56)

**Supersession is explicit, never silent.** The scoreboard keeps two tables side by side: *Current, under the corrected conventions* (since round 11 fixed the count decoder's library size) and *Published, before round 11's correction*, kept verbatim "because the round pages cite them," with the current table declared the superseding one. Alongside, the shared-settings block pins the frozen artifacts by md5 (`norman_stage_a` at `38f51067`, the count decoder at `52a44337`) so every scoreboard row traces to identifiable inputs.

Sources: [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L126-L185), [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L186-L212)

> [!TIP]
> Notice what the two-table scoreboard buys you: no published number is ever rewritten in place. When a convention correction lands, old numbers survive in a clearly labeled table and every round page's citation stays valid — supersession is a new row, not an edit.

## Pre-Registration in Code: The Docstring Protocol

The ledger's shared-settings section states the mechanism in one sentence: *"Each round fixes its endpoint and decision rule before scoring. Since round 7b the protocol is the docstring of the round's comparison script, committed before any number is scored, and the scoring script stops unless it reproduces each run's stored Δr."* Concretely, every round from 7b onward has exactly one comparison script — `20_compare_composition.py` through `27_score_round13.py` — whose module docstring is that round's complete protocol, and the repository README describes them as "one script per round from 7b on, whose docstring is that round's protocol, frozen before any run."

Sources: [index.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/index.md#L186-L212), [README.md](examples/perturbation_response/README.md#L150-L168)

`20_compare_composition.py` is the reference example. Its docstring opens with the header **"PROTOCOL (fixed in writing before any DeepSets run was scored)"** and then walks through every decision in order — each section closing one degree of freedom before data can contaminate it:

| Protocol section | What it locks down |
|---|---|
| Arms | four runs (`flow_add`, `flow_ds`, `vae_add`, `vae_ds`), three seeds each, differing *only* in `--compose deepsets` |
| Predictions | generated by script 19 exactly as 06/09 generate them: 200 cells per pair, generation seed 0, 100 Euler steps, guidance 1 |
| Pairs and genes | the 20 held-out combinations; each pair's top-20 DE genes; log1p-CP10K space |
| Primary endpoint | `log r_p`, the pair's log error relative to the additive reference — with lower-is-better stated |
| Primary family | exactly two contrasts (`flow_ds − flow_add`, `vae_ds − vae_add`), simultaneous over the family |
| Decision rule | improve if the interval lies wholly below 0; worse if wholly above; otherwise inconclusive — and "if neither family improves, the additive composition stays the default" |
| Zero handling, aggregation, missing values | numeric floors, the seed-then-pair averaging order, and the evaluability threshold |
| Beside the primary | an explicit list of descriptive-only metrics, "intervals only, no verdict" |

Sources: [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L1-L85), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L35-L52), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L70-L79)

The protocol is not merely prose — its load-bearing constants are mirrored in code, so the script cannot drift from its own registration. `CONTRASTS`, `PRIMARY`, and `SECONDARY` are module-level constants; `MIN_PAIRS = 18` encodes the docstring's rule that "the primary verdict stands only if at least 18 of the 20 pairs remain; otherwise the primary is reported as not evaluable under this protocol"; and the `verdict()` function mechanically maps interval position to one of the three pre-committed outcomes. The output JSON opens by echoing `"protocol": "composition ablation, frozen before scoring"`, binding each verdict file to its registration.

Sources: [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L106-L117), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L150-L155), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L167-L168)

## Reproduction Guards: Numbers That Must Re-Derive

The second half of the pre-registration contract is enforcement at scoring time. `19_score_interaction.py` — the script that produces the per-pair predictions every round comparison reads — states its guard in the docstring: pair profiles are generated through the same function, in the same order, with the same generator seed as the standing benchmark (06/09), and *"if the run already has a Δ-correlation report, the recomputed per-pair values must match it to 1e-9, or the script stops: a mismatch means the predictions are not the ones the benchmark scored."* Single-gene predictions for the internal metrics are generated *after* the pairs with a separate generator seeded `seed + 1`, so generating them cannot perturb the pair profiles that the primary endpoint reads.

Sources: [19_score_interaction.py](examples/perturbation_response/19_score_interaction.py#L1-L52), [19_score_interaction.py](examples/perturbation_response/19_score_interaction.py#L22-L31)

The guards are layered so that a mismatch can surface at any stage: scoring refuses to re-derive different numbers, comparison scripts refuse missing inputs (`raise SystemExit` naming the absent report and telling you to run 19 first), the primary verdict refuses to be issued from a degraded pair set, and descriptive claims are structurally separated from verdicts in the output JSON. The ECG study implements the same guarantee from the other direction: `08_make_results.py` *generates* every committed number from the frozen run outputs, so "no number on the page is transcribed by hand," and the curated `metrics/summary.json` embeds provenance hashes for the study, its subsets, pretraining and run outputs, plus the full protocol amendment chain (`study_v1.json` → `amend1` → `amend2`, with `in_force` naming the binding version).

| Guard | Where | What it protects | Failure behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-9 reproduction check | `19_score_interaction.py` | predictions match those the benchmark scored | script stops |
| Input existence check | compare scripts (`load_arm`) | comparisons read real, complete reports | `SystemExit` naming the missing file |
| Evaluability threshold (`MIN_PAIRS = 18`) | compare scripts | verdicts are not issued from a degraded pair set | primary reported "not evaluable under this protocol" |
| Verdict function | compare scripts | the decision rule cannot be reinterpreted post hoc | mechanical: below-0 / above-0 / inconclusive |
| Regeneration from frozen outputs | `08_make_results.py` (ECG) | no hand-transcribed numbers in committed results | numbers are built, not typed |
| Provenance hashes | `metrics/summary.json` (ECG) | results trace to exact study/protocol versions | recorded, checked at build time |

Sources: [19_score_interaction.py](examples/perturbation_response/19_score_interaction.py#L39-L42), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L131-L147), [08_make_results.py](examples/ecg_rhythm/08_make_results.py#L1-L19), [summary.json](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/metrics/summary.json#L1-L18)

## The Decision Discipline Around the Ledger

The ledger records verdicts; the *decide* workflow defines how they may be reached. Beyond the pre-committed primary endpoint, three practices are codified in `docs/workflows/04-decide.md`. **Write the decision rule down first**: the operator-algebra round pre-committed that "a null on the in-sample arm kills the idea and we skip the three-seed confirmation," so when the null arrived, following it was "bookkeeping rather than a judgement call made while staring at a difference." **Say the seed count**: one seed is directional; a claim needs seed averaging and a simultaneous interval excluding zero — which is exactly the rule the retracted energy-distance claim violated. And **read nulls honestly**, using `17_eval_bracket_epistasis.py`'s deliberate in-sample (91 training combinations, where power lives) versus held-out (20 combinations, underpowered by construction) split, so an uninformative null is distinguishable from a fatal one.

Sources: [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L29-L42), [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L44-L56), [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L58-L63)

The verdict computation itself is shared infrastructure rather than per-round ad hoc code: `12_compare_arms.py` reads per-perturbation vectors out of existing reports, pairs them (removing the shared difficulty of hard perturbations), resamples the whole contrast family *jointly* to preserve correlations between contrasts sharing an arm, and reports max-$t$ simultaneous intervals. The full statistical machinery — why pairing, why joint resampling, why max-$t$ — is documented in [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference); the ledger's contribution is that the contrast family itself was fixed before the data existed.

Sources: [04-decide.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/workflows/04-decide.md#L5-L27)

## The Same Pattern in the ECG Study

The ECG rhythm package runs the identical discipline at folder granularity. Its `results/` directory is a committed ledger where "methods are developed one controlled setting at a time, and each setting gets its own folder," following the naming convention `NN-<approach>-<question>`. The index states the same pre-registration rule — "each setting asks one question. It fixes its protocol before any model is scored" — and the same commit policy: raw run outputs stay under `output/` and are not committed; what is committed is the interpretation, figures and curated metrics, regenerated from the frozen outputs.

Sources: [results/README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/README.md#L1-L3), [results/README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/README.md#L26-L36)

The setting page (01, JEPA label efficiency) shows the ECG flavor of a round page: a status table linking the protocol JSONs (`configs/study_v1.json` with two numbered amendments), a verbatim blockquote of the question, and the note that the five core labels "were chosen before any model was evaluated." Its shared-settings block mirrors the perturbation ledger's — fixed data version, patient-level splits, the prediction task, and an uncertainty policy ("reported two ways and the two are never merged") — plus an explicit contamination warning: setting 01 examined test fold 10, so later settings should make every choice on validation alone.

Sources: [01-jepa-label-efficiency/README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/README.md#L1-L10), [01-jepa-label-efficiency/README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/01-jepa-label-efficiency/README.md#L41-L49), [results/README.md](examples/ecg_rhythm/results/README.md#L12-L24)

## Adding a Round: The Lifecycle

For a practitioner, a new round is a sequence with exactly one ordering constraint that matters: the protocol commit must precede scoring. Everything else serves that constraint.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Pick one question"] --> B["Write the protocol:<br/>arms, predictions, endpoint,<br/>contrast family, decision rule"]
    B --> C["Commit the comparison script<br/>docstring = the protocol"]
    C --> D["Train arms at fixed seeds"]
    D --> E["Score through 19:<br/>must reproduce stored deltas to 1e-9,<br/>else it stops"]
    E --> F{"Primary evaluable?<br/>18 of 20 pairs minimum"}
    F -->|"yes"| G["Apply the pre-committed rule<br/>via max-t simultaneous intervals"]
    F -->|"no"| H["Report: not evaluable<br/>under this protocol"]
    G --> I["Append the round page<br/>update the scoreboard rows"]
    H --> I
```

The final step follows the ledger's own conventions: the round page restates the settings the round shares plus its own deviations, records the primary endpoint result and secondaries as intervals-only, and appends its row to the scoreboard — under current conventions, with any superseded convention change handled by the two-table rule rather than by editing history.

Sources: [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L170-L177), [20_compare_composition.py](examples/perturbation_response/20_compare_composition.py#L199-L203), [round-01-head-to-head.md](examples/perturbation_response/docs/results/round-01-head-to-head.md#L11-L26)

## Where This Fits in the Toolkit

This page sits at the end of the Evaluation and Methodology group, where the mechanics (probes and metrics, bootstrap statistics, methodology) meet the record-keeping that makes results durable. A productive reading path from here: the statistics behind every ledger interval in [Paired Bootstrap and Simultaneous Inference](20-paired-bootstrap-and-simultaneous-inference), the fuller methodological treatment in [Experimental Methodology Series](21-experimental-methodology-series), the data plumbing these ledgers sit on in [Modality-Agnostic Data Adapters](23-modality-agnostic-data-adapters), and the two studies that exercise the pattern end-to-end in [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline) and [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study). For how the ledger's compute notes connect to infrastructure, see [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-runpod); for where these conventions live in the tree, see [Repository Layout and Conventions](3-repository-layout-and-conventions).


# Modality-Agnostic Data Adapters



Every deep-learning codebase has a moment where modality-specific assumptions leak into the model: an image reshape buried in a training loop, a lead count hard-coded into an encoder, a gene vocabulary welded to a forward pass. `ssllab` draws a hard line against this with its data adapter layer in `src/ssllab/data/`. The rule is simple and enforced everywhere: **each modality adapter's sole job is to emit token tensors of shape `(B, n_tokens, token_dim)`**, and nothing downstream knows or cares where those tokens came from. This page explains the contract, the three adapters that fulfill it, and the supporting machinery — physical-time geometry, cache discipline, and storage dedup — that keeps the seam clean.

Sources: [__init__.py](/src/ssllab/data/__init__.py#L1-L2), [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L1-L6)

## The One Contract: `(B, n_tokens, token_dim)`

The entire architecture rests on a single shape agreement, stated in the package docstring and honored by every module. Images, multi-lead signals, and gene-count vectors all collapse into the same three-dimensional token tensor before they ever reach a model. The downstream backbone — `TinyViT` — is explicit about this: *"Everything here operates on token tensors `(B, N, token_dim)` plus integer position indices `(B, N)` — there is nothing image-specific."* Its first layer, `PatchEmbed`, is just a linear projection from `token_dim` to the model dimension, which is why the same trunk serves the context encoder, the EMA target encoder, and the predictor alike.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph adapters["Modality adapters · ssllab.data"]
        M["mnist.py<br/>images (B, 1, 28, 28)"]
        E["ptbxl.py + signal.py<br/>signals (B, 12, 1000)"]
        P["perturbseq.py<br/>HVG vectors (B, 5000)"]
    end
    T[("The contract<br/>tokens (B, n_tokens, token_dim)")]
    subgraph models["Modality-agnostic stack · ssllab.models"]
        PE["PatchEmbed<br/>Linear(token_dim → embed_dim)"]
        V["TinyViT trunk<br/>context / target / predictor"]
    end
    M -- "patchify: 4×4 grid of 7×7 patches<br/>→ (B, 16, 49)" --> T
    E -- "patchify_1d: 250 ms time patches<br/>→ (B, 40, 12×25)" --> T
    P -- "make_gene_partition + tokenize_cells<br/>→ (B, 50, 100)" --> T
    T --> PE --> V
```

What changes between modalities is *only* the adapter; what stays fixed is the token geometry that `build_jepa(token_dim=..., n_tokens=...)` consumes. The MNIST docstring states the forward-compatibility promise directly: *"A future modality (gene-count vectors, DNA windows) provides a sibling adapter that emits the same `(B, n_tokens, token_dim)` shape; nothing downstream changes"* — and `perturbseq.py` is the proof, since it trains the same JEPA encoder on cells with no architectural change.

Sources: [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L1-L18), [mnist.py](/src/ssllab/data/mnist.py#L1-L15), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L7-L9), [__init__.py](/src/ssllab/data/__init__.py#L1-L59)

## Three Adapters, One Shape

Each adapter pairs a *tokenizer* (modality → tokens) with a *loader factory* (cache → `DataLoader`s). The differences are confined to how the token axis is partitioned and what covariates ride alongside the tokens in the batch.

| | MNIST (image) | PTB-XL (ECG signal) | Perturb-seq (single-cell) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Native input | `(B, 1, 28, 28)` in [0, 1] | `(B, C, L)`, 10 s × 12 leads, int16 µV | `(B, n_hvg)`, 5 000 HVG features |
| Tokenization | spatial `patchify`, 7×7 patches | temporal `patchify_1d`, 250 ms patches | seeded random `make_gene_partition` |
| Output tokens | `(B, 16, 49)` | `(B, N, C·P)` | `(B, 50, 100)` |
| Layout inside a token | pixels, row-major patch grid | **lead-major** sample windows | gene indices from one permutation |
| Normalization | `ToTensor` scaling | `zscore_per_lead` per record | done upstream (`log1p_cpm`) in the cache |
| Batch type | `(x, y)` tuple | dict: `tokens`, `signal`, `row`, `patient_id`, `labels` | dict: `tokens`, `features`, `counts`, `libsize`, `pert_id`, `is_control`, `ctrl_group`, `row` |
| Extra loader attrs | — | `.meta` (geometry, labels, budgets) | `.meta` + `.control_sampler` |

The batch-shape difference is deliberate, not sloppy. MNIST's classic `(x, y)` tuple suffices because images carry no covariates. The bio adapter's docstring justifies its dict batches: *"perturbation modeling needs the covariates (raw counts for an NB decoder, library size, the perturbation label, the control grouping for baseline pairing), not just an image and a class."* The ECG adapter follows the same dict convention for the same reason — labels, patient identity, and the raw signal (for reconstruction heads) must travel with the tokens.

Sources: [mnist.py](/src/ssllab/data/mnist.py#L16-L97), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L101-L116), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L38-L41), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L501-L565), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L23-L25)

## Patching: The Only Modality-Specific Step

**Where the modalities differ, they differ in exactly one place: how a flat token axis is carved out of the raw signal.**

For images, `patchify` reshapes `(B, 1, H, W)` through a permute into `(B, gh·gw, patch·patch)` — 16 patches of 49 pixels each — and validates divisibility loudly rather than rounding (`unpatchify` is the exact inverse for decoder outputs). For signals, `patchify_1d` performs the same reshape along time: `(B, C, L) → (B, N, C·P)`, with the token layout **lead-major** — the first `P` values of a token are lead 0's samples for that window, the next `P` are lead 1's, and so on, a convention the docstring pins down so that inverse transforms and consumers agree.

For cells, there is no spatial or temporal structure to exploit, so `make_gene_partition` invents one: a **deterministic random partition** of the HVG indices into `n_tokens` groups, drawn from a seeded permutation of gene indices. Three implementation details matter. First, it is deterministic in `seed`, so the processing script and training-time loaders agree on the partition — the loader *asserts* equality with the cache's recorded `partition_seed` and raises on mismatch. Second, when `n_hvg` is not divisible by `n_tokens`, the final positions are padded with a `-1` sentinel, which `tokenize_cells` replaces with `pad_value` during the gather. Third, `detokenize_cells` inverts the gather assuming the partition is a permutation, restoring the original `(B, n_hvg)` vector.

Sources: [mnist.py](/src/ssllab/data/mnist.py#L24-L57), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L101-L113), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L88-L141), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L475-L482)

> [!TIP]
> The gene partition is the single knob that silently changes what the model *can* learn: HVG index `j` names the same gene in every cell and split only because selection happens once over all cells, which is what lets the encoder's learned positional table mean anything. Changing `partition_seed` or `n_tokens` without rebuilding the cache is caught at load time — do not bypass that assertion.

## Physical-Time Geometry for Signals

Signal configuration never speaks in samples — it speaks in **Hz and seconds**. `SignalGeometry` is a frozen dataclass holding `fs`, `duration_s`, `patch_s`, and optional `span_s` (masked-span targets for SSL), and every integer quantity is *derived*: `n_samples = fs·duration_s`, `patch_len = fs·patch_s`, `n_tokens = duration_s/patch_s`. The derived values go through `_whole`, which refuses any ratio that is not a whole positive number within a `1e-6` tolerance — *"a ratio that is not a whole number is refused rather than rounded"*. Because geometry is declared in physical time, the same configuration reads correctly at any sampling rate, and `describe()` emits a flat dict for manifests and run reports.

Two supporting pieces complete the signal path. `zscore_per_lead` standardizes each lead of each record over its own time axis, with a flat-lead guard: a disconnected electrode whose standard deviation falls below `eps` maps to zeros instead of dividing by ~0. And `SignalBatcher` is the training fast path — it holds selected recordings as one device-resident `int16` tensor and builds each batch with a single gather, per-lead z-score, and patchify, with no per-item Python work. It deliberately coexists with `DataLoader` rather than replacing it: the batcher is the speed path, the DataLoader remains the general-purpose interface.

Sources: [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L1-L21), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L28-L86), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L89-L98), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L119-L172)

## Loader Semantics: Splits, Budgets, and Attachments

Both heavy adapters return `(train, val, test)` loaders whose split logic is *deterministic and documented in code*. For PTB-XL, splits follow the dataset's `strat_fold` (1–8 train, 9 val, 10 test), which confines each patient to one fold; label budgets are **patient-level and nested** — one seeded permutation of all training patients, where a budget of `k` percent takes the first `ceil(k/100·n)` patients and *every record* of a chosen patient. Because the permutation does not depend on the task, the same patients carry labels across tasks and methods for a given seed — a property the paired-comparison methodology downstream depends on. For Perturb-seq, the `split` parameter selects between `"combo"` (perturbation-level holdout of unseen 2-gene combinations, the headline generalization test) and `"cells"` (random per-cell sanity split).

Each returned loader carries dynamically attached attributes rather than a wrapper class: `.meta` is a plain dict bundling the geometry, vocabulary, split counts, and cache fingerprint, and the perturb-seq loaders additionally attach `.control_sampler`, a `ControlSampler` over the full cell pool for baseline pairing. This keeps the return type `(DataLoader, DataLoader, DataLoader)` — anything that already consumes loaders needs no new plumbing.

Sources: [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L24-L35), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L137-L146), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L530-L560), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L441-L545)

## Cache Discipline: Provenance, Fingerprints, Fail-Loudly Checks

The heavy adapters never touch raw files at train time. Instead, a one-time processing step (e.g. `examples/perturbation_response/00_process_norman.py` for the biology, `build_cache_from_raw` for PTB-XL) writes a torch-native cache that the adapter reads. This split is stated as a design goal: keeping anndata/scanpy out of `ssllab.data.perturbseq` means *"pytest and training never import the heavy stack"* — the module is deliberately torch + numpy + json only.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph raw["Raw sources (never read at train time)"]
        R1["PhysioNet PTB-XL tree<br/>.hea + .dat WFDB records"]
        R2["Norman 2019<br/>processed.h5ad (heavy scanpy stack)"]
    end
    subgraph proc["One-time processing"]
        W1["wfdb16.read_format16<br/>checksum verification"]
        W2["00_process_norman.py<br/>QC · HVG select · normalize"]
    end
    subgraph cache["Torch-native caches"]
        C1["signals.npy (memmapped int16)<br/>records.json · manifest.json"]
        C2["tokens_meta.npz · splits.json<br/>de_genes.json · manifest.json"]
    end
    L["Adapters: load_cache → (train, val, test) loaders"]
    R1 --> W1 --> C1 --> L
    R2 --> W2 --> C2 --> L
```

Integrity is enforced at four distinct layers, each catching a different failure mode:

| Mechanism | Layer | What it catches | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| WFDB first-sample + 16-bit checksum | raw read | truncated downloads, mis-parsed interleave | [wfdb16.py](/src/ssllab/data/wfdb16.py#L86-L115) |
| `artifact_version` check | cache load | caches built by older code silently loading | [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L238-L248) |
| `cache_fingerprint` (MD5 over cell ordering, labels, splits, libsizes) | downstream stores | embeddings computed on one cache looked up by another's row numbers | [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L231-L261) |
| Partition-seed + geometry-vs-cache assertions | loader construction | training on a token geometry the cache disagrees with | [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L472-L482), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L523-L529) |

The fingerprint deserves attention: `cache_fingerprint_from_dir` reads only the three arrays it hashes from the npz (about 1 MB rather than the 4.4 GB of expression matrices), so embedding-store producers can verify row alignment cheaply. The manifest system runs in the other direction too — PTB-XL's `build_cache_from_raw` records the source URL, license, zip SHA-256, label rules, and every derived knob, so any result is traceable to its exact data construction. The synthetic-tree writer (`write_toy_raw_tree`) rounds out the design: smoke tests exercise the *real* reader against tiny PTB-XL-shaped fixtures rather than mocks.

Sources: [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L14-L37), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L259-L374), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L243-L261), [wfdb16.py](/src/ssllab/data/wfdb16.py#L1-L15), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L398-L449)

## Storage: The Data-Lake Layer

Below the adapters sits a purely physical concern: datasets themselves are not tracked in git, and large shared datasets should never be duplicated across projects. `ops/datasets.py` implements **storage dedup by symlink**: keep one project-neutral copy of a large dataset in a "data lake" (located via the `DATA_LAKE_ROOT` env var, with the legacy `SSLLAB_DATA_ROOT` still honored), then link only what a project uses into its local `data/` directory. The lake follows a `<modality>/<sub-topic>/<dataset>` layout (e.g. `scrna/perturb_seq/norman2019`), while the local link defaults to a **flat alias** — the basename — so project code refers to `data/norman2019`, never a deep lake path.

`link_dataset` is idempotent (re-linking refreshes the symlink), refuses to replace a real directory with a link, and links only the named dataset — never the whole tree — so the dependency on shared storage stays explicit and minimal. Local-only data like MNIST needs none of this: torchvision auto-downloads it into `data/` on first use of `get_mnist_dataloaders`.

Sources: [ops/datasets.py](/ops/datasets.py#L1-L49), [ops/datasets.py](/ops/datasets.py#L52-L102), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L1-L26)

## Adding a New Modality: The Checklist

The MNIST docstring doubles as a template for future adapters, and the existing three give a concrete recipe. A new modality requires exactly one sibling module in `src/ssllab/data/` that:

1. **Tokenizes** the native representation into `(B, n_tokens, token_dim)` — spatially (like `patchify`), temporally (like `patchify_1d` with `SignalGeometry`), or by a deterministic partition (like `make_gene_partition`).
2. **Reads from a torch-native cache** with a manifest recording provenance and every knob, and validates `artifact_version` on load.
3. **Raises on disagreement** — geometry mismatches, seed mismatches, non-whole ratios — instead of silently coercing.
4. **Exports through `ssllab.data.__init__`**, alongside the tokenizer and its inverse, so models consume only what the package surface exposes.

If your modality carries covariates a downstream head needs (counts for an NB decoder, demographic labels), emit dict batches like the two heavy adapters do; if it is a plain `(x, y)` problem, the MNIST tuple form remains valid. Nothing in `ssllab.models` changes either way — that is the contract's entire point.

Sources: [mnist.py](/src/ssllab/data/mnist.py#L7-L15), [signal.py](/src/ssllab/data/signal.py#L75-L86), [__init__.py](/src/ssllab/data/__init__.py#L20-L59)

## Where to Go Next

The adapters sit at the boundary between raw data and everything else in this repository, so the natural continuation depends on which direction you are heading. For how the consuming side works, start with [JEPA Module Internals](6-jepa-module-internals) to see the token tensors enter the encoder, and [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview) for the full-module map. To watch the adapters operating end-to-end in a real study, the [Perturbation-Response Pipeline](16-perturbation-response-pipeline) page covers the perturb-seq path (including its one-time processing script), and the [ECG Rhythm Study](17-ecg-rhythm-study) covers the PTB-XL path from cache building through label budgets. Finally, since caches and data lakes are often provisioned on remote machines, [Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod](24-remote-gpu-ops-skypilot-and-runpod) explains the ops layer that stages data where training runs — and [Tutorial Corpus and Reading Paths](25-tutorial-corpus-and-reading-paths) can help you sequence the whole corpus.

Sources: [vit.py](/src/ssllab/models/vit.py#L1-L6), [ptbxl.py](/src/ssllab/data/ptbxl.py#L1-L36), [perturbseq.py](/src/ssllab/data/perturbseq.py#L1-L37)

> [!TIP]
> When debugging a shape error deep in the model stack, trace it back to the adapter boundary first: `dl.meta["token_dim"]` (PTB-XL) or `dl.meta["n_tokens"]` (Perturb-seq) tells you the geometry the loader negotiated with the cache, which is almost always where an inconsistency originates — not in the transformer.

# Remote GPU Ops: SkyPilot and RunPod



Every serious model in ssl-lab eventually outgrows the machine you are sitting at, so the repository ships a small, self-contained remote-training infrastructure at the repo root: the `ops/` package, orchestrated by SkyPilot against RunPod as the cloud provider. This page explains the architecture, walks through the provision → run → fetch workflow, and documents the configuration surface, the safety rails, and the data-staging model. It covers the `ops/` package, the four driver scripts in `examples/ops/`, and the pod entrypoint shell scripts used by the applied studies.

Sources: [README.md](ops/README.md#L1-L14), [README.md](README.md#L148-L160)

## A Deliberately Decoupled Package

The first architectural decision to understand is what `ops` is *not*. It is deliberately decoupled from the SSL library: nothing in `ops/` imports JEPA, and `ssllab` never imports `ops`. Cloud provisioning is treated as scaffolding for practically useful models — necessary to train them, but not part of self-supervised learning itself. This is why `ops/` sits as a top-level package next to `src/` rather than inside `src/ssllab/`, and why it is never installed: Python finds it because the repository root is on the import path (each driver inserts the repo root into `sys.path` itself, and `pyproject.toml` sets `pythonpath = ["."]` for pytest).

Sources: [README.md](ops/README.md#L1-L11), [ops_run_pipeline.py](examples/ops/ops_run_pipeline.py#L36-L40), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L33-L39)

Dependency footprint is split across two optional extras. The `ops` extra pulls in only PyYAML — enough for the compute check and for dry runs, which make zero cloud calls. The `remote` extra adds `skypilot[runpod]>=0.7`, required only when you actually launch pods. This split is load-bearing for the design: every read-only code path (config assembly, YAML generation, cost estimation) works without SkyPilot installed at all, because `gpu_runner.py` imports `sky` lazily inside the `launch` function rather than at module top level.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L25-L27), [README.md](ops/README.md#L16-L22), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L1-L9), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L259-L272)

## Architecture: SkyPilot Orchestrates, RunPod Provides

The second decision is the layering between orchestration and provider. `ops` never calls the RunPod API. It emits provider-neutral SkyPilot task configs in which the provider appears only as the value `cloud: runpod` — a config line, not a hard-coded client. Switching providers is therefore a one-line config change, and every artifact `ops` produces (the generated YAML in `ops/configs/skypilot/generated/`) is inspectable and versionable before any money is spent.

To read the diagram below: the local machine assembles an `InfraConfig` from `gpu_config.yaml`, builds a SkyPilot task dict, writes it as YAML, and hands it to the `sky` CLI. SkyPilot translates the config into a RunPod pod running an NGC PyTorch container, runs the setup and run scripts, and `ops` then rsyncs results back — with teardown handled in a `finally` block so no code path can leave a pod billing unnoticed.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph local["Local machine — repo root"]
        CC["ops_compute_check.py<br/>hardware.detect_hardware"]
        CFG["gpu_config.yaml<br/>→ InfraConfig"]
        BUILD["gpu_runner.build_skypilot_config<br/>(dry-run prints YAML + cost)"]
        GEN[("ops/configs/skypilot/<br/>generated/&lt;job&gt;.yaml")]
        CFG --> BUILD
        BUILD --> GEN
    end
    subgraph sky["SkyPilot CLI — orchestration layer"]
        LAUNCH["sky launch -c &lt;cluster_name&gt;"]
        DOWN["sky down / sky status"]
        RSYNC["rsync -Pavz -u"]
    end
    subgraph pod["RunPod pod — provider (config value, not code)"]
        SETUP["setup: pip install --no-deps .<br/>(NGC-safe install)"]
        JOB["run: set -e; your command"]
        OUT[("&lt;volume&gt;/ssl-lab/output/")]
    end
    CC -->|"no local CUDA"| BUILD
    GEN --> LAUNCH
    LAUNCH --> SETUP --> JOB --> OUT
    OUT -->|"fetch"| RSYNC
    RSYNC -->|"results → output/"| LOCAL["local output/"]
    DOWN -.->|"teardown in finally"| LAUNCH
```

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L1-L9), [README.md](ops/README.md#L13-L14), [gpu_config.yaml](ops/configs/gpu_config.yaml#L1-L5), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L335-L346)

The module interaction is intentionally lean — three small modules plus thin drivers. `hardware.py` answers "what am I on?", `gpu_runner.py` owns the config-to-launch spine, and `datasets.py` handles storage dedup locally. There is no per-model pip registry or task-specific feasibility logic in the infra layer; those belong to individual experiments.

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L10-L12), [hardware.py](ops/hardware.py#L1-L7), [datasets.py](datasets.py#L1-L10)

## Step 0 — The Compute Check

The workflow begins with a pre-flight question: what hardware am I on, and do I need to pay for a pod? `ops_compute_check.py` runs `hardware.detect_hardware`, which probes PyTorch (if importable) to classify the backend as `cuda`, `mps`, or `cpu`, and reports GPU name, VRAM, CPU count, system RAM, and free disk. It is dependency-light by design and carries no task-specific feasibility estimators — deciding whether a *specific* experiment fits is the experiment's job, not the infra's.

Sources: [hardware.py](ops/hardware.py#L1-L7), [ops_compute_check.py](examples/ops/ops_compute_check.py#L1-L12), [hardware.py](ops/hardware.py#L28-L41)

The report ends in a plain-language verdict. A CUDA machine is told it can train locally; anything else is told smoke tests are fine but real training needs a pod, with the exact provisioning command printed. The `--json` flag emits the same report machine-readably, which is how scripts can branch on hardware without parsing formatted text.

Sources: [hardware.py](ops/hardware.py#L79-L101), [ops_compute_check.py](examples/ops/ops_compute_check.py#L38-L45)

## Configuration as Data: InfraConfig and the GPU Catalog

All defaults live in one YAML file, `ops/configs/gpu_config.yaml`, loaded into the `InfraConfig` dataclass. Two fields define project identity: `project` (the folder this project owns on a shared pod volume) and `job_prefix` (the start of every derived job name). Config values can reference the project's volume folder via the `{project_dir}` placeholder, which `InfraConfig.from_yaml` substitutes on load — so porting `ops` to another project means editing two lines, and every downstream path (pip cache, output directory, staged data) follows automatically.

Sources: [gpu_config.yaml](ops/configs/gpu_config.yaml#L7-L13), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L78-L96), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L114-L117)

The GPU catalog, `GPU_SPECS`, maps short CLI names to SkyPilot accelerator strings, VRAM, and indicative hourly rates. These rates are RunPod community-cloud ballparks intended for cost *estimates* only; the code comments and the README both instruct you to verify against live pricing before relying on them. Unknown GPU names are rejected by `apply_overrides` with a helpful choices list, enforced by tests.

| CLI key | SkyPilot accelerator | VRAM | Indicative $/hr |
|---|---|---|---|
| `l4` | `L4:1` | 24 GB | 0.43 |
| `rtx4090` | `RTX4090:1` | 24 GB | 0.69 |
| `rtx5090` | `RTX5090:1` | 32 GB | 0.89 |
| `a40` (default) | `A40:1` | 48 GB | 0.63 |
| `a100` | `A100:1` | 80 GB | 1.19 |
| `h100` | `H100:1` | 80 GB | 2.49 |

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L22-L45), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L120-L128), [test_config.py](ops/tests/test_config.py#L21-L27)

The remaining config fields describe how the project installs itself on the pod and where data and results flow:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `cloud` | `runpod` | Provider string passed to SkyPilot; swapping providers is a config edit |
| `docker_image` | `nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.02-py3` | NGC PyTorch container with optimized CUDA torch |
| `use_volume` / `volume_name` / `volume_mount` | `true` / `"AI lab extension"` / `/runpod-volume` | RunPod network volume; the pod auto-places in the volume's datacenter |
| `workdir` | `.` | Repo root uploaded to the pod |
| `data_path` | `data` | Local input dir; where `link_dataset` symlinks land and staging uploads from |
| `setup_cmd` | `pip install --no-deps .` + light deps | Runs once before the job (see the NGC note below) |
| `output_remote` | `{project_dir}/output` | Where the job writes on the pod — persistent across pod lifecycles |
| `output_local` | `output` | Where rsync fetches results locally |

Sources: [gpu_config.yaml](ops/configs/gpu_config.yaml#L12-L39), [gpu_config.yaml](ops/configs/gpu_config.yaml#L56-L62)

One detail of `setup_cmd` is worth its own explanation because it encodes two hard-won lessons. First, NGC images ship an optimized torch/torchvision; a plain `pip install -e .` would resolve `torch>=2.1` from PyPI and silently overwrite the CUDA builds — hence `pip install --no-deps .` plus only the small non-torch runtime deps. Second, the NGC image's setuptools produces a broken `src`-layout *editable* finder that fails to expose subpackages, so the install must be non-editable (`.`, not `-e .`) so the full tree is copied.

Sources: [gpu_config.yaml](ops/configs/gpu_config.yaml#L40-L54), [test_config.py](ops/tests/test_config.py#L57-L58)

## The Job Pipeline: Build → Dry-Run → Launch → Fetch

`build_skypilot_config` assembles the SkyPilot task dict: job name, workdir, resources (accelerator, cloud, docker image), the `setup` block, and a `run` block that wraps your command in `set -e` so a failing job cannot be masked by trailing echoes, then appends the result-fetch hint. When `use_volume` is set, the config gains a `volumes` key mapping the mount point to the named volume. Every generated task is written to `ops/configs/skypilot/generated/<job>.yaml`, with multi-line scripts rendered as readable YAML literal blocks.

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L176-L206), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L53-L70)

Job names are derived deterministically from the command: the first `.py` argument's stem, with a leading numeric milestone prefix (`01_`, `02_`, …) stripped, joined to the `job_prefix` — so `python examples/jepa_basics/01_train_jepa_mnist.py` becomes `ssl-train-jepa-mnist`. This determinism is what makes pod reuse possible: the cluster name doubles as the rsync host and teardown target.

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L168-L181), [test_config.py](ops/tests/test_config.py#L32-L34), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L293-L307)

The dry-run path is the safety valve: `print_dry_run` writes the YAML, prints the full task, and prints the GPU, cloud, and cost estimate — with no cloud calls and no SkyPilot requirement. It also prints the exact command that would launch for real, so the dry run doubles as documentation of the next action.

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L221-L251)

The live `launch` function wraps the whole lifecycle and embeds three deliberate safety mechanisms. The cluster gets a deterministic name (`-c <job_name>`) so the rsync host and teardown target are unambiguous rather than guessed from SkyPilot's auto-generated names. On failure, the code asks `sky status` whether the pod actually came up before deciding what to report — a live pod is surfaced for inspection (`sky logs`, `ssh`) and torn down, while a never-provisioned cluster is explicitly reported as "nothing to tear down," so failures never read like successes.

> [!TIP]
> The results fetch is `rsync -Pavz -u` — the `-u` (update) flag is load-bearing, not a nicety. It skips files newer on the receiver, so a stale pod (an out-of-date cache on the volume) can never overwrite correct local results with wrong ones. The code comment notes this failure mode has actually happened, and records the reasoning: a result that changes when you re-run the same command is the hardest kind of bug to notice, so the fetch must never be able to move a result backwards.

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L287-L322), [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L323-L334)

Finally, teardown runs in a `try/finally`: a failed job or failed rsync still triggers `sky down` unless you passed teardown-off, so no error path leaves a pod billing silently. When the pod is intentionally kept alive, the code prints the SSH entry point and the exact teardown command for later.

Sources: [gpu_runner.py](ops/gpu_runner.py#L335-L346)

The complete workflow as a how-to flowchart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["1. compute check<br/>ops_compute_check.py"] -->|CUDA present| L["train locally"]
    A -->|no CUDA| B["2. dry-run<br/>ops_run_pipeline.py --gpu a40 -- &lt;cmd&gt;<br/>(YAML + cost, no cloud calls)"]
    B --> B2["adjust: --gpu, --job-name,<br/>--no-volume, --output-dir"]
    B2 --> B
    B --> C{"3. ready?"}
    C -->|"add --execute"| D["sky launch: pod up,<br/>setup_cmd, then your command"]
    D --> E{"job succeeded?"}
    E -->|no| F["diagnose:<br/>sky logs &lt;cluster&gt; · ssh &lt;cluster&gt;"]
    F --> B
    E -->|yes| G["4. fetch: rsync -Pavz -u<br/>→ output/"]
    G --> H{"more sessions?"}
    H -->|yes — default| I["pod kept alive:<br/>reuse with --cluster &lt;name&gt;"]
    H -->|"pass --teardown"| J["sky down &lt;cluster&gt;"]
    I --> K["stage inputs once:<br/>ops_stage_data.py &lt;paths&gt;"]
    K --> D
    I -->|done| J
```

Sources: [README.md](ops/README.md#L24-L53), [ops_run_pipeline.py](examples/ops/ops_run_pipeline.py#L73-L96)

## The Four Driver CLIs

The `examples/ops/` directory holds thin drivers — each puts the repo root on the import path itself, so `ops` needs no installation, only its dependencies. Note the deliberate **asymmetric defaults**: `ops_run_pipeline.py` is dry-run by default (`--execute` to launch) because its unit of work is one job and mistakes are cheap to prevent; `ops_provision_cluster.py` provisions for real by default (`--dry-run` to preview) because its whole purpose is bringing up a pod.

| Script | Purpose | Default behavior | Escape hatch |
|---|---|---|---|
